Neurologic deficits separated in time and space with oligoclonal bands
Fatigable ptosis, diplopia, and proximal weakness worsening with use
Combined upper and lower motor neuron signs without sensory loss
Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis with albuminocytologic dissociation
explain: Distinct patterns of motor, sensory, and fatigable deficits define primary neurological diseases.

prompt: Match each nephrologic condition to its characteristic urinalysis finding.
pairs: Dysmorphic red blood cells and RBC casts
White blood cell casts and urine eosinophils
Fatty casts, oval fat bodies, and Maltese cross pattern
Hyaline casts with normal cellular elements
explain: Urine sediment microscopy provides direct cellular clues to the site of renal injury.

prompt: Match each electrolyte disturbance to its characteristic electrocardiographic abnormality.
pairs: Tall peaked T waves, widened QRS, and loss of P waves
Prominent U waves, ST depression, and flattened T waves
explain: Electrolyte derangements alter cardiac repolarization and refractory periods predictably.

prompt: Match each gastrointestinal condition to its characteristic diagnostic hallmark.
pairs: Duodenal villous atrophy and anti-tTG IgA elevation
Transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and non-caseating granulomas
Continuous mucosal inflammation extending proximally from the rectum
Elevated alkaline phosphatase and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies
Beaded appearance of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts on MRCP
explain: Histopathologic and imaging hallmarks distinguish chronic luminal and biliary GI diseases.

prompt: Match each hematologic malignancy to its defining cytogenetic or molecular abnormality.
explain: Recurrent chromosomal translocations drive specific hematologic oncogenesis.

prompt: Match each vasculitis to its vessel size predilection and characteristic feature.
pairs: Large vessels; temporal artery tenderness and jaw claudication
Large vessels; pulseless disease with aortic arch branch stenosis
Medium vessels; renal/visceral microaneurysms associated with HBV
Small vessels; upper/lower airway granulomas and c-ANCA (PR3)
Small vessels; necrotizing glomerulonephritis and p-ANCA (MPO)
explain: The Chapel Hill consensus classifies vasculitides by vessel caliber and clinicopathologic features.

prompt: Match each type of renal tubular acidosis to its primary pathophysiological defect.
pairs: Impaired distal H+ secretion; urine pH > 5.5, hypokalemic
Generalized proximal tubular transport defect (glucosuria, aminoaciduria)
Loop of Henle NKCC2 cotransporter defect mimicking furosemide
explain: Transport deficiencies along specific nephron segments define RTAs and hereditary tubulopathies.

prompt: Match each infectious agent to its characteristic clinical manifestation in HIV patients.
pairs: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions when CD4 < 100/µL
Subacute meningitis with elevated opening pressure and India ink positivity
Necrotizing chorioretinitis ('pizza pie' retina) when CD4 < 50/µL
Disseminated fever, weight loss, and splenomegaly when CD4 < 50/µL
explain: Opportunistic infections in HIV occur predictably at specific CD4 count thresholds.

prompt: Match each thyroid nodule ultrasound feature to its associated malignant potential.
pairs: High suspicion for papillary thyroid carcinoma
High suspicion for invasive thyroid malignancy
High-risk feature indicating vertical tissue infiltration
Benign feature characteristic of colloid nodules
Very low suspicion / benign hyperplastic nodule
explain: ACR TI-RADS ultrasound features stratify thyroid nodules for fine-needle aspiration.

prompt: Match each acute leukemia to its pathognomonic diagnostic finding.
pairs: TdT positive lymphoblasts common in children
Hypergranular blasts with multiple Auer rods (faggot cells) and DIC
Smudge cells on peripheral blood smear and CD5+ B cells
Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) positive B cells
explain: Cytochemical stains, flow cytometry, and morphology definitively classify leukemias.

prompt: Match each cranial nerve palsy to its characteristic clinical exam finding.
pairs: Eye 'down and out' with ptosis and dilated fixed pupil
Vertical diplopia worsening on downward gaze, head tilt away from lesion
Inability to abduct the affected eye causing horizontal diplopia
Complete ipsilateral facial weakness involving both upper and lower face
Tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion on protrusion
explain: Cranial nerve deficits produce pathognomonic ocular motility, facial, and lingual findings.

prompt: Match each skin lesion to its underlying systemic internal disease.
pairs: Severe insulin resistance or underlying gastric adenocarcinoma
Type 1 diabetes mellitus (yellow atrophic pretibial plaques)
Inflammatory bowel disease or rheumatoid arthritis
Leukocytoclastic small vessel vasculitis or Henoch-Schönlein purpura
explain: Cutaneous manifestations frequently provide the earliest clinical signs of systemic illness.

prompt: Match each inherited cardiomyopathy to its characteristic pathophysiology.
pairs: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction
Four-chamber dilatation with systolic contractile impairment
Fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium with epsilon waves
Bi-atrial enlargement, normal LV size, and speckled myocardium
Stress-induced apical ballooning mimicking anterior STEMI without coronary occlusion
explain: Cardiomyopathies present with distinctive structural, histological, and hemodynamic phenotypes.

prompt: Match each paraneoplastic syndrome to its most common associated primary tumor.
pairs: Myasthenia gravis / Pure red cell aplasia
explain: Paraneoplastic phenomena arise from tumor-derived peptides or cross-reactive autoantibodies.

prompt: Match each cause of acute polyarthritis to its characteristic synovial fluid white blood cell count.
pairs: > 50,000 WBC/µL with > 90% neutrophils and opaque purulent fluid
explain: Synovial fluid leukocyte analysis categorizes joint effusions into non-inflammatory, inflammatory, and septic.

prompt: Match each bleeding disorder to its characteristic coagulation factor profile.
pairs: Isolated prolonged aPTT with deficient Factor VIII activity
Isolated prolonged aPTT with deficient Factor IX activity
Prolonged bleeding time, variable aPTT, reduced vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor
Prolonged PT/INR early, followed by prolonged aPTT, normal platelets
Prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer, thrombocytopenia
explain: Screening coagulation assays pinpoint specific defects in primary vs secondary hemostasis.

prompt: Match each acute glomerulonephritis to its pathognomonic electron microscopic appearance.
pairs: Subepithelial deposits with 'spike and dome' pattern
Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes with no deposits
Subendothelial deposits with mesangial interposition ('tram-track' appearance)
Longitudinal splitting and lamellation of GBM ('basket-weave')
explain: Electron microscopy localizes immune deposits to subepithelial, subendothelial, or mesangial compartments.

prompt: Match each movement disorder to its primary neuroanatomical site of pathology.
pairs: Substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurodegeneration
Caudate nucleus and putamen atrophy with loss of GABAergic neurons
Cerebellar hemisphere or dentate nucleus dysfunction
Lenticular nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus) copper accumulation
explain: Basal ganglia and cerebellar circuitry lesions generate characteristic movement disorders.

prompt: Match each headache disorder to its first-line prophylactic medication.
explain: Preventive headache management utilizes distinct pharmacological classes matched to pathophysiology.

prompt: Match each infectious diarrheal pathogen to its characteristic mechanism of disease.
pairs: Gs-protein ADP-ribosylation causing permanent adenylate cyclase activation and rice-water diarrhea
Heat-labile (cAMP) and heat-stable (cGMP) enterotoxins causing traveler's diarrhea
Ribosomal 60S subunit inhibition causing bloody diarrhea and HUS
Glucosyltransferase toxins A and B disrupting actin cytoskeleton
Adhesion to brush border causing malabsorption, foul flatus, and steatorrhea
explain: Bacterial and parasitic enteric toxins disrupt mucosal transport through specific biochemical cascades.

prompt: Match each central nervous system lesion to its visual field defect.
pairs: Complete ipsilateral anopia (blindness in one eye)
Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky')
Contralateral inferior quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor')
explain: Visual pathway anatomy maps visual field deficits to precise chiasmatic and retrochiasmatic lesions.

prompt: Match each neurodegenerative dementia to its pathognomonic histopathological protein inclusion.
pairs: Extracellular amyloid-beta (Abeta42) plaques and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles
Intracellular alpha-synuclein inclusions in cortical and brainstem neurons
Round tau-positive Pick bodies or TDP-43 inclusions in frontal/temporal lobes
Prion protein (PrPSc) spongiform encephalopathy with 14-3-3 protein in CSF
Tufted astrocytes and globose neurofibrillary tangles composed of 4R tau
explain: Misfolded protein aggregates define the molecular taxonomy of neurodegenerative dementias.

prompt: Match each rare immunodeficiency syndrome to its underlying genetic and biochemical defect.
pairs: BTK gene mutation impairing B-cell tyrosine kinase and light chain rearrangement
CD40L gene mutation on activated T cells impairing immunoglobulin class-switch recombination
IL2RG gene mutation encoding common gamma chain of cytokine receptors
WASP gene mutation causing actin cytoskeleton dysregulation, thrombocytopenia, and eczema
CYBB or NCF gene mutations disabling NADPH oxidase and respiratory burst
explain: Single-gene inborn errors of immunity cause profound cell-mediated and humoral immunodeficiencies.

prompt: Match each diabetic pharmacological agent to its primary mechanism of action.
pairs: Inhibition of hepatic gluconeogenesis via AMPK activation
Inhibition of renal SGLT2 cotransporter increasing urinary glucose excretion
GLP-1 receptor agonism stimulating glucose-dependent insulin secretion
DPP-4 enzyme inhibition prolonging endogenous incretin action
Closure of ATP-sensitive K+ channels in pancreatic beta cells
explain: Distinct molecular targets mediate antihyperglycemic effects across antidiabetic drug classes.

prompt: What is the systolic blood pressure threshold in mmHg defining Stage 1 hypertension according to ACC/AHA guidelines?
explain: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as systolic BP 130-139 mmHg or diastolic 80-89 mmHg.

prompt: What is the diastolic blood pressure threshold in mmHg defining Stage 1 hypertension according to ACC/AHA guidelines?
explain: Diastolic blood pressure >= 80 mmHg defines Stage 1 hypertension.

prompt: What is the systolic blood pressure threshold in mmHg defining Stage 2 hypertension?
explain: Stage 2 hypertension begins at systolic BP >= 140 mmHg or diastolic >= 90 mmHg.

prompt: What is the fasting plasma glucose threshold in mg/dL that establishes a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus on two occasions?
explain: Fasting plasma glucose >= 126 mg/dL confirms diabetes.

prompt: What is the glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) percentage threshold that establishes a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
explain: An HbA1c >= 6.5% is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus.

prompt: What is the normal physiological upper limit of serum potassium in mEq/L in adults?
explain: Normal adult serum potassium is 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L.

prompt: What is the normal physiological lower limit of serum potassium in mEq/L in adults?
explain: Hypokalemia is defined as serum potassium < 3.5 mEq/L.

prompt: What is the normal lower limit of serum sodium in mEq/L below which hyponatremia is diagnosed?
explain: Hyponatremia is defined as serum sodium < 135 mEq/L.

prompt: What is the normal upper limit of serum sodium in mEq/L above which hypernatremia is diagnosed?
explain: Hypernatremia is defined as serum sodium > 145 mEq/L.

prompt: What is the normal adult arterial blood pH value around which acid-base balance is centered?
explain: Normal arterial blood pH ranges tightly between 7.35 and 7.45 (midpoint 7.40).

prompt: What is the 24-hour urine protein threshold in grams per day that defines nephrotic-range proteinuria in adults?
explain: Nephrotic-range proteinuria is defined as > 3.5 grams per 24 hours.

prompt: What is the CD4 count threshold in cells/µL below which an HIV patient is diagnosed with AIDS and requires PCP prophylaxis?
explain: A CD4 count < 200 cells/µL defines AIDS and triggers mandatory PCP prophylaxis.

prompt: What is the CD4 count threshold in cells/µL below which prophylaxis against Toxoplasma gondii is initiated in seropositive HIV patients?
explain: Toxoplasma encephalitis risk escalates sharply below 100 CD4 cells/µL.

prompt: What is the CD4 count threshold in cells/µL below which disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection risk peaks?
explain: Disseminated MAC and CMV retinitis occur predominantly when CD4 falls below 50 cells/µL.

prompt: What is the target international normalized ratio (INR) for an adult with an uncomplicated mechanical aortic valve prosthesis?
explain: Target INR for mechanical aortic valves without additional risk factors is 2.5 (range 2.0-3.0).

prompt: What is the target international normalized ratio (INR) for an adult with a mechanical mitral valve prosthesis?
explain: Mechanical mitral valves carry higher thrombotic risk and target an INR of 3.0 (range 2.5-3.5).

prompt: What is the door-to-balloon time goal in minutes for primary percutaneous coronary intervention in acute STEMI?
explain: ACC/AHA guidelines mandate door-to-balloon time <= 90 minutes for primary PCI.

prompt: What is the door-to-needle time goal in minutes for intravenous fibrinolysis in acute STEMI when PCI is unavailable?
explain: Fibrinolytic therapy should be administered within 30 minutes of hospital arrival if PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes.

prompt: What is the maximum time window in hours from symptom onset for administering intravenous alteplase in acute ischemic stroke?
explain: IV thrombolysis is approved up to 4.5 hours from witnessed onset of acute ischemic stroke.

prompt: What is the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) cut-off in g/dL defining portal hypertension?
explain: A SAAG >= 1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension with 97% accuracy.

prompt: What is the minimum absolute neutrophil count in ascitic fluid in cells/µL that establishes the diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?
explain: Ascitic fluid PMN >= 250/µL confirms SBP.

prompt: What is the normal PR interval upper limit in milliseconds on a resting 12-lead electrocardiogram beyond which first-degree AV block is diagnosed?
explain: A PR interval > 200 ms (one large box) defines first-degree AV block.

prompt: What is the normal QRS complex duration upper limit in milliseconds beyond which complete bundle branch block is diagnosed?
explain: A QRS duration >= 120 ms (3 small boxes) indicates complete bundle branch block or intraventricular conduction delay.

prompt: What is the corrected QT (QTc) interval threshold in milliseconds in adult males above which it is considered prolonged?
explain: QTc > 450 ms in men (and > 460-470 ms in women) indicates prolongation; > 500 ms carries high torsades risk.

prompt: What is the threshold QTc interval in milliseconds above which the risk of Torsades de pointes increases exponentially?
explain: A QTc > 500 ms substantially elevates the danger of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

prompt: What is the threshold platelet count in cells/µL below which spontaneous life-threatening intracranial hemorrhage risk sharply escalates?
explain: Prophylactic platelet transfusion is standard at platelets <= 10,000/µL to prevent spontaneous bleeding.

prompt: What is the maximum recommended sodium correction limit in mEq/L over 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome in chronic hyponatremia?
explain: Current guidelines advise limiting sodium rise to <= 8 mEq/L in 24 hours.

prompt: What is the normal resting mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) threshold in mmHg at or above which pulmonary hypertension is defined?
explain: The 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines revised the definition of pulmonary hypertension to resting mPAP > 20 mmHg.

prompt: What is the normal serum anion gap value in mEq/L around which clinical evaluation is calibrated?
explain: Normal serum anion gap ([Na] - [Cl + HCO3]) is typically 8 to 12 mEq/L.

prompt: What is the post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio threshold below which chronic airflow obstruction is diagnosed in COPD?
explain: GOLD criteria require post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70 to establish fixed obstruction.

prompt: What is the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) threshold in mmHg that defines clinically significant portal hypertension?
explain: An HVPG >= 10 mmHg defines clinically significant portal hypertension.

prompt: What is the HVPG threshold in mmHg above which variceal bleeding occurs almost exclusively?
explain: Variceal hemorrhage rarely happens unless HVPG exceeds 12 mmHg.

prompt: What is the target serum trough level in mcg/mL for vancomycin when treating severe MRSA endocarditis or osteomyelitis?
explain: Target vancomycin trough for severe MRSA infections is 15-20 mcg/mL (or AUC/MIC >= 400).

prompt: What is the normal serum osmolality midpoint value in mOsm/kg H2O?
explain: Normal serum osmolality is 275 to 295 mOsm/kg (mean ~285 mOsm/kg).

prompt: What is the fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) percentage threshold below which prerenal acute kidney injury is indicated?
explain: A FeNa < 1% reflects avid sodium reabsorption characteristic of prerenal azotemia.

prompt: What is the fractional excretion of urea (FeUrea) percentage threshold below which prerenal azotemia is indicated in patients receiving diuretics?
explain: When diuretics invalidate FeNa, a FeUrea < 35% indicates prerenal hypoperfusion.

prompt: What is the minimum percentage of clonal plasma cells on bone marrow biopsy required to establish a diagnosis of multiple myeloma?
explain: Diagnostic criteria mandate >= 10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells (or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) plus CRAB features.

prompt: What is the target hemoglobin A1c percentage recommended by the ADA for most non-pregnant adults with diabetes mellitus?
explain: An HbA1c < 7.0% is the standard target to minimize microvascular complications without excessive hypoglycemia.

prompt: What is the target LDL cholesterol level in mg/dL for patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease at very high risk?
explain: Recent guidelines recommend LDL-C < 55 mg/dL (or >= 50% reduction) for very high-risk patients.

prompt: What is the light-to-serum protein ratio threshold in Light's criteria defining an exudative pleural effusion?
explain: Pleural fluid protein / serum protein > 0.5 establishes an exudate.

prompt: What is the light-to-serum LDH ratio threshold in Light's criteria defining an exudative pleural effusion?
explain: Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH > 0.6 establishes an exudate.

prompt: What is the minimum score on the Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis that classifies a patient as having 'high probability'?
explain: A Wells DVT score >= 3 points indicates high pre-test probability.

prompt: What is the cutoff score on the Wells criteria for pulmonary embolism above which PE is considered 'likely'?
explain: A score > 4 points on the Wells PE criteria indicates PE is likely, prompting imaging rather than D-dimer alone.

prompt: What is the Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale score threshold that strongly supports a diagnosis of overt thyroid storm?
explain: A score >= 45 highly suggests thyroid storm; 25-44 suggests impending storm, and < 25 makes it unlikely.

prompt: What is the threshold absolute neutrophil count (ANC) in cells/µL defining severe neutropenia?
explain: Severe neutropenia is defined as ANC < 500 cells/µL, carrying dramatic infection vulnerability.

prompt: What is the typical half-life of albumin in human plasma in days?
explain: Albumin has a biological half-life of approximately 20 days (19-21 days), making it a marker of chronic rather than acute hepatic function.

prompt: What is the percentage threshold of severe ADAMTS13 activity deficiency that confirms the diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)?
explain: Severe ADAMTS13 activity < 10% is pathognomonic for TTP.

prompt: What is the length of the CAG trinucleotide repeat threshold in the HTT gene above which Huntington disease manifests with full penetrance?
explain: >= 40 CAG repeats in the huntingtin gene confers 100% lifetime penetrance of Huntington disease.

prompt: What is the normal 24-hour urinary free cortisol upper reference limit in micrograms per 24 hours in adults?
explain: Normal adult urinary free cortisol is typically < 50 mcg/24hr (values > 3x upper limit confirm Cushing syndrome).

prompt: Which virulence factor of Staphylococcus aureus binds the Fc portion of IgG, preventing opsonization and complement activation?
explain: Protein A on the S. aureus cell wall binds the Fc domain of IgG antibodies upside down, preventing Fc-receptor mediated phagocytosis.

prompt: Which catalase-negative, beta-hemolytic gram-positive coccus is bacitracin-sensitive and pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) positive?
explain: Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) is characterized by beta-hemolysis, susceptibility to bacitracin, and positive PYR test.

prompt: Which organism is the most common cause of community-acquired lobar pneumonia in adults, appearing as lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci with optochin susceptibility?
explain: Streptococcus pneumoniae displays alpha-hemolysis, bile solubility, and optochin ("P" disc) sensitivity.

prompt: Which gram-positive coccus is novobiocin-resistant and a frequent cause of uncomplicated urinary tract infections in sexually active young women?
explain: Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus saprophyticus is distinguished from S. epidermidis by its resistance to novobiocin.

prompt: Which spore-forming gram-positive rod produces an exotoxin consisting of protective antigen, lethal factor, and edema factor, the latter functioning as an adenylate cyclase?
explain: Anthrax edema factor is a calmodulin-dependent adenylate cyclase that elevates intracellular cAMP, causing extensive tissue edema.

prompt: What is the mechanism of action of tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) produced by Clostridium tetani?
choices: Cleaves synaptobrevin (SNARE), blocking release of inhibitory GABA and glycine from Renshaw cells
Cleaves SNAP-25, blocking acetylcholine release at the motor end plate
Inactivates the 60S ribosomal subunit by cleaving rRNA
explain: Tetanospasmin undergoes retrograde axonal transport to spinal inhibitory interneurons, cleaving synaptobrevin and producing spastic paralysis.

prompt: Which non-spore-forming, facultative intracellular gram-positive rod exhibits "tumbling motility" at 25°C and cold enrichment at 4°C, causing neonatal and immunocompromised meningitis?
explain: Listeria monocytogenes grows at refrigeration temperatures (cold enrichment), shows end-over-end tumbling motility, and uses actin rockets to spread cell-to-cell.

prompt: Which gram-positive filamentous rod is branching, strictly anaerobic, non-acid-fast, and forms yellow "sulfur granules" in draining sinus tracts?
explain: Actinomyces israelii is an oral commensal causing cervicofacial abscesses with sulfur granules under anaerobic conditions.

prompt: Which virulence factor of Neisseria meningitidis is primarily responsible for the rapid progression of septic shock and petechial purpura fulminans?
explain: Meningococcal lipooligosaccharide (LOS) lacks the O-antigen polysaccharide chain, causing massive TNF-alpha and IL-1 cytokine release upon shedding.

prompt: On which selective culture medium containing vancomycin, polymyxin (colistin), nystatin, and trimethoprim is Neisseria gonorrhoeae routinely isolated?
explain: Thayer-Martin medium uses selective antibiotics to inhibit gram-positives (vancomycin), gram-negatives (colistin), fungi (nystatin), and Proteus (trimethoprim).

prompt: Which lactose-fermenting, indole-positive gram-negative rod is the most common cause of community-acquired urinary tract infections and gram-negative bacteremia?
explain: Uropathogenic E. coli utilizes P-fimbriae to adhere to urothelium; it ferments lactose (pink on MacConkey) and is indole-positive.

prompt: Which gram-negative non-motile rod possesses a prominent antiphagocytic mucoid capsule, ferments lactose, and causes severe necrotizing "currant jelly" sputum pneumonia in alcoholics?
explain: Klebsiella produces abundant polysaccharide capsules yielding thick, mucoid colonies and currant-jelly sputum with cavitary upper-lobe pneumonia.

prompt: Which non-lactose fermenting, oxidase-positive, gram-negative rod produces pyocyanin and pyoverdine pigments and is a classic pathogen in burn victims and cystic fibrosis?
explain: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an obligate aerobe, oxidase-positive, produces blue-green pigments, and utilizes Exotoxin A to inactivate EF-2.

prompt: What is the primary mechanism of action of cholera toxin produced by Vibrio cholerae?
choices: Constitutively activates Gs alpha-subunit by ADP-ribosylation, elevating intracellular cAMP and CFTR chloride secretion
Inactivates Gi alpha-subunit, preventing inhibition of adenylate cyclase
Cleaves 28S rRNA in the 60S ribosomal subunit
Blocks acetylcholine release at presynaptic junctions
explain: Cholera toxin permanently ADP-ribosylates Gs, locking adenylate cyclase in the ON state, flooding intestinal crypts with chloride and watery "rice-water" diarrhea.

prompt: Which curved, microaerophilic gram-negative rod is oxidase-positive, grows at 42°C, and is the most common bacterial trigger for Guillain-Barré syndrome?
explain: Campylobacter jejuni grows at 42°C and produces inflammatory bloody diarrhea; molecular mimicry between its LOS and host gangliosides (GM1) induces Guillain-Barré.

prompt: Which enzyme produced abundantly by Helicobacter pylori hydrolyzes urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, allowing bacterial survival in acidic gastric juice?
explain: Bacterial urease generates an alkaline ammonia cloud that neutralizes gastric hydrochloric acid in the immediate microenvironment.

prompt: Which lipid component of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis cell wall inhibits phagosome-lysosome fusion inside infected macrophages?
explain: Sulfatides (sulfolipids) inhibit phagolysosomal fusion, permitting intracellular mycobacterial replication; cord factor inhibits leukocyte migration and induces TNF-alpha.

prompt: Which bacterial pathogen lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall completely, incorporates host cholesterol into its triple-layered membrane, and causes "walking pneumonia" with cold agglutinins?
explain: Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a cell wall (rendering beta-lactams useless) and induces IgM cold agglutinins against RBC I-antigens.

prompt: Which stage of the Chlamydia trachomatis developmental lifecycle is metabolically inert, spore-like, and infectious when entering host cells?
explain: Elementary bodies "Enter" (infectious), while Reticulate bodies "Replicate" intracellularly via binary fission.

prompt: What painless, indurated genital ulcer with clean base characterizes the primary stage of Treponema pallidum infection?
explain: Primary syphilis presents with a solitary, painless, indurated chancre; chancroid (H. ducreyi) produces a painful, soft ulcer.

prompt: Which tick vector transmits Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of Lyme disease, in the northeastern United States?
explain: Ixodes scapularis nymphs transmit Borrelia burgdorferi (as well as Babesia microti and Anaplasma phagocytophilum).

prompt: Which enveloped double-stranded DNA virus establishes latency in the sensory neurons of the trigeminal ganglia?
choices: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) exclusively in sacral ganglia
explain: HSV-1 typically establishes latent infection in sensory neurons of the trigeminal ganglion, reactivating as herpes labialis.

prompt: Which herpesvirus binds the CD21 (CR2) complement receptor on B-lymphocytes, causing infectious mononucleosis and atypical reactive CD8+ T-lymphocytes (Downey cells)?
explain: EBV envelope gp350 binds CD21 on B cells; atypical reactive lymphocytes in peripheral blood are cytotoxic CD8+ T cells responding to infected B cells.

prompt: What histological finding in urine or tissue biopsy is pathognomonic for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection?
choices: Cowdry type A eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions
explain: CMV-infected cells demonstrate cytomegaly with prominent basophilic intranuclear "owl's eye" inclusions.

prompt: Which non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus infects erythroid progenitor cells, causing aplastic crises in sickle cell patients and hydrops fetalis during pregnancy?
explain: Parvovirus B19 has a linear ssDNA genome and binds the erythrocyte P-antigen (globoside), halting red blood cell production.

prompt: Which surface glycoprotein of the Influenza A virus mediates viral attachment to host cell sialic acid receptors and viral entry via endocytosis?
explain: Hemagglutinin binds terminal sialic acid on host respiratory epithelial glycoproteins, while neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release progeny virions.

prompt: What genetic mechanism responsible for major global influenza pandemics involves genetic reassortment of segmented RNA between animal and human viral strains?
explain: Antigenic shift is genetic reassortment of segmented genome segments creating novel HA/NA subtypes; antigenic drift is minor random point mutation.

prompt: Which member of the Paramyxoviridae family possesses a fusion (F) protein that induces host cells to merge into multinucleated giant cells (syncytia), causing bronchiolitis in infants?
explain: RSV uses its F protein to fuse epithelial cells into giant syncytia, causing acute bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants; prevented with palivizumab.

prompt: Which bullet-shaped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA rhabdovirus travels via retrograde axoplasmic flow along peripheral nerves to the CNS, forming eosinophilic Negri bodies in Purkinje cells?
explain: Rabies virus binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction and travels retrograde to the brainstem and hippocampus.

prompt: Which flavivirus is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, causes severe retro-orbital headache, "breakbone" arthralgias, and can trigger life-threatening hemorrhagic fever upon secondary re-infection?
explain: Secondary infection with a different dengue serotype triggers antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), leading to massive capillary leak and dengue shock syndrome.

prompt: Which HIV-1 viral envelope glycoprotein mediates initial high-affinity attachment to host cell surface CD4 receptors?
explain: Surface gp120 attaches to CD4 and chemokine coreceptors (CCR5 or CXCR4); transmembrane gp41 mediates viral membrane fusion.

prompt: Which opportunistic yeast exhibits germ tube formation at 37°C, pseudohyphae on tissue biopsy, and causes thrush, diaper dermatitis, and candidemia in hospitalized patients?
explain: Candida albicans is a polymorphic fungus forming true germ tubes at 37°C and pseudohyphae with budding blastoconidia.

prompt: Which heavily encapsulated yeast is found in pigeon droppings, displays narrow-based budding, stains positive with India ink and mucicarmine, and causes chronic meningitis in immunocompromised patients?
explain: Cryptococcus neoformans possesses a thick polysaccharide glucuronoxylomannan capsule visualized as clear halos on India ink.

prompt: Which monomorphic mold is characterized by acute-angle (45-degree) branching, regular septate hyphae, and can form a "fungus ball" (aspergilloma) inside preexisting tuberculous lung cavities?
explain: Aspergillus has narrow, septate hyphae branching dichotomously at 45° angles and produces fruiting bodies (conidiophores) in air-filled spaces.

prompt: Which mold exhibits broad, non-septate (pauciseptate) hyphae branching at wide right angles (90 degrees) and characteristically causes rhinocerebral angioinvasion in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis?
explain: Mucorales thrive in high glucose and ketone acidotic environments, penetrating cribriform plates and blood vessels with right-angle non-septate hyphae.

prompt: Which thermally dimorphic fungus is endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, resides intracellularly inside macrophages, and is associated with bird and bat guano in caves?
explain: Histoplasma capsulatum forms tiny oval yeast cells (2-4 um) packed inside reticuloendothelial macrophages.

prompt: Which dimorphic fungus endemic to the southwestern United States (San Joaquin Valley) forms large thick-walled spherules filled with endospores in tissue biopsies?
explain: Coccidioides forms arthroconidia in soil, which transform inside human lungs into massive 20-60 um spherules containing endospores.

prompt: Which flagellated protozoan trophozoite is pear-shaped with two nuclei and four pairs of flagella ("falling leaf motility"), causing non-bloody, foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea in hikers drinking untreated water?
explain: Giardia trophozoites attach to duodenal brush border via ventral sucking discs without mucosal invasion, causing fat malabsorption and steatorrhea.

prompt: Which amoebic protozoan causes dysentery with flask-shaped intestinal ulcers and can travel via the portal vein to produce a solitary "anchovy paste" liver abscess?
explain: Entamoeba histolytica invades the colonic submucosa to form flask-shaped ulcers and contains engulfed RBCs (erythrophagocytosis) in trophozoites.

prompt: Which intracellular coccidian parasite is transmitted via feline feces or undercooked meat, causing multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in AIDS patients and chorioretinitis in congenital infection?
explain: Toxoplasma gondii tachyzoites and bradyzoite cysts cause cerebral abscesses with surrounding ring enhancement and classic congenital triad (hydrocephalus, calcifications, chorioretinitis).

prompt: Which Plasmodium species is the most virulent cause of malaria, featuring irregular 48-hour fever spikes, banana-shaped gametocytes, and sequestration in microvessels causing cerebral malaria?
explain: P. falciparum parasitizes erythrocytes of all ages, expresses PfEMP1 to adhere to endothelial ICAM-1, and shows distinctive crescent/banana-shaped gametocytes.

prompt: Which tick-borne intraerythrocytic protozoan transmitted by Ixodes scapularis resembles malaria on blood smear but characteristically displays tetrads in a "Maltese cross" arrangement?
explain: Babesia microti trophozoites form pleomorphic intraerythrocytic ring forms and pathognomonic cruciform tetrads ("Maltese cross") without hemozoin pigment.

prompt: Which protozoan transmitted by the reduviid ("kissing") bug causes Chagas disease, manifesting with dilated cardiomyopathy, megacolon, and megaesophagus?
explain: T. cruzi amastigotes destroy autonomic myenteric ganglia and cardiac conduction fibers, producing dilated cardiomyopathy, apical aneurysm, and gastrointestinal megadisease.

prompt: Which common pediatric nematode (pinworm) deposits eggs on the perianal folds at night, causing nocturnal pruritus ani diagnosed via the cellophane "tape test"?
explain: Gravid female Enterobius vermicularis worms migrate out of the anus at night to deposit asymmetric, flat-sided eggs.

prompt: Which cestode (pork tapeworm) causes neurocysticercosis with seizures and "swiss-cheese" calcified cysts in the brain when humans accidentally ingest its eggs from contaminated feces?
explain: Ingestion of T. solium eggs (fecal-oral) produces larval cysticercosis in human tissues/brain, whereas eating undercooked pork containing larvae causes simple intestinal tapeworm infection.

prompt: Which blood fluke utilizes freshwater snails as intermediate hosts, penetrates human skin via cercariae, and resides in the vesical venous plexus, causing hematuria and squamous cell bladder cancer?
explain: Schistosoma haematobium eggs have a terminal spine; chronic granulomatous inflammation in the bladder wall predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma.

prompt: What genetic mechanism confers high-level methicillin resistance in Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)?
choices: Mutations in DNA gyrase subunit A
Upregulation of the MexAB multidrug efflux pump
explain: The staphylococcal cassette chromosome SCCmec carries the mecA gene, which synthesizes PBP2a, conferring resistance to virtually all beta-lactams.

prompt: What altered cell wall peptidoglycan precursor confers vancomycin resistance in Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococci (VRE)?
choices: Substitution of terminal D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac
Loss of outer membrane OprD porin channels
Enzymatic acetylation of aminoglycoside hydroxyl groups
explain: The vanA operon encodes ligases that synthesize D-alanyl-D-lactate instead of D-Ala-D-Ala, decreasing vancomycin binding affinity 1,000-fold.

prompt: Which process of bacterial horizontal gene transfer involves the uptake and genomic incorporation of naked extracellular DNA fragments from the surrounding environment?
explain: Transformation is the direct uptake of naked environmental DNA by competent bacteria (classically Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria).

prompt: Which process of bacterial genetic exchange requires direct cell-to-cell contact mediated by a sex pilus encoded by the F plasmid?
explain: Bacterial conjugation involves transfer of single-stranded plasmid DNA from donor (F+) to recipient (F-) bacteria across a mating bridge.

prompt: Which bacterial toxin produced by Clostridium perfringens is an alpha-toxin that functions as a lecithinase (phospholipase C), cleaving cell membrane phospholipids to cause myonecrosis and gas gangrene?
explain: C. perfringens alpha-toxin hydrolyzes phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin, destroying cell membranes and causing gas gangrene.

prompt: Which gram-negative coccobacillus requires both Factor X (hematin) and Factor V (NAD+) for growth on chocolate agar?
explain: H. influenzae requires both X factor (hematin) and V factor (NAD), which are released by heated erythrocytes in chocolate agar.

prompt: Which zoonotic organism transmitted by domestic cat and dog bites causes acute cellulitis within 24 hours and is a small, encapsulated bipolar-staining gram-negative rod?
explain: Pasteurella multocida causes rapid-onset wound infection (<24 hours) following cat or dog bites; sensitive to amoxicillin-clavulanate.

prompt: What form of leprosy is characterized by a strong cell-mediated TH1 immune response, few hypopigmented skin lesions with anesthetic centers, and low bacterial load?
explain: Tuberculoid leprosy features strong cell-mediated immunity (positive lepromin skin test), granulomas, and localized asymmetric hypopigmented plaques.

prompt: Which spirochete transmitted via exposure to animal urine-contaminated water causes Weil disease, characterized by severe jaundice, azotemia, hemorrhage, and conjunctival suffusion?
explain: Leptospira interrogans is a hook-ended spirochete causing leptospirosis; severe icteric illness with renal failure is known as Weil disease.

prompt: Which polyomavirus establishes latent infection in the renal parenchyma and reactivates in renal transplant recipients to cause graft nephropathy and ureteral stenosis?
explain: BK virus causes polyomavirus-associated nephropathy in kidney allograft recipients; JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).

prompt: Which naked, positive-sense single-stranded RNA picornavirus is acid-stable and transmitted via the fecal-oral route, causing acute self-limited viral hepatitis without a chronic carrier state?
explain: HAV is an enterovirus-like picornavirus causing acute jaundice via contaminated shellfish/water; it never progresses to chronic hepatitis.

prompt: Which dimorphic fungus causes "rose gardener disease" following cutaneous thorn prick inoculation, producing subcutaneous nodules that spread proximally along lymphatic drainage?
explain: Sporothrix schenckii forms cigar-shaped budding yeasts in tissue and causes nodular lymphocutaneous lesions treated with itraconazole.

prompt: Which tissue nematode transmitted by blackfly (Simulium) bites in tropical Africa causes river blindness (onchocerciasis) and pruritic "lizard skin"?
explain: Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae migrate through ocular tissues causing sclerosing keratitis and blindness; treated with ivermectin.

prompt: What pseudomembranous enterotoxin and cytotoxin are produced by Clostridioides difficile following broad-spectrum clindamycin or cephalosporin antibiotic exposure?
explain: C. difficile Toxin A causes watery diarrhea while Toxin B glycosylates Rho GTPases, disrupting the actin cytoskeleton and killing enterocytes.

prompt: Which gram-negative rod produces swarming motility on blood agar and hydrolyzes urea, predisposing to magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) staghorn calculi?
explain: Proteus urease alkalinizes urine (pH >8.0), promoting precipitation of struvite (ammonium magnesium phosphate) staghorn stones.

prompt: Which zoonotic gram-negative rod transmitted by unpasteurized goat dairy products causes undulant fever and resides chronically in reticuloendothelial macrophages?
explain: Brucella species cause undulant fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and osteomyelitis following consumption of unpasteurized milk or cheese.

prompt: Which naked, segmented double-stranded RNA reovirus is the most common cause of severe dehydrating infantile diarrhea worldwide, prevented by live oral vaccination?
explain: Rotavirus has an 11-segment dsRNA genome and encodes the NSP4 viral enterotoxin, blunting villi and causing secretory diarrhea.

prompt: Which coagulase-negative staphylococcus is a prominent producer of extracellular polysaccharide biofilms on prosthetic joints, intravascular catheters, and artificial heart valves?
explain: S. epidermidis produces an adherent glycocalyx biofilm that protects the bacteria from antimicrobials and host phagocytes.

prompt: Which test reliably differentiates Staphylococcus species (catalase-positive) from Streptococcus species (catalase-negative)?
explain: Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen gas, creating visible bubbles in staphylococci.

prompt: Which enteric pathogen is non-motile, does not produce H2S, has a very low infectious dose (<100 organisms), and invades M cells to cause bacillary dysentery?
explain: Shigella species are acid-resistant, non-motile, H2S-negative, and spread cell-to-cell via actin polymerisation.

prompt: Which non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus causes acute epidemic hemorrhagic cystitis in children and pharyngoconjunctival fever in summer camps?
explain: Adenovirus has fiber spikes projecting from its icosahedral capsid and causes conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, and acute hemorrhagic cystitis.

prompt: Which paramyxovirus causes acute parotitis, orchitis (risking male infertility), and aseptic meningitis, preventable with the MMR vaccine?
explain: Mumps virus replicates in upper respiratory epithelium and spreads to parotid glands, testes, pancreas, and meninges.

prompt: Which protozoan flagellate transmitted through sexual intercourse causes foul-smelling, greenish-yellow frothy vaginal discharge with a "strawberry cervix"?
explain: Trichomonas vaginalis exists only as a motile trophozoite (no cyst stage), displaying corkscrew motility on wet mount.

prompt: Which large intestinal roundworm can cause mechanical intestinal obstruction in children and migrates through the pulmonary alveoli during its larval lifecycle?
explain: Ascaris lumbricoides is the largest human intestinal nematode; heavy worm burdens can knot together and obstruct the ileocecal valve.

prompt: What is the mechanism of action of diphtheria toxin produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae?
explain: Diphtheria toxin is an AB toxin that catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of diphthamide on EF-2, halting peptide elongation.

prompt: Which bacterial zoonosis is transmitted by aerosols from infected sheep placenta and amniotic fluid, causing Q fever without an arthropod vector?
explain: Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular bacterium with spore-like resistance that causes Q fever culture-negative endocarditis.

prompt: Which positive-sense enveloped single-stranded RNA virus in the Togaviridae family causes "German measles" with posterior auricular lymphadenopathy and congenital cataract/deafness/PDA?
explain: Rubella (German measles) is a togavirus causing mild fever, maculopapular rash, and postauricular lymphadenopathy; highly teratogenic.

prompt: Which atypical opportunistic fungus has a cholesterol-containing cell membrane, forms "crushed ping-pong ball" cysts on silver stain, and causes interstitial pneumonia in AIDS?
explain: Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungus lacking ergosterol (unresponsive to azoles/amphotericin) that stains black with methenamine silver; treated with TMP-SMX.

prompt: Which cestode acquired from eating raw freshwater fish can grow up to 10 meters in the human intestine and causes megaloblastic anemia via vitamin B12 competition?
explain: Diphyllobothrium latum consumes up to 80% of ingested dietary vitamin B12, causing subacute combined degeneration and megaloblastic anemia.

prompt: Which gram-positive rod is a facultative intracellular pathogen that escapes the phagolysosome using the pore-forming toxin listeriolysin O and moves via actin polymerization?
explain: Listeriolysin O punches pores in phagosomes; ActA polymerizes host actin to form "actin rockets" that push Listeria into neighboring cells.

prompt: Which organism causes bubonic plague with exquisitely tender swollen lymph nodes (buboes), transmitted by the Xenopsylla cheopis rodent flea?
explain: Yersinia pestis is a gram-negative rod with bipolar "safety pin" staining that produces bubonic plague with septicemic shock.

prompt: Which human herpesvirus is the etiological agent of exanthem subitum (roseola infantum), causing several days of high fever followed by a lace-like rash as the fever breaks?
explain: HHV-6 infects CD4+ T-lymphocytes, causing high fever in infants that terminates abruptly as a macular blanching rash appears.

prompt: Which RNA filovirus causes severe hemorrhagic fever with extensive mucosal bleeding, shock, and DIC, transmitted via contact with bodily fluids from infected individuals or fruit bats?
explain: Ebola and Marburg are filamentous negative-sense ssRNA viruses causing severe microvascular endothelial breakdown and fatal hemorrhagic fever.

prompt: Which enzyme produced by extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing Enterobacteriaceae hydrolyzes third-generation cephalosporins and aztreonam?
explain: ESBLs are plasmid-mediated beta-lactamases that confer resistance to penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam; carbapenems remain the treatment of choice.

prompt: Which superantigen produced by Streptococcus pyogenes causes streptococcal toxic shock-like syndrome and scarlet fever?
explain: SpeA crosslinks MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells to the T-cell receptor beta chain, activating massive non-specific polyclonal T-cell cytokine release.

prompt: Which organism causes whooping cough by producing pertussis toxin, which ADP-ribosylates and inhibits the Gi alpha-subunit?
explain: Pertussis toxin permanently disables Gi, keeping adenylate cyclase constitutively active and causing lymphocytosis and whooping cough paroxysms.

prompt: Which organism causes typhus with a rash that begins on the trunk and spreads to the extremities (sparing the face, palms, and soles), transmitted by the human body louse?
explain: Rickettsia prowazekii causes epidemic louse-borne typhus with central-to-peripheral rash; R. rickettsii causes RMSF with peripheral-to-central rash on palms and soles.

prompt: Which human herpesvirus is the causative agent of Kaposi sarcoma, presenting as violaceous vascular cutaneous plaques in patients with AIDS?
explain: HHV-8 encodes viral oncogenes including a VEGF homologue that induces spindle-cell vascular proliferation and Kaposi sarcoma.

prompt: Which nematode acquired by walking barefoot on fecally contaminated soil can cause autoinfection and fatal hyperinfection syndrome in immunocompromised patients?
explain: Strongyloides rhabditiform larvae can molt into filariform larvae within the human gut lumen, reinvading the intestinal wall or perianal skin (autoinfection).

prompt: Which gram-negative coccobacillus is transmitted by aerosol inhalation from aquatic biofilms and cooling towers, requires charcoal yeast extract agar, and causes severe atypical pneumonia with hyponatremia?
explain: Legionella pneumophila requires iron and L-cysteine on BCYE agar, causing Legionnaires disease with confusion, diarrhea, and hyponatremia.

prompt: What systemic febrile reaction can occur within hours of initiating penicillin treatment for spirochetal syphilis, caused by massive release of endotoxin-like pyrogens from dying treponemes?
explain: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute cytokine surge causing fever, chills, tachycardia, and flushing following rapid lysis of Treponema pallidum.

prompt: Which picornavirus is the most common cause of the common cold (acute rhinitis), possesses over 100 serotypes, and binds intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1)?
explain: Rhinovirus is an acid-labile picornavirus that replicates optimally at 33°C in the cooler nasal mucosa and binds host ICAM-1.

prompt: Which superficial dermatophyte is a dimorphic lipophilic fungus that causes pityriasis (tinea) versicolor, displaying "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on KOH preparation?
explain: Malassezia furfur degrades skin lipids to generate dicarboxylic acids that inhibit melanogenesis, producing hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules.

prompt: Which protozoan transmitted by sandflies (Phlebotomus) invades reticuloendothelial macrophages to cause visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia?
explain: Leishmania donovani amastigotes replicate inside splenic, hepatic, and bone marrow macrophages, causing spiking fevers, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia.

prompt: Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-negative and does not ferment mannitol.
explain: S. aureus produces coagulase and ferments mannitol, distinguishing it from coagulase-negative staphylococci.

prompt: Streptococcus pneumoniae is resistant to optochin and insoluble in bile salts.
explain: S. pneumoniae is sensitive to optochin and lyses rapidly in bile salts (bile soluble), distinguishing it from viridans streptococci.

prompt: Streptococcus pyogenes produces streptolysin O, which is antigenic and stimulates the production of ASO antibodies.
explain: Anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titers document recent pharyngeal infection in suspected acute rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis.

prompt: Enterococci can grow in 6.5% NaCl and hydrolyze esculin in the presence of 40% bile.
explain: Enterococcus faecalis and E. faecium tolerate high salt concentrations (6.5% NaCl) and hydrolyze bile esculin.

prompt: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) produces the CAMP factor that synergistically enlarges the hemolysis zone of S. aureus.
explain: The CAMP test reveals arrowhead hemolysis when S. agalactiae is streaked perpendicularly to beta-lysin-producing S. aureus.

prompt: Bacillus anthracis is the only bacterium that possesses a polypeptide capsule composed of poly-D-glutamic acid.
explain: Unlike virtually all other bacterial capsules which are polysaccharides, the anthrax capsule consists of poly-D-glutamic acid.

prompt: Clostridium botulinum toxin produces spastic paralysis by blocking glycine release in spinal Renshaw cells.
explain: Botulinum neurotoxin blocks acetylcholine release at peripheral motor end plates, producing flaccid (not spastic) paralysis.

prompt: Listeria monocytogenes can cross the placenta and cause granulomatosis infantiseptica in neonates.
explain: Transplacental transmission of Listeria causes disseminated microabscesses and granulomas (granulomatosis infantiseptica) or neonatal meningitis.

prompt: Corynebacterium diphtheriae appears as pleomorphic club-shaped rods with metachromatic granules on Löffler medium.
explain: Albert or Neisser stains highlight polyphosphate volutin (metachromatic) granules in club-shaped corynebacteria.

prompt: Nocardia asteroides is an anaerobic organism that forms yellow sulfur granules in tissue biopsies.
explain: Nocardia is an obligate aerobe with branching beaded filaments that is weakly acid-fast; Actinomyces is the anaerobe with sulfur granules.

prompt: Neisseria gonorrhoeae ferments both maltose and glucose, whereas Neisseria meningitidis ferments only glucose.
explain: Meningococcus ferments Maltose and Glucose (M and G); Gonococcus ferments only Glucose (G).

prompt: Neisseria gonorrhoeae possesses an antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule that protects it from complement lysis.
explain: N. gonorrhoeae lacks a capsule; N. meningitidis possesses a polysaccharide capsule.

prompt: Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive, gram-negative diplococcus that causes otitis media and sinusitis in children.
explain: Moraxella catarrhalis is an aerobic diplococcus commonly causing pediatric otitis media and exacerbations of COPD.

prompt: Escherichia coli O157:H7 ferments sorbitol rapidly on MacConkey sorbitol agar.
explain: Unlike most commensal E. coli, EHEC O157:H7 does not ferment sorbitol and forms colorless colonies on MacConkey-sorbitol agar.

prompt: Salmonella species are motile, produce hydrogen sulfide (H2S), and tolerate stomach acid in very low doses (<10 organisms).
explain: Salmonella is acid-labile and requires a high infectious dose (>10^5 organisms) to survive the gastric barrier; Shigella has a low infectious dose.

prompt: Shigella sonnei and dysenteriae spread from enterocyte to enterocyte by polymerizing host actin filaments.
explain: Shigella invades M cells and uses actin rockets to move horizontally through colonic epithelium without entering the bloodstream.

prompt: Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces Exotoxin A, which inactivates elongation factor-2 (EF-2) identically to diphtheria toxin.
explain: Both Exotoxin A and diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylate EF-2, terminating host cellular protein translation.

prompt: Bacteroides fragilis is the most abundant strictly anaerobic bacterium in the normal human colonic microbiota.
explain: B. fragilis is an obligate anaerobe with a modified LPS capsule that predominates in intra-abdominal abscesses following perforation.

prompt: Campylobacter jejuni is a comma-shaped rod that grows best at 42°C on Skirrow selective medium.
explain: Thermophilic Campylobacter jejuni grows at 42°C under microaerophilic conditions.

prompt: Vibrio vulnificus wound infections are acquired from exposure to warm seawater or raw oysters and can cause fatal necrotizing fasciitis in patients with hemochromatosis.
explain: V. vulnificus utilizes excess host iron to fuel rapid proliferation, causing hemorrhagic bullae and septic shock in patients with chronic liver disease.

prompt: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an obligate anaerobe that preferentially replicates in the lung bases due to low oxygen tension.
explain: Secondary reactivation tuberculosis predilects the apical and posterior segments of upper lobes where ventilation-perfusion ratios are highest.

prompt: Mycoplasma pneumoniae can be treated effectively with beta-lactam penicillins and cephalosporins.
explain: Mycoplasma completely lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall; all beta-lactams and glycopeptides are entirely ineffective.

prompt: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D through K cause trachoma, the leading cause of preventable infectious blindness worldwide.
explain: Serovars A, B, Ba, and C cause blinding trachoma; serovars D-K cause sexually transmitted urethritis and PID.

prompt: Rickettsia rickettsii causes a petechial rash that begins on the trunk and spreads outward to the limbs.
explain: Rocky Mountain spotted fever causes necrotizing vasculitis with an inward centripetal rash starting on wrists/ankles and spreading to trunk and palms.

prompt: Coxiella burnetii infection requires an arthropod tick vector for transmission to humans.
explain: Coxiella burnetii is transmitted by inhalation of dried aerosols from barnyard animal placental fluids, requiring no tick vector.

prompt: Treponema pallidum can be cultured readily on standard synthetic laboratory agar media.
explain: T. pallidum is an obligate parasite that has never been cultured continuously in vitro on artificial media.

prompt: The VDRL and RPR screening tests for syphilis detect antibodies specific to Treponema pallidum antigens.
explain: Non-treponemal tests detect IgM/IgG antibodies directed against cardiolipin released from damaged host cells and treponemes.

prompt: Erythema migrans is the classic targetoid expanding skin rash of early localized Lyme disease.
explain: The "bull's-eye" erythema migrans rash develops 7-14 days after an Ixodes tick bite transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi.

prompt: Leptospirosis can present with conjunctival suffusion without purulent discharge.
explain: Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival suffusion (erythema without pus) is a pathognomonic diagnostic sign of acute leptospirosis.

prompt: Gummas are soft, non-cancerous granulomatous growths characteristic of tertiary syphilis.
explain: Tertiary syphilis produces destructive gummatous necrosis in bone, skin, liver, and subcutaneous tissues.

prompt: All herpesviruses establish lifelong latent infection within host cells following primary infection.
explain: Herpesviridae (HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, EBV, CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7, HHV-8) characteristically establish permanent latency.

prompt: Varicella-zoster virus establishes latency in the anterior horn motor neurons of the spinal cord.
explain: Following childhood chickenpox, VZV remains dormant in sensory ganglia and reactivates as dermatomal herpes zoster (shingles).

prompt: Epstein-Barr virus infection is associated with an elevated heterophile antibody titer (Monospot positive).
explain: EBV infection drives polyclonal B-cell activation, generating heterophile IgM antibodies that agglutinate sheep or horse erythrocytes.

prompt: Rubella is the most common congenital viral infection in the United States.
explain: Congenital CMV causes sensorineural hearing loss, periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, and blueberry muffin rash.

prompt: Parvovirus B19 is an enveloped double-stranded DNA virus.
explain: Parvovirus B19 is a non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus (the only human pathogenic ssDNA virus).

prompt: Hepatitis B virus is a single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus that replicates without any reverse transcription step.
explain: HBV is a hepadnavirus containing DNA polymerase with reverse transcriptase activity that copies pregenomic RNA.

prompt: High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 cause condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts).
explain: Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 cause benign genital warts; types 16 and 18 cause cervical and oropharyngeal dysplasias and carcinomas.

prompt: Adenovirus is an enveloped virus that is easily inactivated by lipid solvents and hand sanitizer.
explain: Adenovirus is a non-enveloped (naked) capsid virus that is extremely stable in the environment and resistant to lipid solvents.

prompt: Poxviruses are the only DNA viruses that replicate entirely within the cytoplasm of host cells.
explain: Poxviruses (e.g., variola, molluscum contagiosum) encode their own DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, allowing cytoplasmic replication.

prompt: JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) by destroying oligodendrocytes in AIDS patients.
explain: Reactivation of latent JC polyomavirus selectively lyses myelin-producing oligodendrocytes, producing demyelinating brain lesions.

prompt: Poliovirus is an enterovirus transmitted by the fecal-oral route that destroys anterior horn motor neurons.
explain: Poliovirus replicates in oropharynx and Peyer patches, enters blood, and selectively destroys anterior horn cells causing flaccid paralysis.

prompt: Rhinoviruses are acid-stable viruses that replicate well in the low pH environment of the stomach.
explain: Rhinoviruses are acid-labile (destroyed by stomach acid), explaining why they cause upper respiratory but not gastrointestinal infections.

prompt: Hepatitis C virus is a flavivirus that frequently progresses to chronic infection in >75% of infected individuals.
explain: Lack of 3'-to-5' proofreading in HCV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase generates hypervariable quasispecies, evading immunity and favoring chronicity.

prompt: Influenza viruses possess a single, continuous non-segmented negative-sense RNA genome.
explain: Influenza A and B viruses possess an 8-segmented negative-sense RNA genome, enabling antigenic shift via reassortment.

prompt: Koplik spots on buccal mucosa are pathognomonic for rubella (German measles) infection.
explain: Koplik spots are small bluish-white ulcers on an erythematous base opposite the lower molars, appearing before the measles rash.

prompt: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) possesses hemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface spikes.
explain: RSV lacks hemagglutinin and neuraminidase; it relies on its G (attachment) protein and F (fusion) glycoprotein.

prompt: Rotavirus is an enveloped single-stranded DNA virus.
explain: Rotavirus (Reoviridae) has an 11-segmented double-stranded RNA genome and a wheel-like triple-layered capsid.

prompt: Rabies virus vaccine can be administered post-exposure because of the virus's prolonged incubation period.
explain: Slow retrograde transport along peripheral nerves (weeks to months) allows active immunization and rabies immunoglobulin to prevent disease.

prompt: Ebola virus is a positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus.
explain: Ebola is a filamentous, negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Filoviridae family.

prompt: Zika virus infection during pregnancy can cause severe congenital microcephaly and cerebral calcifications.
explain: Zika virus crosses the placental barrier and infects neural progenitor cells, impairing brain development and causing microcephaly.

prompt: The HIV-1 viral genome consists of a single double-stranded DNA molecule.
explain: HIV virions are diploid, containing two identical copies of positive-sense ssRNA alongside reverse transcriptase and integrase.

prompt: Chemokine receptor CXCR4 is the coreceptor used by macrophage-tropic (M-tropic) strains of HIV-1.
explain: Early transmitted R5 strains bind CCR5 coreceptors; homozygous CCR5-delta-32 mutations confer high resistance to HIV-1.

prompt: Human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1) causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and tropical spastic paraparesis.
explain: HTLV-1 encodes the Tax oncoprotein, driving malignant proliferation of CD4+ T-lymphocytes.

prompt: Candida albicans forms pseudohyphae and budding yeasts in cold temperatures and true germ tubes at 37°C.
explain: Candida forms pseudohyphae and budding yeast at 20°C, and forms germ tubes and hyphae in human serum at 37°C.

prompt: Cryptococcus neoformans is an intracellular dimorphic fungus that forms spherules in tissue.
explain: Cryptococcus is an extracellular, monomorphic encapsulated yeast; Coccidioides forms spherules.

prompt: Aspergillus fumigatus produces broad, non-septate hyphae that branch at right angles.
explain: Aspergillus hyphae are narrow, regular, septate, and branch dichotomously at 45°.

prompt: Mucor and Rhizopus species invade blood vessels through internal elastic lamina, causing tissue infarction.
explain: Zygomycetes are strongly angioinvasive, causing rapid vascular thrombosis and black necrotic eschars.

prompt: Histoplasma capsulatum yeast cells are characteristically found multiplying inside host macrophages.
explain: Histoplasma survives inside phagolysosomes of macrophages, appearing as small oval yeasts with pseudocapsules.

prompt: Blastomyces dermatitidis is characterized in tissue by narrow-based budding yeasts surrounded by a thick polysaccharide capsule.
explain: Blastomyces forms large round yeasts (8-15 um) with single broad-based buds ("Broad-Based Budding").

prompt: Coccidioides immitis forms large endospore-filled spherules in tissue at 37°C.
explain: Coccidioides is unique among dimorphic fungi because its parasitic tissue form is a large endosporulating spherule, not a yeast.

prompt: Pneumocystis jirovecii cell membranes contain high concentrations of ergosterol.
explain: Pneumocystis cell membranes contain cholesterol rather than ergosterol, explaining why amphotericin B and azoles are ineffective.

prompt: Giardia duodenalis causes bloody diarrhea by deeply invading the colonic mucosa.
explain: Giardia is non-invasive; it attaches to duodenal enterocytes with ventral sucking discs, causing non-bloody steatorrhea.

prompt: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites can ingest erythrocytes (erythrophagocytosis).
explain: Presence of ingested red blood cells inside trophozoite cytoplasm distinguishes pathogenic E. histolytica from commensal amoebas.

prompt: Cryptosporidium oocysts are best identified in stool with India ink staining.
explain: Cryptosporidium oocysts (4-5 um) are acid-fast, appearing as bright red spherical bodies in stool smears.

prompt: Dogs are the definitive hosts for Toxoplasma gondii, where the sexual reproductive cycle occurs.
explain: Felines are the only definitive hosts shedding infective Toxoplasma oocysts; humans and other animals serve as intermediate hosts.

prompt: Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium malariae can form dormant hypnozoites in hepatocytes that cause late clinical relapses.
explain: P. vivax and P. ovale hypnozoites remain dormant in liver parenchyma; primaquine or tafenoquine is required to eradicate them.

prompt: Babesia microti is transmitted to humans by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito.
explain: Babesia is transmitted by the Ixodes scapularis tick; Anopheles mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium (malaria).

prompt: Trypanosoma cruzi is transmitted by reduviid bugs depositing infected feces near bite wounds.
explain: T. cruzi metacyclic trypomastigotes are excreted in bug feces during feeding and rubbed into the bite wound or conjunctiva.

prompt: Enterobius vermicularis diagnosis is confirmed by finding characteristic eggs on a perianal cellulose tape prep.
explain: Stool examination is rarely positive; applying transparent adhesive tape to the perianal fold in the morning captures the flat-sided eggs.

prompt: Ingestion of undercooked pork containing larval cysticerci of Taenia solium causes human neurocysticercosis.
explain: Eating undercooked pork containing cysts causes adult intestinal tapeworm infection; neurocysticercosis occurs when humans ingest eggs from feces.

prompt: Schistosoma haematobium infection is strongly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder.
explain: Chronic mechanical irritation and egg granulomas in the bladder wall lead to squamous metaplasia and malignant transformation.

prompt: MRSA resistance to oxacillin and nafcillin is mediated by enzymatic degradation via beta-lactamase.
explain: MRSA resistance is mediated by altered PBP2a encoded by mecA, which has low affinity for beta-lactams.

prompt: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) resist vancomycin mainly by producing an enzyme that degrades the drug.
explain: The vanA and vanB operons synthesize D-Ala-D-Lac, decreasing vancomycin hydrogen-bonding affinity.

prompt: Bacterial beta-lactamase inhibitors such as clavulanic acid and tazobactam restore the activity of penicillins against MRSA.
explain: Beta-lactamase inhibitors only block beta-lactamases; they cannot overcome the low-affinity PBP2a target in MRSA.

prompt: Efflux pumps can confer multidrug resistance by actively extruding tetracyclines, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones from the bacterial cell.
explain: Membrane-bound active efflux transporters (e.g., TetA, MexAB) pump diverse antimicrobials out of the cytoplasm.

prompt: Fluoroquinolone resistance frequently arises through point mutations in bacterial DNA gyrase (gyrA) and topoisomerase IV (parC).
explain: Target-site mutations in the quinolone resistance-determining regions (QRDR) prevent drug binding.

prompt: Bacterial transformation requires viable direct donor-to-recipient physical contact.
explain: Transformation is the uptake of free, naked environmental DNA; conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact.

prompt: Generalized transduction is mediated by lytic bacteriophages packaging random host bacterial DNA fragments.
explain: During lytic phage assembly, fragments of host chromosome are mistakenly packaged into phage heads and injected into recipient cells.

prompt: Specialized transduction transfers specific bacterial genes adjacent to the prophage integration site in temperate phages.
explain: Imprecise excision of a lysogenic prophage (e.g., lambda phage) carries flanking bacterial genes into new host cells.

prompt: Transposons can jump between bacterial chromosomes and plasmids, facilitating the spread of multi-drug resistance.
explain: Transposable genetic elements ("jumping genes") encode transposases that excise and insert resistance genes across replicons.

prompt: Clostridioides difficile spores are resistant to alcohol-based hand sanitizers and require soap and water washing for physical removal.
explain: Bacterial endospores resist alcohol hand rubs; mechanical friction with soap and water is mandatory to rinse them away.

prompt: Helicobacter pylori colonization is strongly associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma.
explain: Chronic H. pylori gastritis causes mucosal atrophy/dysplasia predisposing to adenocarcinoma, while antigenic drive fuels clonal B-cell MALT lymphoma.

prompt: Treponema pallidum cannot be visualized by standard light microscopy and requires darkfield microscopy or silver staining.
explain: Treponemes have a very narrow diameter (0.15 um) below the resolving power of brightfield light microscopy.

prompt: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD).
explain: EBV latency programs drive B-cell and epithelial transformation, predisposing to these malignancies.

prompt: Echinococcus granulosus causes large hydatid cysts with "hydatid sand" in the liver that can cause fatal anaphylaxis if ruptured during surgery.
explain: Hydatid cyst fluid contains highly antigenic larval proteins; spillage during surgical resection triggers life-threatening anaphylactic shock.

prompt: Bartonella henselae infection causes cat scratch disease in immunocompetent individuals and bacillary angiomatosis in AIDS patients.
explain: Bartonella henselae causes self-limited regional lymphadenopathy in healthy hosts and vascular proliferative bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised AIDS patients.

prompt: Pasteurella multocida is a common cause of rapidly progressive soft tissue cellulitis following domestic cat or dog bites.
explain: Pasteurella is part of normal animal oral flora, causing acute erythema, swelling, and purulence within 24 hours of bite injury.

prompt: Rabies virus exhibits an exceptionally short incubation period of under 24 hours, precluding post-exposure vaccination.
explain: Rabies travels slowly along peripheral axons, typically incubating over 1 to 3 months; this long delay allows post-exposure active vaccination and immune globulin to prevent clinical disease.

prompt: Malassezia furfur causes tinea versicolor and requires lipid supplementation to grow in laboratory culture.
explain: Malassezia is a lipophilic yeast that depends on exogenous fatty acids for growth, requiring olive oil overlay on agar.

prompt: Trichomonas vaginalis exists in both an active motile trophozoite stage and an environmentally hardy cyst stage.
explain: Trichomonas vaginalis possesses only a motile flagellated trophozoite stage and completely lacks a cyst form, necessitating direct sexual transmission.

prompt: Arrange the sequential biochemical steps of the classic Gram staining procedure in order:
items: Application of primary crystal violet stain to the heat-fixed bacterial smear
Application of Gram iodine as a mordant to form insoluble crystal violet-iodine complexes
Decolorization with acetone or 95% ethanol to extract lipid from gram-negative outer membranes
Application of safranin counterstain to color decolorized gram-negative cells pink
Microscopic examination: Gram-positives appear purple and gram-negatives appear pink/red
explain: Gram staining proceeds from crystal violet to iodine mordant, alcohol decolorization, and safranin counterstaining.

prompt: Order the sequential steps of the Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast staining protocol for mycobacteria:
items: Application of primary carbolfuchsin stain containing phenol to penetrate waxy mycolic acids
Application of heat to facilitate dye penetration into the lipid-rich mycobacterial cell wall
Decolorization with acid-alcohol solution (3% HCl in 95% ethanol)
Application of methylene blue counterstain to color non-acid-fast background material blue
Microscopic evaluation: Acid-fast bacilli retain bright red/pink carbolfuchsin against a blue background
explain: Ziehl-Neelsen uses carbolfuchsin with heat, followed by acid-alcohol decolorization and methylene blue counterstaining.

prompt: Arrange the sequential steps of the HIV-1 replication lifecycle from viral attachment to budding:
items: gp120 binds host CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4 coreceptors, triggering gp41-mediated membrane fusion
Uncoating and reverse transcription of viral genomic RNA into double-stranded complementary DNA
Translocation of cDNA into the nucleus and integration into host genome via viral integrase
Transcription of proviral DNA by host RNA polymerase II into viral mRNAs and genomic RNA
Assembly at host plasma membrane, budding, and proteolytic cleavage into mature virions by viral protease
explain: HIV attaches/fuses, reverse transcribes, integrates proviral cDNA, transcribes viral mRNA, and matures via protease cleavage.

prompt: Order the sequential stages of Influenza A infection and cellular processing:
items: Hemagglutinin binding to sialic acid residues on host respiratory epithelial surface
Receptor-mediated endocytosis of the intact virion into host endosomes
Acidification of endosome opening M2 proton channels and triggering nucleocapsid uncoating
Nuclear import of segmented negative-sense viral RNA and cap-snatching transcription
Budding from host membrane and neuraminidase-mediated cleavage of sialic acid to release virions
explain: Influenza binds via HA, enters by endocytosis, uncoats via M2 proton channels, replicates in the nucleus, and releases via NA.

prompt: Arrange the progressive clinical stages of untreated Treponema pallidum (Syphilis) infection:
items: Primary syphilis: Solitary painless indurated chancre at site of inoculation resolving in 3-6 weeks
Secondary syphilis: Disseminated maculopapular rash on palms/soles, condyloma lata, and lymphadenopathy
Early and late latent syphilis: Seropositive asymptomatic dormancy lasting years to decades
Tertiary syphilis: Destructive gummatous necrosis of skin/bone and ascending syphilitic aortitis
Neurosyphilis: Tabes dorsalis (posterior column degeneration) and general paresis with Argyll Robertson pupils
explain: Syphilis progresses from primary chancre to secondary bacteremic rash, latent dormancy, and tertiary gummas/neurosyphilis.

prompt: Order the chronological stages of untreated Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi infection):
items: Stage 1 (Early localized): Expanding erythema migrans targetoid rash accompanied by flu-like symptoms (days)
Stage 2 (Early disseminated): Multiple secondary annular lesions and transient migratory arthralgias (weeks)
Stage 2 (Carditis & Neuroborreliosis): Atrioventricular conduction blocks and bilateral cranial nerve VII (facial) palsy
Stage 3 (Late disseminated): Chronic asymmetrical oligoarthritis, typically involving the knee joint (months to years)
Stage 3 (Late chronic encephalopathy): Subacute cognitive dysfunction and peripheral polyneuropathy
explain: Lyme disease begins with erythema migrans, disseminates to AV blocks/Bilateral Bell palsy, and culminates in chronic knee arthritis.

prompt: Arrange the sequential steps in the Plasmodium falciparum malaria lifecycle within the human host:
items: Inoculation of motile sporozoites into subcutaneous tissue by biting female Anopheles mosquito
Migration through bloodstream to hepatocytes and exoerythrocytic schizogony (asymptomatic liver stage)
Rupture of mature hepatic schizonts releasing thousands of merozoites into circulating blood
Erythrocytic invasion, trophozoite ring-form development, and schizont formation causing red cell lysis
Differentiation of a subpopulation of merozoites into sexual micro- and macrogametocytes
explain: Sporozoites invade hepatocytes, hepatic schizonts release merozoites into erythrocytes, and repeating RBC lysis causes malaria paroxysms.

prompt: Order the developmental migration of Ascaris lumbricoides within the human body following egg ingestion:
items: Ingestion of embryonated eggs from fecally contaminated soil or unwashed food
Hatching of rhabditiform larvae in the duodenum and penetration of the intestinal wall
Migration via mesenteric venules into the portal vein, inferior vena cava, and right heart
Sequestration in pulmonary capillaries, alveolar penetration, and bronchial ascent (Loeffler syndrome)
Swallowing of coughed-up larvae down the esophagus into the small intestine where adults mature
explain: Ascaris eggs hatch in the gut, larvae migrate through the portal blood to lungs, ascend the trachea, are swallowed, and mature in the intestine.

prompt: Arrange the lifecycle steps of Schistosoma mansoni from freshwater cercaria to adult intravascular pairing:
items: Free-swimming fork-tailed cercariae penetrate intact human skin during freshwater contact
Shedding of tail to form schistosomulae and entry into cutaneous venules
Passage through venous circulation, right heart, and lungs into systemic arterial circulation
Maturation and pairing of adult male and female flukes in the intrahepatic portal veins
Retrograde migration of paired adults to mesenteric venules to lay eggs causing pipe-stem fibrosis
explain: Cercariae penetrate skin, migrate through lungs to liver, pair up, and settle in mesenteric venules to deposit fibrogenic eggs.

prompt: Order the pathophysiological sequence of Clostridioides difficile colitis following antibiotic exposure:
items: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy disrupts normal gut colonic anaerobic microflora
Ingested C. difficile endospores germinate into vegetative bacilli in the colonic lumen
Production and luminal secretion of large clostridial exotoxins Toxin A (enterotoxin) and Toxin B (cytotoxin)
Toxin-mediated glucosylation of host Rho GTPases, causing enterocyte cytoskeletal collapse and apoptosis
Formation of mucosal pseudomembranes composed of fibrin, mucin, necrotic enterocytes, and neutrophils
explain: Antibiotics deplete competing flora, allowing C. difficile germination, toxin A/B release, enterocyte death, and pseudomembranes.

prompt: Arrange the sequence of events during Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi enteric fever pathogenesis:
