items: Oral ingestion of contaminated food/water and invasion of ileal mucosal M cells in Peyer patches
Phagocytosis by intestinal macrophages and survival within unacidified phagosomes
Dissemination via mesenteric lymph nodes into the bloodstream producing transient primary bacteremia
Colonization and multiplication within the reticuloendothelial system (liver, spleen, bone marrow)
Secondary bacteremia with step-ladder fevers, faint salmon-colored rose spots, and biliary seeding
explain: S. Typhi invades Peyer patches, survives in macrophages, enters primary bacteremia, multiplies in RES, and causes secondary bacteremia.

prompt: Order the sequential stages of primary pulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection:
items: Inhalation of infectious droplet nuclei into the mid-to-lower lung zones
Phagocytosis of mycobacteria by alveolar macrophages with inhibition of phagolysosome fusion
Bacterial replication triggering dendritic cell migration to regional hilar lymph nodes
Activation of CD4+ TH1 cells and secretion of interferon-gamma to activate macrophages (2-3 weeks)
Formation of a fibrocaseous Ghon complex (peripheral subpleural lung focus plus calcified hilar lymph node)
explain: Inhaled M. tuberculosis replicates in macrophages, stimulates TH1 cells to secrete IFN-gamma, and forms a calcified Ghon complex.

prompt: Arrange the clinical and immunological sequence of Hepatitis B virus infection following acute transmission:
items: Appearance of Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) as the first serological marker in blood
Appearance of Hepatitis B envelope antigen (HBeAg) and HBV DNA indicating active high replication
Development of anti-HBc IgM antibodies marking acute clinical phase with elevated transaminases
Disappearance of HBsAg followed by the "window period" before anti-HBs becomes detectable
Appearance of protective anti-HBs antibodies alongside anti-HBc IgG indicating resolved natural infection
explain: HBsAg and HBeAg rise first, followed by anti-HBc IgM, the window period, and permanent recovery with anti-HBs and anti-HBc IgG.

prompt: Order the sequential events in F-plasmid mediated bacterial conjugation:
items: Donor (F+) bacterium extends sex pilus and makes physical contact with recipient (F-) bacterium
Retraction of pilus draws bacterial membranes into close contact to form a stable mating bridge
Relaxosome enzyme nicks a single strand of the circular F plasmid at the origin of transfer (oriT)
Rolling circle replication feeds the single-stranded nicked DNA across the bridge into recipient
Complementary strand synthesis occurs in both donor and recipient, converting recipient into an F+ cell
explain: Conjugation requires pilus contact, membrane bridge formation, relaxosome nicking, rolling circle transfer, and conversion to F+.

prompt: Arrange the sequence of events in Bacillus anthracis cutaneous anthrax development:
items: Inoculation of anthrax endospores from animal hides or wool into a microscopic cutaneous abrasion
Germination of dormant spores into vegetative encapsulated bacilli within dermal tissue
Secretion of tripartite toxin: Protective antigen (PA), lethal factor (LF), and edema factor (EF)
Development of an initial painless, pruritic papule that rapidly progresses to a vesicle with surrounding gelatinous edema
Central vesicular rupture and ulceration yielding a pathognomonic painless black necrotic eschar
explain: Spores enter skin, germinate, release edema and lethal toxins, forming an edematous vesicle that ruptures into a black eschar.

prompt: Order the sequence of pathophysiological events in Clostridium tetani intoxication:
items: Spore contamination of a deep puncture wound creating a localized anaerobic necrotic environment
Germination of spores and local elaboration of zinc metalloprotease toxin tetanospasmin
Retrograde intra-axonal transport of tetanospasmin along lower motor neurons to the spinal cord
Trans-synaptic entry into inhibitory interneurons and enzymatic cleavage of synaptobrevin (VAMP)
Blockade of GABA and glycine exocytosis producing uninhibited alpha-motor neuron firing and spastic paralysis
explain: Tetanus spores germinate in wounds, tetanospasmin travels retrograde to spinal interneurons, cleaves synaptobrevin, and blocks GABA/glycine.

prompt: Arrange the steps in the pathogenesis of Bordetella pertussis from colonization to paroxysmal cough:
items: Inhalation of infectious respiratory droplets and attachment to ciliated respiratory epithelium via filamentous hemagglutinin
Secretion of tracheal cytotoxin, which paralyzes and destroys ciliated bronchial epithelial cells
Secretion of pertussis toxin, which ADP-ribosylates Gi alpha, keeping adenylate cyclase constitutively active
Catarrhal stage (1-2 weeks): Low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and highly contagious mild coughing
Paroxysmal stage (2-6 weeks): Severe bouts of coughing with classic inspiratory "whoop" and post-tussive emesis
explain: Pertussis attaches via FHA, destroys cilia via tracheal cytotoxin, paralyzes Gi via pertussis toxin, and causes whooping cough.

prompt: Order the clinical and morphological progression of Sporothrix schenckii lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis:
items: Traumatic inoculation of fungal conidia or hyphae into the dermis via a contaminated rose thorn or splinter
Transformation of inoculated mycelium into cigar-shaped budding yeast cells at body temperature (37°C)
Formation of a primary painless erythematous papule or nodule at the puncture site several weeks later
Ulceration of the primary lesion into an indolent draining chancre-like ulcer
Proximal spread of secondary subcutaneous nodules along the regional lymphatic drainage tract
explain: Rose thorn prick inoculates Sporothrix, which transforms into yeast, forms a primary ulcer, and ascends lymphatic channels.

prompt: Arrange the sequential steps in the transmission and lifecycle of Taenia solium causing Neurocysticercosis:
items: Ingestion of food or water contaminated with Taenia solium eggs shed in the feces of an adult tapeworm carrier
Gastric acid and intestinal enzymes dissolve egg shell, liberating microscopic oncospheres
Oncospheres actively penetrate the intestinal mucosa and enter mesenteric blood vessels
Hematogenous dissemination to the brain, skeletal muscle, and eyes
Encystment into fluid-filled cysticercus larvae in the brain parenchyma triggering seizures upon larval degeneration
explain: Fecal-oral egg ingestion liberates oncospheres, which penetrate the gut and encyst in the brain as neurocysticercosis.

prompt: Order the chronological clinical progression of Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) from primary infection to reactivation:
items: Inhalation of respiratory droplets and primary replication in nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue
Viremia with widespread dissemination to the skin, causing vesicular chickenpox rash in "different stages of healing"
Retrograde axonal transport of viral particles from cutaneous lesions to dorsal root and trigeminal sensory ganglia
Establishment of lifelong viral latency within sensory neurons without active replication
Reactivation decades later during waning cell-mediated immunity, migrating anterograde as a painful dermatomal shingles rash
explain: VZV causes chickenpox, ascends sensory nerves to establish dorsal root ganglion latency, and reactivates as dermatomal herpes zoster.

prompt: Arrange the sequential stages of Rabies virus infection from animal bite to encephalitic death:
items: Inoculation of rabies virions into skeletal muscle via the bite of an infected rabid animal (e.g., bat, dog)
Local viral replication in myocytes and binding to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions
Retrograde axoplasmic transport along peripheral motor neurons at 50-100 mm/day toward the spinal cord
Ascent through spinal cord and rapid replication within brainstem, hippocampus, and Purkinje cells (Negri bodies)
Anterograde centrifugal spread along autonomic nerves to salivary glands, cornea, and skin with terminal hydrophobia and coma
explain: Rabies replicates in muscle, enters motor nerves at ACh receptors, travels retrograde to the brain, forms Negri bodies, and causes fatal encephalitis.

prompt: Order the pathophysiological events in Staphylococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS):
items: Vaginal colonization by S. aureus in the presence of a superabsorbent tampon or surgical wound
Synthesis and secretion of Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1)
Systemic absorption of TSST-1 into circulating blood without bacterial bacteremia
TSST-1 crosslinks MHC class II molecules directly to V-beta domains of T-cell receptors without antigen processing
Massive polyclonal activation of up to 20% of all T cells, unleashing a cytokine storm (IL-1, IL-2, TNF) and shock
explain: TSST-1 superantigen crosslinks MHC II and TCR V-beta, activating 20% of T cells and causing a massive cytokine storm and shock.

prompt: Arrange the migration and developmental steps of Hookworms (Necator americanus / Ancylostoma duodenale):
items: Infective filariform larvae in warm, moist soil penetrate bare human foot skin
Larvae enter venous circulation and travel to pulmonary capillaries
Larvae break into alveolar airspaces, ascend the tracheobronchial tree, and are swallowed
Adult worms attach to mucosal villi of the jejunum via cutting plates or teeth
Chronic sucking of intestinal blood and secretion of anticoagulants leading to severe microcytic iron deficiency anemia
explain: Hookworm larvae penetrate bare feet, migrate through lungs, are swallowed, and bite jejunal villi to cause iron deficiency anemia.

prompt: Order the stages of Helicobacter pylori-induced gastric mucosal disease from colonization to peptic ulcer:
items: Motile flagellar movement through gastric mucus layer toward surface foveolar epithelium
Urease activity produces an alkaline ammonia cloud that neutralizes local gastric acid
Bacterial BabA and SabA adhesins attach tightly to Lewis antigens on gastric epithelial cells
CagA and VacA virulence factors induce host IL-8 secretion and severe mucosal neutrophil infiltration
Chronic active antral gastritis increases gastrin secretion and acid output, eroding duodenal mucosa into an ulcer
explain: H. pylori uses flagella and urease to survive, adhesins to attach, and CagA/VacA to trigger inflammation and ulceration.

prompt: Arrange the sequence of events in Neisseria meningitidis invasive meningococcemia:
items: Nasopharyngeal colonization and adherence to non-ciliated epithelial cells via type IV pili
Transcytosis across mucosal barrier into subepithelial capillaries and entry into bloodstream
Circulating survival mediated by antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule and factor H binding protein
Rapid shedding of lipooligosaccharide (LOS) blebs triggering widespread endothelial damage and DIC
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhagic infarction (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), purpura fulminans, and shock
explain: Meningococcus crosses mucosa, survives via capsule, sheds LOS endotoxin, and causes purpura fulminans and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

prompt: Order the clinical phases of Dengue virus infection from mosquito bite to severe dengue:
items: Transmission of Dengue virus by the bite of an infected female Aedes aegypti mosquito
Febrile phase: Sudden onset high fever, severe retro-orbital headache, and "breakbone" musculoskeletal pain (days 1-3)
Critical phase: Defervescence accompanied by massive plasma leakage, pleural effusions, and ascites (days 3-7)
Thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy progressing to Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever and Dengue Shock Syndrome
Convalescent phase: Resorption of extravasated fluid, stabilization of vital signs, and recovery rash
explain: Dengue progresses from mosquito inoculation to febrile breakbone pain, critical plasma leakage/shock, and convalescence.

prompt: Arrange the pathogenesis steps of Rhinocerebral Mucormycosis in a patient with Diabetic Ketoacidosis:
items: Inhalation of environmental sporangiospores of Rhizopus or Mucor into the paranasal sinuses
Acidotic and hyperglycemic conditions allow fungal utilization of free serum iron via rhizopus ketoreductase
Germination into broad, non-septate hyphae branching at wide right angles (90 degrees)
Direct angioinvasion through blood vessel walls, internal elastic lamina, and cribriform plate
Extensive ischemic necrosis of the palate, orbit, and cavernous sinus, producing a black necrotic eschar
explain: DKA facilitates Mucor germination; hyphae invade vessels and cribriform plate, causing fatal rhinocerebral necrosis.

prompt: Order the steps of Listeria monocytogenes intracellular survival and cell-to-cell spread:
items: InlA and InlB internalins bind host E-cadherin and Met receptors, triggering receptor-mediated endocytosis
Secretion of pore-forming toxin listeriolysin O (LLO) and phospholipases to lyse the phagolysosomal membrane
Escape into host cell cytoplasm and rapid nutrient acquisition and replication
ActA surface protein recruits host Arp2/3 complex to polymerize host actin into an "actin rocket" tail
Propulsion into adjacent cell membrane forming a double-membrane pseudopod that is engulfed by the neighbor
explain: Listeria enters via internalins, escapes vacuoles with LLO, replicates, polymerizes actin rockets with ActA, and spreads cell-to-cell.

prompt: Arrange the diagnostic evaluation sequence for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis:
items: Collection of three consecutive early morning sputum specimens at least 8 hours apart
Immediate Ziehl-Neelsen or fluorochrome auramine-rhodamine acid-fast smear microscopy
Rapid nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT / GeneXpert MTB/RIF) to detect M. tuberculosis and rifampin resistance
Inoculation onto liquid broth medium (MGIT) and solid Löwenstein-Jensen egg-based agar
Confirmation of growth and phenotypic automated antimicrobial susceptibility testing (2-6 weeks)
explain: TB workup requires 3 sputum samples, AFB microscopy, rapid GeneXpert NAAT, and liquid/solid LJ culture with susceptibility.

prompt: Order the developmental lifecycle of Toxoplasma gondii during congenital transmission:
items: Primary infection of a non-immune pregnant mother via ingestion of undercooked cyst-laden meat or cat oocysts
Tachyzoites disseminate hematogenously and infect maternal syncytiotrophoblasts in the placenta
Transplacental crossing of rapidly replicating tachyzoites into the fetal circulation
Invasion of fetal brain parenchyma, ventricular ependyma, and developing retina
Development of classic congenital triad: Chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications
explain: Maternal primary infection leads to parasitemia, placental crossing, fetal CNS invasion, and the congenital triad.

prompt: Match each gram-positive coccus to its primary diagnostic microbiological hallmark:
explain: Classical diagnostic algorithms differentiate staphylococci and streptococci using coagulase, novobiocin, bacitracin, and optochin.

prompt: Match each gram-positive rod to its hallmark disease or clinical feature:
pairs: Poly-D-glutamate capsule and black necrotic eschar
Tetanospasmin blocking GABA/glycine with spastic paralysis
Preformed neurotoxin blocking ACh with flaccid paralysis
explain: Gram-positive bacilli produce distinctive potent exotoxins or possess unique structural adaptations.

prompt: Match each gram-negative rod to its definitive growth characteristic or biochemical test:
pairs: Lactose fermenter (pink on MacConkey) and indole-positive
Mucoid lactose fermenter with thick polysaccharide capsule
Urease-positive with swarming motility on agar
explain: Gram-negative bacilli are classified by lactose fermentation, oxidase, urease, and temperature preferences.

prompt: Match each bacterial exotoxin to its exact intracellular molecular mechanism:
pairs: Permanently activates Gs alpha via ADP-ribosylation, elevating cAMP
Inactivates Gi alpha via ADP-ribosylation, preventing cAMP inhibition

Internal autoinfection cycle leading to hyperinfection in steroids
Periorbital edema, myalgias, and encysted larvae in striated muscle

explain: Bacterial resistance operates via target modification, enzymatic inactivation, or target bypass.

Buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar with iron and cysteine
explain: Fastidious microorganisms require unique growth factors, blood products, or selective antibiotics.

Antiphagocytic surface protein and driver of rheumatic molecular mimicry

Antiphagocytic polysaccharide shield preventing C3b opsonization
Endotoxin triggering severe capillary leak, DIC, and shock

Dog and cat oral flora causing rapid cellulitis following bites

Rabbits, rodents, and ticks (tularemia ulceroglandular disease)
Rodents and prairie dogs via Xenopsylla flea bites (plague)

Bunyavirus from deer mouse feces causing acute pulmonary syndrome

prompt: What optimal incubation temperature in degrees Celsius is used to demonstrate characteristic "tumbling motility" in Listeria monocytogenes?
explain: Listeria exhibits tumbling motility at room temperature (20-25°C), which is downregulated at 37°C.

prompt: What optimal incubation temperature in degrees Celsius is used on Skirrow agar to select for Campylobacter jejuni over other enteric bacteria?
explain: Campylobacter jejuni is thermophilic and grows optimally at 42°C, suppressing commensal bowel flora.

prompt: What concentration percentage of sodium chloride (NaCl) in broth is tolerated by Enterococcus faecalis for diagnostic growth?
explain: Enterococci grow readily in 6.5% NaCl broth, differentiating them from non-enterococcal group D streptococci.

prompt: How many base pairs are contained in the standard deletion responsible for the protective human CCR5-delta-32 mutation that confers resistance to HIV-1?
explain: A 32-base-pair deletion in the CCR5 gene causes a frameshift resulting in non-functional coreceptors.

prompt: How many distinct RNA genome segments are contained within the Influenza A virus nucleocapsid?
explain: Influenza A and B viruses possess 8 distinct negative-sense single-stranded RNA segments.

prompt: How many double-stranded RNA genome segments are contained within the human Rotavirus capsid?
explain: Rotaviruses possess an 11-segmented double-stranded RNA genome.

prompt: What is the minimum infectious dose (approximate number of organisms) required to cause clinical bacillary dysentery in Shigella dysenteriae?
explain: Shigella is extremely acid-resistant; as few as 10 to 100 viable organisms can establish infection.

prompt: What minimum infectious dose in organisms is typically required for Salmonella enterica serovars to overcome the gastric acid barrier?
explain: Salmonella is acid-labile and generally requires >100,000 organisms to establish enteric disease.

prompt: What minimum bacterial colony forming units (CFU) per milliliter in clean-catch midstream urine defines significant bacteriuria in acute cystitis?
explain: Classic diagnostic criteria define significant bacteriuria as >=10^5 CFU/mL in asymptomatic or symptomatic patients.

prompt: How many days is the typical average incubation period for acute Hepatitis B virus infection from exposure to clinical symptoms?
explain: The incubation period for Hepatitis B ranges from 30 to 180 days, averaging approximately 90 days (3 months).

prompt: How many days is the typical average incubation period for acute Hepatitis A virus infection?
explain: Hepatitis A has an incubation period of 15 to 50 days, with a median of approximately 28 days (4 weeks).

prompt: How many days is the typical incubation period of the common cold caused by Rhinovirus?
explain: Rhinovirus has a short incubation period averaging 1 to 3 days (typically ~2 days).

prompt: Within how many hours of symptom onset must neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir) be initiated to provide significant clinical benefit in acute influenza?
explain: Antivirals for influenza are most effective when started within 48 hours of initial symptom onset.

prompt: Within how many hours of high-risk occupational HIV exposure must post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) be initiated for maximum efficacy?
explain: PEP should be initiated as soon as possible and strictly within 72 hours of exposure for 28 days.

prompt: What CD4+ T-cell count threshold per microliter defines stage 3 HIV infection (clinical AIDS)?
explain: A CD4+ T-lymphocyte count falling below 200 cells/mcL defines progression to clinical AIDS.

prompt: At what CD4+ T-cell count threshold per microliter is daily azithromycin prophylaxis initiated to prevent Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) in advanced AIDS?
explain: MAC prophylaxis is historically recommended when the CD4 count falls below 50 cells/mcL.

prompt: At what CD4+ count per microliter is primary trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis initiated to prevent Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis in seropositive HIV patients?
explain: Toxoplasma encephalitis prophylaxis is indicated when CD4 drops below 100 cells/mcL.

prompt: At what induration diameter in millimeters is a tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test considered positive in an HIV-infected individual?
explain: In immunocompromised patients (HIV, organ transplants), an induration >=5 mm is considered positive.

prompt: At what induration diameter in millimeters is a PPD skin test considered positive in healthcare workers and immigrants from high-prevalence countries?
explain: Healthcare personnel and residents from endemic regions are considered positive at >=10 mm induration.

prompt: At what induration diameter in millimeters is a PPD skin test considered positive in a healthy individual with zero known TB risk factors?
explain: Individuals with no known risk factors require >=15 mm of induration to be considered positive.

prompt: What angle in degrees defines the classical dichotomous hyphal branching pattern of Aspergillus species on histopathology?
explain: Aspergillus displays acute-angle branching characteristically at approximately 45 degrees.

prompt: What angle in degrees defines the wide branching pattern of Mucor and Rhizopus species hyphae on tissue biopsy?
explain: Mucorales exhibit broad, non-septate hyphae branching at wide angles of approximately 90 degrees.

prompt: What is the diameter in micrometers of a typical oval intracellular Histoplasma capsulatum yeast cell inside a macrophage?
explain: Histoplasma yeast cells are small, measuring 2 to 4 micrometers (average ~3 um).

prompt: What is the average diameter in micrometers of a mature Coccidioides immitis thick-walled spherule in pulmonary tissue?
explain: Coccidioides spherules range from 20 to 60 micrometers (average ~40 um), filled with endospores.

prompt: How many days after initial Treponema pallidum inoculation does a primary syphilitic chancre typically manifest?
explain: The incubation period for primary syphilis ranges from 10 to 90 days, averaging approximately 21 days (3 weeks).

prompt: How many weeks after primary infection does disseminated secondary syphilis typically appear?
explain: Secondary syphilis develops approximately 6 to 12 weeks (average ~8 weeks) after the primary chancre.

prompt: Within how many hours of initiating penicillin treatment for secondary syphilis does the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction typically begin?
explain: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction typically begins 1 to 2 hours after the first penicillin dose.

prompt: How many hours is the typical febrile paroxysm cycle interval in tertian malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale?
explain: P. vivax and P. ovale exhibit a 48-hour (tertian) erythrocyte cycle.

prompt: How many hours is the febrile paroxysm cycle interval in quartan malaria caused by Plasmodium malariae?
explain: Plasmodium malariae produces a 72-hour (quartan) fever cycle.

prompt: What maximum length in meters can an adult Diphyllobothrium latum tapeworm reach inside the human small intestine?
explain: Diphyllobothrium latum is the largest human tapeworm, routinely growing to 10 meters (over 30 feet).

prompt: How many pairs of flagella are present on a mature Giardia duodenalis trophozoite?
explain: Giardia trophozoites possess 4 pairs of flagella (8 flagella total) conferring their tumbling motility.

prompt: How many nuclei are present inside a mature infectious Entamoeba histolytica cyst passed in human feces?
explain: Mature infectious E. histolytica cysts contain exactly 4 nuclei and elongated chromatoid bars.

prompt: How many nuclei are present inside a mature Giardia duodenalis cyst?
explain: Mature Giardia cysts contain 4 nuclei, while active vegetative trophozoites contain 2 nuclei.

prompt: How many pairs of suction hooks are present on the scolex of Taenia solium?
explain: Taenia solium possesses a rostellum with 2 rows of hooks alongside 4 large suckers.

prompt: What sedimentation coefficient in Svedberg units characterizes the complete intact bacterial ribosome?
explain: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, composed of a 30S small subunit and a 50S large subunit.

prompt: What sedimentation coefficient in Svedberg units characterizes the small bacterial ribosomal subunit targeted by aminoglycosides?
explain: The bacterial small subunit is 30S, containing 16S rRNA.

prompt: What sedimentation coefficient in Svedberg units characterizes the large bacterial ribosomal subunit targeted by macrolides?
explain: The bacterial large subunit is 50S, containing 23S and 5S rRNAs.

prompt: What Svedberg unit characterizes the eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosome?
explain: Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, composed of 40S and 60S subunits.

prompt: What Svedberg unit characterizes the bacterial ribosomal RNA targeted by DNA sequencing for species identification?
explain: 16S rRNA sequencing is the gold standard molecular fingerprint for bacterial taxonomy.

prompt: By what approximate factor does the substitution of D-Ala-D-Lac for D-Ala-D-Ala in VRE decrease vancomycin binding affinity?
explain: The loss of a critical hydrogen bond decreases vancomycin binding affinity by approximately 1,000-fold.

prompt: What percentage of adults infected acutely with Hepatitis B virus successfully clear the virus spontaneously without developing chronic hepatitis?
explain: Approximately 95% of immunocompetent adults clear acute HBV, whereas >90% of perinatally infected neonates develop chronic infection.

prompt: What percentage of neonates vertically infected with Hepatitis B virus develop chronic persistent infection?
explain: Due to immune tolerance, approximately 90% of neonates infected at birth become chronic carriers.

prompt: What percentage of adults infected with Hepatitis C virus fail to clear the virus and progress to chronic hepatitis?
explain: Approximately 75 to 85% (average ~80%) of individuals infected with HCV develop chronic persistent infection.

prompt: How many days of isolation are historically recommended following the onset of parotitis in mumps to prevent secondary spread?
explain: CDC guidelines recommend droplet isolation for 5 days after parotid gland swelling begins.

prompt: How many weeks of post-exposure antiretroviral prophylaxis (PEP) are standardly prescribed following occupational HIV exposure?
explain: Standard HIV PEP duration is exactly 28 days (4 weeks) of three-drug antiretroviral therapy.

prompt: How many viral genes are encoded within the HIV-1 genome?
explain: HIV-1 encodes 9 genes: gag, pol, env, tat, rev, nef, vif, vpr, and vpu.

prompt: How many serotypes of Poliovirus exist worldwide (Type 1, 2, and 3)?
explain: Poliovirus exists as exactly 3 serotypes: Mahoney (type 1), Lansing (type 2), and Leon (type 3).

prompt: How many serotypes of Dengue virus exist that can cause severe secondary infection via antibody-dependent enhancement?
explain: Dengue virus exists as 4 distinct serotypes (DENV-1 through DENV-4).

prompt: How many copies of genomic RNA are packaged inside a single mature HIV-1 retrovirus particle?
explain: HIV-1 is a diploid retrovirus containing exactly two identical positive-sense single-stranded RNA molecules.

prompt: At what gestational age in weeks is routine universal screening for gestational diabetes mellitus performed using a 50-g oral glucose challenge test?
explain: Universal screening for gestational diabetes is routinely performed at 24-28 weeks gestation when human placental lactogen levels peak.

prompt: What is the recommended dose of folic acid for a low-risk pregnant woman started at least 1 month prior to conception to prevent neural tube defects?
explain: 0.4 mg (400 mcg) daily is standard for low-risk women; 4 mg daily is reserved for women with a prior neural tube defect-affected pregnancy.

prompt: Which diagnostic criterion differentiates preeclampsia with severe features from preeclampsia without severe features?
choices: Blood pressure >= 160/110 mmHg, platelets < 100,000/µL, or elevated transaminases
Mild ankle edema in late pregnancy
explain: Severe features include BP >= 160/110, thrombocytopenia, doubling of liver enzymes, severe RUQ pain, creatinine > 1.1, or pulmonary edema.

prompt: What is the first-line intravenous medication for seizure prophylaxis in women with severe preeclampsia or eclampsia?
explain: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for eclamptic seizure prevention and treatment.

prompt: What is the specific antidote for magnesium toxicity manifesting with loss of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression?
explain: 10% calcium gluconate (1 g IV over 3-5 minutes) rapidly antagonizes the neuromuscular effects of hypermagnesemia.

prompt: Which condition presents in the third trimester with sudden-onset painful vaginal bleeding, uterine hypertonicity, and fetal distress?
explain: Placental abruption classically causes painful third-trimester bleeding with a tense, tender uterus.

prompt: Which condition is characterized by painless, bright red third-trimester vaginal bleeding in a patient with a low-lying placenta covering the internal cervical os?
explain: Placenta previa presents with painless vaginal bleeding; digital vaginal exam is strictly contraindicated until location is confirmed by ultrasound.

prompt: What is the most common cause of primary postpartum hemorrhage occurring within 24 hours of delivery?
explain: Uterine atony ('Tone') accounts for 70-80% of all primary postpartum hemorrhages.

prompt: What is the initial medication of choice for active management of third stage of labor and treatment of uterine atony?
explain: Oxytocin infusion is the first-line uterotonic agent for prevention and management of uterine atony.

prompt: Which uterotonic drug is contraindicated in a patient with preeclampsia or chronic hypertension due to risk of stroke?
explain: Methylergonovine produces generalized vasoconstriction and is contraindicated in hypertensive disorders.

prompt: Which uterotonic agent is contraindicated in a postpartum patient with active asthma?
explain: Carboprost stimulates prostaglandin F2-alpha receptors, provoking bronchoconstriction; it is contraindicated in asthma.

prompt: What is the most common anatomical site of an ectopic pregnancy?
explain: Over 70-80% of tubal ectopic pregnancies occur in the ampullary portion of the fallopian tube.

prompt: What is the initial diagnostic test of choice when evaluating suspected ectopic pregnancy in an early pregnant patient?
explain: Transvaginal sonography combined with serial quantitative serum beta-hCG is the gold standard diagnostic algorithm.

prompt: What is the discriminatory zone of serum beta-hCG (in mIU/mL) above which an intrauterine gestational sac should reliably be seen on transvaginal ultrasound?
explain: At a beta-hCG between 1,500 and 2,000 mIU/mL, transvaginal ultrasound should visualize an intrauterine gestational sac; absence strongly suggests ectopic pregnancy.

prompt: Which medical agent is first-line for medical management of an unruptured ectopic pregnancy in a stable patient meeting eligibility criteria?
explain: Systemic intramuscular methotrexate (folate antagonist) is standard for hemodynamically stable patients with unruptured ectopic pregnancies.

prompt: When is anti-D immune globulin (RhoGAM) routinely administered to an Rh-negative, unsensitized pregnant woman?
choices: At 28 weeks and within 72 hours postpartum
At 12 weeks gestation only, at the dating scan
At 36 weeks gestation only, before labor
explain: Standard prophylaxis is 300 mcg at 28 weeks gestation and a second dose within 72 hours postpartum if the newborn is Rh-positive.

prompt: What screening test is universally performed at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks gestation to identify colonization that requires intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?
choices: Rectovaginal culture for Group B Streptococcus
Endocervical NAAT swab for Neisseria gonorrhoeae
explain: Universal rectovaginal swab culture at 35-37 weeks screens for GBS colonization.

prompt: What is the first-line intrapartum antibiotic of choice for maternal Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis during labor?
explain: IV penicillin G (5 million units initial dose, then 2.5-3.0 million units every 4 hours) is the preferred regimen.

prompt: What is the definition of the active phase of the first stage of labor according to contemporary ACOG/SMFM guidelines?
choices: Cervical dilation of 6 cm or more
explain: Active labor is modernly defined as starting at 6 cm dilation; dilation before 6 cm constitutes the latent phase.

prompt: Which clinical sign is characterized by bluish discoloration of the cervix and vagina visible on speculum exam in early pregnancy?
explain: Chadwick sign is violet-blue pelvic congestion of the cervix and vaginal mucosa caused by elevated local venous vascularity.

prompt: What is the classic diagnostic triad of symptoms in endometriosis?
choices: Menorrhagia, hot flashes, and weight gain
Pruritus vulvae, vaginal dryness, and hirsutism
explain: Endometriosis presents classically with cyclic pelvic pain (dysmenorrhea), deep dyspareunia, and subfertility.

prompt: What is the gold standard diagnostic method for confirming endometriosis and visualizing endometriotic implants?
explain: Diagnostic laparoscopy allows direct inspection of 'powder-burn' or 'chocolate' lesions and histological confirmation.

prompt: Which bacterial pathogen is the most common cause of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in sexually active young women?
explain: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the predominant sexually transmitted organisms initiating ascending PID.

prompt: What is the classic physical exam finding of 'strawberry cervix' (punctate cervical hemorrhages) pathognomonic for?
explain: Punctate cervical petechial microhemorrhages (strawberry cervix / colpitis macularis) are classic for Trichomonas.

prompt: What microscopic finding on saline wet mount confirms the diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis?
explain: Clue cells (squamous cells stippled with coccobacilli) are the hallmark microscopic feature of bacterial vaginosis.

prompt: What is the first-line oral pharmacological treatment for bacterial vaginosis in non-pregnant and pregnant patients?
choices: Oral Metronidazole (500 mg twice daily for 7 days)
explain: Oral metronidazole 500 mg BID for 7 days (or topical metronidazole/clindamycin) is first-line.

prompt: Which high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) genotypes are responsible for approximately 70% of invasive cervical cancers worldwide?
explain: High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 cause the overwhelming majority of cervical squamous carcinomas and adenocarcinomas.

prompt: What is the recommended screening cervical cytology (Pap smear) guideline for an average-risk woman aged 21 to 29 years?
choices: Cytology plus HPV co-testing every 5 years
explain: USPSTF guidelines recommend cervical cytology alone every 3 years for women aged 21-29; HPV co-testing is not recommended before age 30.

prompt: Which benign ovarian neoplasm is composed of tissues derived from all three germ cell layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm)?
explain: Mature cystic teratomas (dermoids) contain differentiated ectodermal (hair, sebaceous), mesodermal (bone, cartilage), and endodermal elements.

prompt: What is the most common cause of abnormal uterine bleeding in postmenopausal women that must be biopsied to rule out malignancy?
explain: Endometrial atrophy is the most frequent cause (60-80%), but postmenopausal bleeding is considered endometrial cancer until proven otherwise by endometrial biopsy.

prompt: What is the endometrial stripe thickness threshold on transvaginal ultrasound below which endometrial carcinoma is highly unlikely in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding?
explain: An endometrial thickness <= 4 mm on TVUS has >99% negative predictive value for endometrial cancer in postmenopausal bleeding.

prompt: Which condition is characterized by the classic Rotterdam criteria: hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound?
explain: Rotterdam consensus requires 2 of 3 features: oligo/anovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound.

prompt: What is the first-line oral medication for ovulation induction in anovulatory women with polycystic ovary syndrome seeking fertility?
explain: Letrozole produces higher live birth and ovulation rates compared to clomiphene in women with PCOS.

prompt: Which hormonal profile is characteristic of premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) in a female under 40 years of age?
choices: Elevated FSH, elevated LH, and low estradiol
Low FSH, low LH, and low estradiol
explain: Loss of ovarian follicular activity removes negative feedback, causing markedly elevated FSH/LH alongside depleted estradiol.

prompt: What is the classic diagnostic triad of symptoms in ectopic pregnancy?
choices: Unilateral pelvic pain, amenorrhea, and abnormal vaginal bleeding
High fever, foul lochia, and uterine tenderness
Severe bilateral leg edema, hyperreflexia, and scotoma
Painless gross hematuria, flank mass, and weight loss
explain: The triad of missed period, unilateral lower abdominal pain, and spotting warrants prompt ectopic evaluation.

prompt: Which surgical emergency presents with sudden-onset severe unilateral lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and an enlarged ovarian mass on Doppler showing decreased or absent venous/arterial flow?
explain: Ovarian torsion is twisting of the adnexa on its infundibulopelvic and utero-ovarian ligaments, causing vascular compromise.

prompt: What is the definitive surgical management for suspected acute ovarian torsion to preserve ovarian viability?
choices: Emergency diagnostic laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian preservation
Percutaneous cyst aspiration under local anesthesia
explain: Laparoscopic untwisting (detorsion) with preservation of the ovary is standard, even if the ovary appears dusky or congested.

prompt: Which obstetric complication is characterized by umbilical cord prolapse through the internal cervical os ahead of the presenting fetal part?
explain: Overt cord prolapse is an acute emergency where the cord slips into the vagina, risking fatal fetal compression.

prompt: What is the immediate maneuver when overt umbilical cord prolapse is diagnosed while preparing for emergent cesarean delivery?
choices: Manual elevation of the presenting fetal part off the cord and placing mother in knee-chest position
Immediate manual replacement of the cord back into the uterus
explain: The examiner keeps their gloved hand in the vagina elevating the fetal head off the umbilical cord until emergency cesarean delivery is executed.

prompt: What is the defining clinical characteristic of uterine rupture during a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC)?
choices: Sudden loss of fetal heart rate, loss of fetal station, and severe abdominal pain
Gradual cessation of contractions with normal fetal heart rate
Onset of painless bright red bleeding with elevated fetal station
Sudden increase in intrauterine contraction pressure > 100 mmHg
explain: Acute fetal heart rate decelerations, loss of fetal station on digital exam, and severe pain are cardinal signs of uterine rupture.

prompt: Which fetal heart rate deceleration pattern is caused by transient fetal head compression during uterine contractions and is considered benign?
explain: Early decelerations mirror contractions (nadir matches peak of contraction) due to vagal stimulation from head compression.

prompt: Which fetal heart rate deceleration pattern is caused by uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia?
explain: Late decelerations begin after the contraction starts, nadir after the peak, and return to baseline after the contraction ends, signaling uteroplacental compromise.

prompt: Which fetal heart rate deceleration pattern is characterized by abrupt decrease and abrupt return to baseline, caused by umbilical cord compression?
explain: Variable decelerations show sharp, jagged drops (onset to nadir < 30 sec) reflecting transient umbilical cord occlusion.

prompt: What is the classic diagnostic finding of complete hydatidiform mole on pelvic ultrasound?
choices: 'Snowstorm' appearance and absence of fetal tissue
Large ovarian dermoid cyst with calcifications
Thin-walled empty gestational sac with no yolk sac seen
explain: Diffuse hydropic swelling of chorionic villi produces the classic 'snowstorm' or 'bunch of grapes' appearance on ultrasound.

prompt: What is the karyotype in the vast majority (90%) of complete hydatidiform moles?
explain: Complete moles are diploid (46,XX) androgenetic, resulting from fertilization of an empty ovum by a single sperm that duplicates.

prompt: Which serum tumor marker is monitored serially to surveillance for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (choriocarcinoma) after molar evacuation?
explain: Serial weekly beta-hCG monitoring until normal for 3 consecutive weeks, then monthly for 6 months, detects persistent invasive GTN.

prompt: Which clinical condition is defined by the absence of menses by age 15 in the presence of normal secondary sexual characteristics?
explain: Primary amenorrhea is failure of menarche by age 15 with normal secondary sexual characteristics (or by age 13 without breast development).

prompt: Which congenital anomaly is characterized by 46,XX karyotype, normal ovaries, normal external female genitalia, and complete congenital absence of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina?
explain: MRKH features 46,XX, normal female secondary sexual characteristics and testosterone levels, but absent uterus and upper vagina.

prompt: Which genetic condition features a 46,XY karyotype, functioning testes, high testosterone, complete androgen resistance, absent uterus, and external female phenotype with scant pubic hair?
explain: Non-functional androgen receptors in a 46,XY individual produce female external phenotype, undescended testes, and absent pubic hair.

prompt: Which postpartum infection presents on postoperative day 2 to 3 following cesarean delivery with fever, uterine fundal tenderness, and purulent, foul-smelling lochia?
explain: Postpartum endometritis is a polymicrobial ascending infection presenting with fever, fundal tenderness, and foul lochia.

prompt: What is the standard first-line intravenous antibiotic regimen for postpartum endometritis following cesarean section?
explain: IV clindamycin (anaerobic coverage) plus gentamicin (gram-negative coverage) is the gold standard regimen until afebrile for 24-48 hours.

prompt: What is the initial management for a lactating woman presenting with acute mastitis characterized by a wedge-shaped painful, erythematous, warm breast segment, fever, and flu-like symptoms?
explain: Antistaphylococcal antibiotics (dicloxacillin/cephalexin) and continued milk emptying prevent progression to breast abscess.

prompt: Which type of urinary incontinence presents with sudden, compelling urges to void followed by involuntary urine leakage due to detrusor overactivity?
explain: Urge incontinence is involuntary loss of urine accompanied by urgency, mediated by uninhibited detrusor smooth muscle contractions.

prompt: Which maneuver involves hyperflexion and abduction of the maternal hips against the abdomen to resolve shoulder dystocia during delivery?
explain: McRoberts maneuver flattens the sacral promontory and cephalad-rotates the pubic symphysis, releasing the anterior fetal shoulder.

prompt: Which maneuver for refractory shoulder dystocia involves deliberate cephalic replacement of the fetal head back into the pelvis followed by emergency cesarean delivery?
explain: The Zavanelli maneuver reverses the cardinal movements of labor, pushing the fetal head back into the vagina prior to emergency cesarean.

prompt: Which clinical test is performed on maternal blood to quantify the volume of feto-maternal hemorrhage to guide additional anti-D immune globulin dosing?
explain: The Kleihauer-Betke acid elution test identifies acid-resistant fetal hemoglobin (HbF) cells to calculate fetal hemorrhage volume.

prompt: Which test differentiates fetal blood from maternal blood in vaginal bleeding (e.g. distinguishing vasa previa bleeding from maternal bleeding)?
explain: The Apt test uses potassium hydroxide (alkali); adult hemoglobin turns yellow-brown while fetal hemoglobin resists alkali and stays pink.

prompt: What is the pathognomonic diagnostic finding of amniotic fluid on microscopy when evaluating suspected rupture of membranes?
explain: Amniotic fluid crystallizes in a delicate palm-leaf or fern-like pattern on air-dried glass slides due to high sodium chloride and protein.

prompt: What is the pH threshold of vaginal fluid on Nitrazine paper indicating rupture of amniotic membranes?
explain: Normal vaginal pH is 3.8-4.5; amniotic fluid is basic (pH 7.0-7.5), turning Nitrazine paper deep blue at pH > 6.5.

prompt: Which condition is characterized by painless, progressive cervical dilation and effacement in the second trimester in the absence of uterine contractions, leading to pregnancy loss?
explain: Cervical insufficiency features painless mid-trimester dilation treated prophylactically with cervical cerclage.

prompt: What is the recommended gestational age for elective placement of a prophylactic cervical cerclage in a woman with a history of cervical insufficiency?
explain: Elective cerclage is placed at the end of the first trimester (12-14 weeks) after confirming fetal viability and normal sonographic anatomy.

prompt: Which abnormal placentation involves chorionic villi adhering directly to the myometrium without invading into the muscle layer?
explain: Placenta accreta is direct adherence to myometrium; increta invades into myometrium; percreta penetrates through serosa into adjacent organs.

prompt: Which abnormal placentation involves chorionic villi penetrating completely through the full thickness of the myometrium and uterine serosa, potentially invading the urinary bladder?
explain: Placenta percreta penetrates through the serosa and frequently invades the anterior bladder wall.

prompt: What is the strongest risk factor for placenta accreta spectrum?
explain: The combination of prior cesarean delivery and an anterior low-lying placenta previa escalates accreta risk up to 40-60%.

prompt: Which condition is defined as the arrest of descent of the fetal head in the second stage of labor?
explain: Second-stage arrest is diagnosed after at least 3 hours (nulliparas without epidural) or 4 hours (with epidural) of adequate pushing.

prompt: Which monozygotic twin gestation carries the unique risk of Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)?
explain: Monochorionic diamniotic twins share a single placenta with unbalanced arteriovenous anastomoses, leading to TTTS.

prompt: What is the definitive in utero treatment of choice for severe Stage II-IV Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)?
explain: Fetoscopic laser ablation of inter-twin vascular anastomoses on the placental surface is the gold standard therapy.

prompt: Which monozygotic twin gestation carries high risk of catastrophic umbilical cord entanglement, mandating elective delivery by cesarean at 32 to 34 weeks?
explain: Sharing a single amniotic sac puts MoMo twins at high risk of cord knotting, requiring inpatient monitoring and planned delivery at 32-34 weeks.

prompt: Which infectious pathogen in pregnancy causes neonatal triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications?
explain: Congenital toxoplasmosis presents with the classic Sabin triad: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications.

prompt: Which congenital viral infection presents with periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, and 'blueberry muffin' petechiae?
explain: Congenital CMV characteristically produces periventricular calcifications and is the leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural deafness.

prompt: Which maternal infection causes the classic congenital triad of sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)?
explain: Gregg triad of congenital rubella consists of cataracts, sensorineural hearing loss, and congenital heart defects (PDA).

prompt: What is the primary fetal complication of maternal Parvovirus B19 infection during the second trimester?
explain: Parvovirus B19 attacks fetal erythroid progenitors in the liver, precipitating profound aplastic anemia and hydrops fetalis.

prompt: Which ultrasound marker measured on fetal Doppler provides non-invasive detection of moderate-to-severe fetal anemia?
choices: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity > 1.5 MoM
explain: Elevated MCA peak systolic velocity (>1.5 multiples of the median) reliably detects fetal anemia due to hyperdynamic circulation.

prompt: Which ovarian germ cell tumor contains functional thyroid tissue and can cause clinical thyrotoxicosis?
explain: Struma ovarii is a monodermal teratoma composed predominantly of mature thyroid tissue capable of secreting thyroid hormone.

prompt: Which ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor secretes estrogen and manifests with precocious puberty in young girls or postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial hyperplasia in older women?
explain: Granulosa cell tumors secrete estradiol and inhibin, producing Call-Exner bodies on histopathology.

prompt: Which ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor secretes androgens (testosterone), causing rapid defeminization, hirsutism, and virilization in young women?
explain: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors produce marked virilization, clitoromegaly, and voice deepening due to testosterone hypersecretion.

prompt: Which ovarian malignant germ cell tumor is the female counterpart of testicular seminoma and responds exquisitely to radiotherapy and chemotherapy?
explain: Dysgerminoma is the most common malignant germ cell tumor in young females, producing LDH and responding to chemotherapy/radiation.

prompt: Which ovarian tumor characteristically produces elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and contains Schiller-Duval bodies on histology?
explain: Yolk sac tumors produce high AFP and pathognomonic Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid structures).

prompt: Which rare dermatologic disorder of the vulva presents in postmenopausal women with porcelain-white atrophic plaques, parchment-like skin, and loss of normal vulvar architecture?
explain: Lichen sclerosus causes severe pruritus, parchment paper skin, resorption of labia minora, and carries a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

prompt: What is the first-line medical therapy for vulvar lichen sclerosus to relieve pruritus and prevent architectural distortion?
explain: Ultra-potent topical corticosteroids (clobetasol) applied for 12 weeks are the established first-line therapy.

prompt: Which drug is an oral selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that acts as an antagonist in breast tissue and an agonist in endometrial tissue, increasing the risk of endometrial cancer?
explain: Tamoxifen exerts pro-estrogenic effects on the endometrium, predisposing to endometrial polyps, hyperplasia, and adenocarcinoma.

prompt: Which selective estrogen receptor modulator acts as an antagonist in both breast and endometrial tissues, used for osteoporosis prevention without increasing endometrial cancer risk?
explain: Raloxifene is estrogenic in bone and anti-estrogenic in breast and endometrium, carrying zero increased endometrial cancer risk.

prompt: What is the defining clinical feature of Asherman syndrome (intrauterine synechiae)?
choices: Severe cyclic dysmenorrhea with adnexal mass
explain: Trauma to the basalis layer of the endometrium from postpartum or postabortal D&C leads to fibrous adhesions and secondary amenorrhea.

prompt: What is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic gold standard for Asherman syndrome?
explain: Hysteroscopic direct visualization allows targeted sharp or blunt division of intrauterine synechiae.

prompt: Which congenital genetic syndrome is characterized by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, delayed puberty, and anosmia or hyposmia due to defective embryonic migration of GnRH neurons?
explain: Kallmann syndrome features failure of olfactory and GnRH neurons to migrate from the cribriform plate to the hypothalamus.

prompt: Which syndrome features the triad of fibrous dysplasia of bone, café-au-lait skin spots with jagged borders ('Coast of Maine'), and autonomous peripheral precocious puberty?
explain: Activating postzygotic mutations in GNAS1 lead to autonomous endocrine hyperfunction, bone lesions, and precocious puberty.

prompt: Which rare maternal obstetric catastrophe presents during labor or immediately postpartum with sudden cardiovascular collapse, profound hypoxemia, DIC, and seizure?
explain: Amniotic fluid entry into maternal circulation triggers an anaphylactoid reaction causing pulmonary vasospasm, cardiogenic shock, and massive DIC.

prompt: What is the initial emergency step in managing acute puerperal uterine inversion before the placenta has separated?
choices: Immediate manual replacement of the inverted uterus without removing the placenta first
Immediate manual removal of the placenta from the inverted uterus
Administration of high-dose intravenous oxytocin bolus immediately
explain: The uterus must be manually replaced immediately; removing the placenta first triggers massive, catastrophic hemorrhage.

prompt: In a patient with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY), when is gonadectomy recommended to prevent malignant degeneration of cryptorchid intra-abdominal testes?
explain: Gonadectomy is deferred until after spontaneous puberty to allow endogenous aromatization of testicular androgens to estrogens, ensuring normal breast development and growth.

prompt: Which antiepileptic drug used in pregnancy is associated with the highest risk of major congenital malformations, specifically neural tube defects?
explain: Valproic acid carries a 1-2% risk of neural tube defects (spina bifida) along with craniofacial and cardiovascular anomalies.

prompt: Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated in patients presenting with third-trimester vaginal bleeding prior to ultrasound evaluation.
explain: Digital examination can precipitate massive catastrophic hemorrhage if placenta previa is present.

prompt: Placenta previa is characterized by painful vaginal bleeding and high uterine resting tone.
explain: Placenta previa classically presents with painless bright red bleeding; painful bleeding is characteristic of placental abruption.

prompt: Magnesium sulfate is administered in severe preeclampsia primarily to lower maternal blood pressure.
explain: Magnesium sulfate is an anticonvulsant used for seizure prophylaxis; antihypertensives like labetalol or hydralazine are used for BP control.

prompt: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the earliest clinical physical sign of magnesium toxicity.
explain: Patellar reflex disappears at serum magnesium levels of 8-10 mg/dL, preceding respiratory depression (12-15 mg/dL).

prompt: Naloxone is the specific antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity.
explain: 10% calcium gluconate IV directly antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction.

prompt: Retained placental tissue is the most common cause of primary postpartum hemorrhage.
explain: Atony ('Tone') causes over 70% of early postpartum hemorrhages.

prompt: Methylergonovine can be safely administered to treat postpartum hemorrhage in patients with severe hypertension.
explain: Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction and can provoke severe hypertensive crisis or stroke.

prompt: Carboprost tromethamine (PGF2-alpha) is contraindicated in postpartum patients with active bronchial asthma.
explain: PGF2-alpha causes smooth muscle constriction, precipitating severe bronchospasm in asthmatics.

prompt: An ectopic pregnancy can be definitively ruled out if serum beta-hCG is below 1,000 mIU/mL.
explain: Ectopic pregnancies can present at any beta-hCG level and can rupture even at low titers.

prompt: Methotrexate is an acceptable medical therapy for an unruptured ectopic pregnancy in a hemodynamically stable patient.
explain: Single- or multi-dose methotrexate is the standard medical alternative to surgery in selected patients.

prompt: RhoGAM (anti-D immune globulin) is given to Rh-positive mothers to protect Rh-negative fetuses.
explain: RhoGAM is given to unsensitized Rh-negative mothers carrying (or potentially carrying) an Rh-positive fetus.

prompt: Routine universal screening for Group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonization is performed at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks gestation.
explain: ACOG recommends rectovaginal culture at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks to guide intrapartum prophylaxis.

prompt: Intravenous vancomycin is the first-line intrapartum antibiotic of choice for maternal GBS colonization.
explain: Penicillin G (or IV ampicillin) is the primary first-line choice.

prompt: Active labor is officially defined as starting at 6 cm of cervical dilation.
explain: Contemporary obstetrics recognizes 6 cm dilation as the onset of active labor.

prompt: The second stage of labor begins with complete cervical dilation (10 cm) and ends with delivery of the placenta.
explain: Second stage encompasses full dilation through infant delivery.

prompt: The third stage of labor begins after fetal delivery and ends with expulsion of the placenta.
explain: Placental delivery defines completion of the third stage.

prompt: Normal fetal heart rate baseline ranges between 60 and 100 beats per minute.
explain: A baseline FHR of 110-160 bpm is the normal physiological range.

prompt: Early decelerations in fetal heart rate monitoring indicate uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia.
explain: Early decelerations result from vagal response to fetal head compression and do not indicate hypoxia.

prompt: Late decelerations are caused by fetal head compression during uterine contractions.
explain: Late decelerations reflect uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia; early decelerations reflect head compression.

prompt: Variable decelerations are caused by fetal head compression.
explain: Sharp variable decelerations indicate umbilical cord occlusion.

prompt: Endometriosis is characterized by the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity.
explain: Ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus defines endometriosis.

prompt: Endometriosis is definitively diagnosed by serum CA-125 measurement alone.
explain: Definitive diagnosis requires direct visualization by laparoscopy with histological confirmation; CA-125 is non-specific.

prompt: Cervical cancer screening with Pap smear should begin at age 18 in sexually active individuals.
explain: Screening begins at age 21 regardless of sexual debut, as adolescent HPV infections typically clear spontaneously.

prompt: Between ages 21 and 29, cervical cytology alone is recommended every 3 years for average-risk women.
explain: Cytology alone every 3 years without HPV co-testing is the standard guideline for ages 21-29.

prompt: HPV genotypes 6 and 11 cause the majority of cervical carcinomas.
explain: High-risk HPV 16 and 18 account for ~70% of all invasive cervical cancers.

prompt: HPV genotypes 6 and 11 are low-risk types responsible for condyloma acuminata (genital warts).
explain: HPV 6 and 11 cause >90% of benign anogenital warts.

prompt: Bacterial vaginosis is characterized by an acidic vaginal pH below 4.5.
explain: Bacterial vaginosis elevates vaginal pH above 4.5 due to loss of hydrogen peroxide-producing lactobacilli.

prompt: Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent coccobacilli, characteristic of vulvovaginal candidiasis.
explain: Clue cells seen on saline wet mount confirm bacterial vaginosis.

prompt: Trichomoniasis is caused by a flagellated protozoan and presents with frothy green-yellow vaginal discharge.
explain: Trichomonas vaginalis is a motile protozoan causing malodorous frothy discharge and cervical petechiae.

prompt: Both the patient and their sexual partner must be treated simultaneously for Trichomonas vaginalis infection.
explain: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection requiring partner treatment to prevent ping-pong reinfection.

prompt: Vulvovaginal candidiasis is characterized by clue cells on wet mount and a vaginal pH above 4.5.
explain: Candida thrives at normal acidic vaginal pH (<4.5) and presents with thick white cottage-cheese discharge.

prompt: Postmenopausal vaginal bleeding is considered endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.
explain: Any postmenopausal bleeding warrants prompt endometrial evaluation to exclude adenocarcinoma.

prompt: An endometrial stripe thickness of 3 mm on transvaginal ultrasound virtually excludes endometrial cancer in a postmenopausal woman.
explain: Endometrial thickness <= 4 mm has a negative predictive value >99% for endometrial malignancy.

prompt: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is associated with hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance.
explain: Compensatory hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian theca cell androgen production and inhibits hepatic SHBG.

prompt: Letrozole is the first-line oral ovulation induction agent for infertile anovulatory women with PCOS.
explain: Letrozole (aromatase inhibitor) yields superior live birth rates compared to clomiphene in PCOS.

prompt: In ovarian torsion, the ovary should be immediately removed without untwisting due to fear of pulmonary embolism.
explain: Current surgical standard is conservative detorsion and cystectomy/pexopexy; detorsion does not increase PE risk and preserves fertility.

prompt: Overt umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate elevation of the presenting part and emergency cesarean section.
explain: Cord compression causes rapid fetal asphyxia; digital elevation relieves pressure until cesarean delivery.

prompt: Sudden loss of fetal station on digital vaginal exam during labor strongly suggests uterine rupture.
explain: Uterine rupture permits the fetus to extrude into the peritoneal cavity, resulting in recession of the presenting part.

prompt: Complete hydatidiform moles are typically triploid and contain fetal tissue.
explain: Complete moles arise from fertilization of an empty ovum by a sperm that duplicates its genome (46,XX androgenetic).

prompt: Partial hydatidiform moles are typically triploid (69,XXY or 69,XXX) and contain fetal tissue.
explain: Partial moles result from fertilization of a normal ovum by two sperm, yielding triploid tissue and fetal parts.

prompt: Serum beta-hCG is monitored serially following suction evacuation of a hydatidiform mole to detect gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
explain: Persistent or plateauing beta-hCG signifies invasive mole or choriocarcinoma.

prompt: Primary amenorrhea is diagnosed if menarche has not occurred by age 12 in a patient with normal breast development.
explain: Failure of menarche by age 15 with secondary sexual characteristics meets criteria for primary amenorrhea.

prompt: Patients with Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome have a 46,XY karyotype.
explain: MRKH is Müllerian agenesis in genetic females (46,XX) with normal ovaries; 46,XY describes androgen insensitivity.

prompt: Patients with Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) have functioning intra-abdominal testes and high testosterone.
explain: CAIS patients are genetic males (46,XY) with testes producing male-range testosterone, but non-responsive androgen receptors.

prompt: Postpartum endometritis is treated with oral amoxicillin as an outpatient in most cesarean section cases.
explain: Post-cesarean endometritis is a severe polymicrobial infection requiring inpatient IV clindamycin and gentamicin.

prompt: Lactating women with acute puerperal mastitis should immediately cease breastfeeding from the affected breast.
explain: Continued frequent nursing or pumping is essential to prevent milk stasis and progression to abscess.

prompt: Stress urinary incontinence is characterized by involuntary leakage of urine associated with coughing, sneezing, or laughing.
explain: Hypermobility of the bladder neck or intrinsic sphincter deficiency causes stress leakage during intra-abdominal pressure spikes.

prompt: Pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises) is first-line conservative therapy for stress urinary incontinence.
explain: Kegel exercises strengthen the levator ani and pubococcygeus, improving urethral coaptation.

prompt: The McRoberts maneuver for shoulder dystocia involves applying firm fundal pressure.
explain: McRoberts maneuver flattens the lumbosacral angle and rotates the symphysis pubis cephalad.

prompt: Fundal pressure is strongly recommended to assist in delivering the shoulders during shoulder dystocia.
explain: Fundal pressure is strictly contraindicated in shoulder dystocia as it impacts the anterior shoulder further and causes uterine rupture or brachial plexus injury.

prompt: Suprapubic pressure (not fundal pressure) should be applied to dislodge the anterior shoulder in shoulder dystocia.
explain: Firm downward suprapubic pressure pushes the anterior shoulder under the pubic bone.

prompt: The Kleihauer-Betke test relies on the resistance of adult hemoglobin to acid elution compared to fetal hemoglobin.
explain: Adult hemoglobin elutes in acid, leaving pale ghost cells, while fetal hemoglobin resists acid and stains bright pink.

prompt: The Apt test differentiates maternal blood from fetal blood using an alkali denaturation technique.
explain: Fetal hemoglobin resists alkali denaturation (stays pink), whereas adult maternal hemoglobin turns yellow-brown.

prompt: Ferning of amniotic fluid on a glass slide is caused by crystallization of sodium chloride in the presence of protein.
explain: Arborization (ferning) of dried amniotic fluid on air-drying confirms rupture of membranes.

prompt: Amniotic fluid is acidic, so Nitrazine paper turns yellow when the amniotic membranes have ruptured.
explain: Amniotic fluid is alkaline (pH 7.0-7.5), turning Nitrazine paper blue (vaginal secretions are acidic, pH 3.8-4.5).

prompt: Cervical cerclage is placed electively between 12 and 14 weeks gestation in patients with confirmed cervical insufficiency.
explain: Prophylactic cerclage is performed at the end of the first trimester before cervical effacement occurs.

prompt: Placenta accreta occurs when chorionic villi invade completely through the uterine serosa into adjacent pelvic structures.
explain: Invasion through the serosa defines placenta percreta; accreta is adherence directly to myometrium without muscular penetration.

prompt: Dichorionic diamniotic (DiDi) twin pregnancies are the specific subgroup at risk for Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome.
explain: Unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses in a shared single placenta cause TTTS in MoDi twins.

prompt: Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of communicating placental vessels is the treatment of choice for severe TTTS.
explain: Laser ablation of anastomoses interrupts vascular shunting and optimizes survival of both twins.

prompt: Monochorionic monoamniotic (MoMo) twins are delivered electively by cesarean section between 32 and 34 weeks gestation.
explain: MoMo twins face high risk of fatal cord entanglement, mandating planned preterm cesarean delivery.

prompt: Congenital toxoplasmosis classically causes a triad of cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus, and sensorineural deafness.
explain: The Sabin triad characterizes congenital toxoplasma infection.

prompt: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children.
explain: CMV infection in utero is the leading infectious etiology of progressive sensorineural hearing impairment.

prompt: Parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy can cause severe fetal aplastic anemia and non-immune hydrops fetalis.
explain: Viral destruction of fetal erythroid precursors causes profound anemia, high-output heart failure, and hydrops.

prompt: Doppler measurement of middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) is a reliable non-invasive test for fetal anemia.
explain: An MCA-PSV > 1.5 MoM correlates with moderate-to-severe fetal anemia, guiding intrauterine transfusion.

prompt: Granulosa cell tumors of the ovary produce alpha-fetoprotein and feature Schiller-Duval bodies on histological examination.
explain: Call-Exner bodies (microfollicular structures with central eosinophilic fluid) and estrogen secretion define granulosa tumors.

prompt: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors of the ovary typically secrete estrogen and cause precocious puberty.
explain: Sertoli-Leydig tumors secrete androgens, producing rapid virilization, clitoromegaly, and hirsutism.

prompt: Yolk sac tumors of the ovary secrete alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and display Schiller-Duval bodies.
explain: Schiller-Duval bodies and elevated serum AFP are pathognomonic for endodermal sinus (yolk sac) tumors.

prompt: Dysgerminoma is the most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumor in young females and produces serum LDH.
explain: Dysgerminomas are radiosensitive germ cell tumors associated with elevated lactate dehydrogenase.

prompt: Vulvar lichen sclerosus is treated first-line with ultra-potent topical corticosteroids such as clobetasol propionate.
explain: Clobetasol 0.05% ointment is the established therapy to arrest atrophy and prevent architecture resorption.

prompt: Tamoxifen exerts pro-estrogenic effects on breast tissue but anti-estrogenic effects on the endometrium.
explain: Tissue-selective receptor modulation by tamoxifen increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma.

prompt: Raloxifene increases the risk of endometrial cancer similar to tamoxifen.
explain: Raloxifene is an estrogen antagonist in both breast and endometrium, avoiding the endometrial cancer risk of tamoxifen.

prompt: Asherman syndrome consists of intrauterine fibrous synechiae typically resulting from vigorous postpartum curettage.
explain: Mechanical destruction of the basal endometrial layer causes scarring and secondary amenorrhea.

prompt: Amniotic fluid embolism is an unpredictable, catastrophic obstetric event presenting with cardiovascular collapse, hypoxemia, and DIC.
explain: Anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy triggers profound bronchospasm, pulmonary vasospasm, and consumptive coagulopathy.

prompt: In acute uterine inversion, the placenta should be detached manually before attempting uterine replacement.
explain: Removing the placenta before uterine replacement causes massive life-threatening hemorrhage; replace the uterus first.

prompt: Kallmann syndrome is characterized by hypergonadotropic hypogonadism associated with anosmia or hyposmia.
explain: Impaired migration of GnRH and olfactory neurons results in delayed puberty and loss of smell.

prompt: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by a germline mutation transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern.
explain: McCune-Albright is caused by a somatic mosaic postzygotic mutation in GNAS1; germline transmission is lethal.

prompt: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, gonadectomy is routinely performed in infancy before puberty.
explain: Gonadectomy is deferred until after spontaneous completion of puberty to allow normal estrogen-driven breast development.

prompt: Swyer syndrome is 46,XY pure gonadal dysgenesis presenting with female external phenotype and streak gonads.
explain: Mutation in SRY prevents testicular differentiation in a 46,XY individual, yielding uterus and streak gonads.

prompt: Streak gonads in patients with a Y chromosome (such as Swyer syndrome) carry a high risk of gonadoblastoma and should be removed.
explain: Presence of Y chromosome material in dysgenetic gonads carries a 20-30% malignancy risk, mandating prophylactic gonadectomy.

prompt: Unilateral bloody nipple discharge without a palpable breast mass is most commonly caused by invasive ductal carcinoma.
explain: Benign intraductal papilloma is the leading cause of unilateral serosanguinous nipple discharge.

prompt: Inflammatory breast cancer characteristically presents as an aggressive erythematous, edematous lesion resembling mastitis with peau d'orange.
explain: Dermal lymphatic invasion by tumor cells obstructs drainage, causing erythema and orange-peel (peau d'orange) skin dimpling.

prompt: Bartholin gland cysts are located in the labia minora at the 12 o'clock position.
explain: Bartholin glands are located in the posterior labia majora at the 4 and 8 o'clock positions.

prompt: Surgical Word catheter placement is a standard treatment for a symptomatic, drained Bartholin gland abscess.
explain: A Word catheter left in place for 4-6 weeks permits epithelialization of a permanent draining tract.

prompt: A tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) in pelvic inflammatory disease always requires immediate emergency surgical hysterectomy.
explain: Most unruptured TOAs (>70%) resolve with inpatient intravenous antibiotic therapy alone; surgery is reserved for rupture or medical failure.

prompt: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis presenting with RUQ pain and 'violin-string' adhesions between the liver capsule and abdominal wall.
explain: Ascending Chlamydia or Gonococcus infection inflames the hepatic capsule, creating pathognomonic violin-string adhesions.

prompt: In a pregnant patient with appendicitis, the appendix is typically displaced caudally and medially deep into the pelvis as the uterus enlarges.
explain: The enlarging gravid uterus pushes the cecum and appendix upward and outward toward the RUQ by the third trimester.

prompt: Pudendal nerve block for second-stage vaginal delivery anesthesia is placed using the ischial spines as the primary landmark.
explain: The pudendal nerve passes behind the sacrospinous ligament near the ischial spine, the anatomical target for local infiltration.

prompt: The bishop score evaluates five pelvic factors: cervical dilation, effacement, consistency, position, and fetal station.
explain: The Bishop score calculates pelvic readiness for labor induction across these five clinical criteria.

prompt: A Bishop score greater than 8 indicates a favorable cervix with a high likelihood of successful vaginal delivery following induction.
explain: A score >= 8 predicts induction success comparable to spontaneous labor.

prompt: External cephalic version (ECV) for breech presentation is routinely performed at 28 weeks gestation.
explain: ECV is performed at or after 37 weeks gestation when spontaneous version is unlikely and delivery is safe if complications arise.

prompt: Order the normal anatomical stages of human labor from first onset to the immediate postpartum period.
items: First stage: onset of regular contractions to complete cervical dilation (10 cm)
Second stage: complete cervical dilation to delivery of the infant
Third stage: delivery of the infant to complete expulsion of the placenta
Fourth stage: immediate two-hour postpartum hemodynamic recovery and monitoring
explain: Labor progresses systematically through first, second, third, and fourth stages into the puerperium.

prompt: Order the cardinal movements of labor executed by the fetal head during normal vaginal cephalic delivery.
items: Engagement of the biparietal diameter in the pelvic inlet
Descent of the presenting part through the birth canal
Flexion of the fetal head against the pelvic floor
Internal rotation to an occiput anterior position
Extension of the fetal head delivering under the pubic symphysis
explain: Engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, and expulsion are the classic cardinal movements.

prompt: Order the diagnostic workup for a woman of reproductive age presenting with acute lower abdominal pain and abnormal vaginal bleeding.
items: Obtain immediate point-of-care urine pregnancy test
Quantify serum beta-hCG and obtain complete blood count and type/screen
Perform transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to locate pregnancy and evaluate adnexa
Assess for gestational sac within the endometrial cavity relative to discriminatory zone
Initiate medical management (methotrexate) or surgical laparoscopy if ectopic confirmed
explain: Pregnancy exclusion precedes quantitative beta-hCG, transvaginal ultrasound, discriminatory zone assessment, and intervention.

prompt: Order the sequential steps in managing active postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony.
items: Initiate continuous vigorous bimanual uterine massage and fluid resuscitation
Administer second-line uterotonics (methylergonovine, carboprost, or misoprostol)
Insert intrauterine balloon tamponade (Bakri balloon) if bleeding persists
Perform surgical intervention (B-Lynch compression suture, uterine artery ligation, or hysterectomy)
explain: Management escalates from bimanual massage to oxytocin, secondary uterotonics, balloon tamponade, and surgical devascularization.

prompt: Order the chronological prenatal screening schedule for an uncomplicated pregnancy.
items: First trimester: dating ultrasound, nuchal translucency, and aneuploidy screening (10-13 weeks)
Second trimester: quad screen or maternal AFP and anatomy ultrasound (18-20 weeks)
Gestational diabetes screening (50-g glucose challenge) and CBC at 24-28 weeks
Group B Streptococcus (GBS) rectovaginal screening at 35-37 weeks
Weekly cervical assessment and labor management at 36-40 weeks
explain: Prenatal care follows a strict trimester schedule: first-trimester dating, mid-trimester anatomy, 28-week GDM, and 36-week GBS.

prompt: Order the stages of the female menstrual cycle from the onset of menses.
items: Early follicular phase: menses and recruitment of primordial follicles by FSH
Late follicular phase: selection of dominant follicle producing peak estradiol
Ovulatory phase: estradiol trigger of the LH surge and oocyte release
Early luteal phase: corpus luteum formation and peak progesterone production
Late luteal phase: luteolysis, progesterone withdrawal, and endometrial shedding
explain: The cycle proceeds from menses through follicular maturation, LH-mediated ovulation, luteal synthesis, and luteolysis.

prompt: Order the sequential management steps for an acute eclamptic seizure.
items: Maintain maternal airway, position mother in left lateral decubitus, and administer supplemental oxygen
Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose (4 to 6 grams over 15-20 minutes)
Administer intravenous antihypertensive (labetalol or hydralazine) if systolic BP >= 160 or diastolic >= 110
Initiate continuous magnesium sulfate maintenance infusion (1 to 2 g/hr)
Proceed with definitive delivery of the fetus once mother is hemodynamically stabilized
explain: Airway/oxygenation precedes magnesium loading, BP control, maintenance magnesium, and planned delivery.

prompt: Order the five anatomical components evaluated in calculating the Bishop score for cervical favorability.
items: Fetal station relative to ischial spines
