explain: Dilation, effacement, station, consistency, and position comprise the Bishop score.

prompt: Order the diagnostic workup for a postmenopausal female presenting with spontaneous vaginal bleeding.
items: Perform detailed pelvic bimanual and speculum examination
Perform transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to measure endometrial stripe thickness
Identify endometrial thickness > 4 mm or persistent bleeding
Perform diagnostic hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage if biopsy is non-diagnostic
explain: Speculum exam and TVUS measure stripe thickness; thickness > 4 mm dictates endometrial biopsy and hysteroscopy.

prompt: Order the emergency obstetric maneuvers for resolving shoulder dystocia (HELPERR mnemonic).
items: Call for Help and request neonatal and anesthesia teams
Evaluate for Episiotomy to increase posterior working space
Perform McRoberts maneuver (hyperflexion of maternal legs onto abdomen)
Apply firm Suprapubic Pressure pushing anterior shoulder downward and forward
Perform Enter rotational maneuvers (Rubin or Woods corkscrew) or Remove posterior arm
explain: The HELPERR mnemonic standardizes shoulder dystocia relief: Help, Episiotomy, Leg flexion (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter maneuvers, Remove arm.

prompt: Order the clinical evaluation steps for suspected preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM).
items: Perform sterile speculum examination avoiding digital examination
Visualize pooling of clear fluid in the posterior vaginal fornix
Perform Nitrazine test demonstrating alkaline fluid (pH > 6.5, blue color)
Perform microscopic examination demonstrating arborization and ferning of dried fluid
Perform obstetric ultrasound to confirm decreased amniotic fluid index (oligohydramnios)
explain: Sterile speculum inspection identifies pooling, confirmed by Nitrazine alkalinity, ferning arborization, and ultrasound.

prompt: Order the management steps for confirmed preterm premature rupture of membranes at 31 weeks gestation.
items: Confirm gestational age at 31 weeks and admit to inpatient obstetric unit
Administer intramuscular betamethasone (two doses 24 hours apart) for fetal lung maturity
Initiate latency antibiotic regimen (ampicillin and erythromycin / azithromycin for 7 days)
Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
Plan delivery at 34 weeks gestation or sooner if intrauterine infection develops
explain: Admission, corticosteroids for lung maturity, latency antibiotics, magnesium neuroprotection, and delivery at 34 weeks form standard care.

prompt: Order the diagnostic evaluation of secondary amenorrhea in a reproductive-aged female.
items: Exclude pregnancy with urine or serum beta-hCG
Measure serum TSH, prolactin, and FSH levels
Perform medroxyprogesterone acetate withdrawal challenge test (10 mg daily for 10 days)
Observe for withdrawal bleeding: bleeding confirms anovulation (e.g. PCOS)
If no bleeding, perform estrogen-progesterone challenge test followed by pelvic imaging to assess outflow tract
explain: Excluding pregnancy, checking TSH/prolactin/FSH, and progesterone withdrawal challenge establish the diagnostic tier.

prompt: Order the management steps for a patient with acute pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) requiring hospital admission.
items: Establish clinical criteria: pelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness
Obtain endocervical swabs for NAAT gonorrhea and chlamydia and rule out ectopic pregnancy
Perform pelvic ultrasound to exclude tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA)
Initiate IV cefotetan (or cefoxitin) plus oral/IV doxycycline (or IV ampicillin-sulbactam + doxycycline)
Transition to oral therapy after 24-48 hours of sustained clinical improvement to complete 14 days total
explain: Clinical diagnosis and ruling out TOA/ectopic precede parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics, completing 14 days total.

prompt: Order the steps of Pap smear screening triage for a 32-year-old female with atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US).
items: Review cervical cytology showing ASC-US result
Perform reflex high-risk HPV DNA testing on the liquid cytology specimen
If high-risk HPV is negative, repeat co-testing in 3 years
If high-risk HPV is positive, perform diagnostic colposcopy with directed biopsies
Perform endocervical curettage (ECC) if squamocolumnar junction is not fully visualized
explain: ASC-US is managed with reflex HPV testing; positive high-risk HPV mandates colposcopy and directed biopsy.

prompt: Order the surgical steps of an uncomplicated low transverse cesarean section.
items: Pfannenstiel horizontal suprapubic skin incision and division of subcutaneous tissue
Transverse incision of rectus sheath fascia and blunt midline separation of rectus muscles
Sharp entry into parietal peritoneum and creation of bladder flap
Low transverse hysterotomy incision into lower uterine segment
Delivery of infant, cord clamping, delivery of placenta, and two-layer hysterotomy closure
explain: Pfannenstiel entry, fascial division, peritoneal opening, hysterotomy, delivery, and layered uterine closure are standard.

prompt: Order the chronological progression of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) monitoring after evacuation of a hydatidiform mole.
items: Perform suction curettage to evacuate molar tissue from uterine cavity
Obtain baseline quantitative serum beta-hCG within 48 hours post-procedure
Monitor serum beta-hCG weekly until levels become undetectable for 3 consecutive weeks
Monitor serum beta-hCG monthly for an additional 6 consecutive months
Enforce strict contraception throughout the entire surveillance period
explain: Suction evacuation is followed by weekly hCG until zero for 3 weeks, then monthly for 6 months while maintaining contraception.

prompt: Order the workup and management of Rh(D) alloimmunization in an Rh-negative pregnant woman.
items: Obtain maternal blood type and indirect Coombs antibody screen at first prenatal visit
Identify anti-D antibody and determine initial maternal antibody titer
Repeat anti-D titers every 4 weeks until critical titer (1:16 to 1:32) is reached
Perform serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) Doppler if critical titer exceeded
Perform percutaneous umbilical blood sampling and intrauterine fetal blood transfusion if severe anemia detected
explain: Antibody screening, serial titers to critical threshold (1:16), MCA Doppler monitoring, and cordocentesis transfusion protect the fetus.

prompt: Order the sequential steps in managing overt umbilical cord prolapse.
items: Identify pulsing or visible umbilical cord protruding into the vagina
Call immediately for emergency cesarean delivery and obstetric/anesthesia backup
Insert gloved hand into vagina and manually elevate presenting fetal part off the cord
Place patient in steep Trendelenburg or knee-chest position and fill bladder with 500 mL saline
Transport emergently to operating room with hand continuously elevating fetal head until delivery
explain: Immediate diagnosis, emergency call, manual fetal head elevation, positioning, and continuous hand elevation until cesarean save the infant.

prompt: Order the diagnostic workup for a 28-year-old woman presenting with suspected polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
items: Evaluate menstrual history for oligo-ovulation or amenorrhea (< 9 menses per year)
Assess clinical hyperandrogenism (modified Ferriman-Gallwey hirsutism score) and serum total/free testosterone
Exclude mimic conditions by checking TSH, prolactin, and early morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Perform pelvic transvaginal ultrasound showing >= 20 follicles per ovary or ovarian volume >= 10 mL
Confirm diagnosis using Rotterdam criteria (2 of 3 features present) and screen for metabolic syndrome
explain: Menstrual history, androgen assessment, exclusion of mimics (CAH, prolactin), ultrasound morphology, and Rotterdam criteria confirm PCOS.

prompt: Order the surgical steps of laparoscopic salpingectomy for a ruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy.
items: Establish pneumoperitoneum and insert umbilical and lower quadrant laparoscopic trocars
Evacuate hemoperitoneum and visualize the affected fallopian tube
Grasp fallopian tube and identify the mesosalpinx containing tubal branch vessels
Coagulate and transect mesosalpinx along the length of the tube using bipolar energy
Transect tube at the isthmus/cornual junction, place in specimen retrieval bag, and extract
explain: Laparoscopic entry, hemoperitoneum evacuation, mesosalpinx coagulation, isthmic transection, and contained extraction form safe salpingectomy.

prompt: Order the stages in the management of acute puerperal uterine inversion.
items: Recognize acute uterine inversion and call immediately for emergency resuscitation and anesthesia
Do NOT remove the adherent placenta prior to replacement
Administer uterine relaxant (nitroglycerin, terbutaline, or general anesthesia) if contraction ring is present
Perform Johnson maneuver: apply steady upward manual pressure along the axis of the birth canal
Administer high-dose intravenous oxytocin infusion immediately after uterus is successfully replaced
explain: Immediate recognition, keeping placenta attached, uterine relaxation, manual Johnson replacement, and post-replacement oxytocin are critical.

prompt: Order the clinical steps of External Cephalic Version (ECV) for a persistent breech presentation at 37 weeks.
items: Confirm singleton breech presentation and normal amniotic fluid index on ultrasound at 37 weeks
Perform reactive non-stress test (NST) confirming fetal well-being
Administer subcutaneous tocolytic (terbutaline) 15-30 minutes prior to procedure
Apply gentle bimanual manipulation lifting fetal breech and guiding fetal head into pelvis
Repeat ultrasound and non-stress test post-procedure and administer RhoGAM if mother is Rh-negative
explain: Ultrasound confirmation at 37 weeks, reactive NST, terbutaline tocolysis, bimanual version, and post-procedure NST/RhoGAM define ECV.

prompt: Order the staging laparotomy steps for apparent early-stage epithelial ovarian carcinoma.
items: Perform vertical midline laparotomy and collect peritoneal washings (pelvis, gutters, diaphragm)
Perform total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH-BSO)
Perform bilateral pelvic and para-aortic lymph node dissection up to renal vessels
Perform peritoneal biopsies of diaphragmatic peritoneum, paracolic gutters, and pelvic peritoneum
explain: Washings, TAH-BSO, omentectomy, pelvic/para-aortic lymphadenectomy, and systematic peritoneal biopsies comprise complete staging.

prompt: Order the diagnostic evaluation of primary amenorrhea in a 16-year-old female with breast development and absent uterus.
items: Confirm presence of normal secondary sexual characteristics (breast development) and absent menses
Perform pelvic transvaginal ultrasound or MRI confirming absent uterus and upper vagina
Distinguish 46,XX (Müllerian agenesis / MRKH) from 46,XY (Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome)
Measure serum testosterone: female level confirms MRKH, whereas male level confirms CAIS
explain: Normal breasts with absent uterus prompts karyotyping; serum testosterone differentiates 46,XX MRKH from 46,XY CAIS.

prompt: Order the steps in managing a woman with postpartum choriocarcinoma.
items: Identify plateauing or rising beta-hCG titers after pregnancy event
Perform pelvic ultrasound showing hypervascular myometrial invasive mass
Perform staging metastatic workup (chest CT, brain MRI, abdominal/pelvic CT)
Calculate FIGO / WHO prognostic scoring index
Initiate single-agent chemotherapy (methotrexate) for low-risk, or multi-agent EMA-CO for high-risk disease
explain: Rising hCG, pelvic imaging, metastatic staging, WHO risk scoring, and tailored chemotherapy cure gestational choriocarcinoma.

prompt: Order the clinical protocol for induction of labor with an unfavorable cervix (Bishop score 3).
items: Confirm clinical indication for labor induction and assess fetal well-being with reactive NST
Initiate cervical ripening with mechanical Foley balloon catheter or vaginal prostaglandin E2/E1
Reassess cervical Bishop score after 12 hours of ripening
Initiate intravenous oxytocin infusion once Bishop score is favorable (> 6-8)
Perform artificial rupture of membranes (amniotomy) once active labor is established
explain: Unfavorable cervix requires pre-induction ripening (prostaglandin/balloon) before oxytocin infusion and amniotomy.

prompt: Order the surgical steps of emergency peripartum hysterectomy for catastrophic placenta percreta.
items: Deliver infant through high fundal hysterotomy avoiding anterior placental incision
Leave placenta completely undisturbed in situ and rapidly close hysterotomy incision
Ligate and divide round ligaments and open retroperitoneal space
Isolate and divide uterine vessels with serial clamping
Dissect bladder flap off anterior lower uterine segment and perform total hysterectomy
explain: Fundal delivery sparing placenta, closing uterus, retroperitoneal dissection, uterine vessel control, and bladder dissection optimize survival.

prompt: Order the sequential steps in managing suspected Amniotic Fluid Embolism (AFE).
items: Recognize sudden cardiovascular collapse, profound cyanosis, and seizure during labor
Initiate immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation and high-flow 100% oxygen with endotracheal intubation
Displace gravid uterus manually to the left to relieve aortocaval compression
Execute immediate perimortem cesarean delivery within 4 to 5 minutes of arrest if mother does not achieve ROSC
Administer aggressive blood component resuscitation (1:1:1 PRBC, FFP, platelets) for fulminant DIC
explain: Immediate CPR/airway, left uterine displacement, perimortem cesarean delivery within 5 minutes, and balanced transfusion for DIC are life-saving.

prompt: Order the stepwise medical management of severe hyperemesis gravidarum.
items: Dietary modification with frequent small meals and ginger supplementation
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) monotherapy or combined with doxylamine
Add-on dopamine antagonist (promethazine, prochlorperazine, or metoclopramide)
Intravenous fluid rehydration with thiamine supplementation prior to dextrose
explain: Stepwise escalation proceeds from lifestyle/pyridoxine-doxylamine to dopamine antagonists, ondansetron, and IV fluids with thiamine to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

prompt: Match each obstetric third-trimester bleeding condition to its characteristic presentation.
pairs: Painless bright red vaginal bleeding in the third trimester
Painful vaginal bleeding with uterine hypertonus and fetal distress
Sudden abdominal pain, loss of fetal station, and maternal shock
Painless bleeding immediately following rupture of membranes with fetal bradycardia
Painless postcoital spotting with normal ultrasound
explain: Clinical pain, timing of membrane rupture, and uterine tone differentiate third-trimester hemorrhage.

prompt: Match each hypertensive disorder of pregnancy to its defining diagnostic criteria.
pairs: BP >= 140/90 mmHg documented before pregnancy or before 20 weeks gestation
New-onset BP >= 140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks without proteinuria or severe features
New-onset BP >= 140/90 after 20 weeks with proteinuria >= 300 mg/24hr
BP >= 160/110 mmHg, platelets < 100,000, or severe end-organ damage
New-onset grand mal seizures in a patient with preeclampsia
explain: Gestational age at onset, proteinuria, and end-organ features define hypertensive pregnancy categories.

prompt: Match each postpartum hemorrhage etiology ('the 4 Ts') to its classic cause.
pairs: Uterine atony secondary to overdistension or prolonged labor
Lacerations of the cervix, vagina, or perineum and uterine rupture
Retained placental fragments, succenturiate lobe, or invasive placenta
Preexisting coagulopathy, DIC, or severe preeclampsia
Excessive umbilical cord traction precipitating acute uterine inversion
explain: The 4 Ts mnemonic categorizes the underlying causes of postpartum hemorrhage.

prompt: Match each infectious vulvovaginitis to its classic clinical diagnostic feature.
pairs: Thin grey-white discharge, fishy amine odor with 10% KOH, and clue cells
Frothy yellow-green discharge, strawberry cervix, and motile protozoa
Thick cottage-cheese discharge, intense pruritus, pseudohyphae on KOH
Pale, dry, thinned vaginal epithelium with elevated pH in postmenopausal female
Painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base with tender lymphadenopathy
explain: Discharge characteristics, microscopy, and physical signs differentiate vaginitis etiologies.

prompt: Match each fetal heart rate pattern to its underlying pathophysiologic etiology.
pairs: Fetal head compression causing benign vagal reflex
Severe fetal anemia or profound acidemia
Reassuring fetal movement and intact sympathetic tone
explain: Cardiotocography patterns correspond directly to mechanical or hypoxic physiological states.

prompt: Match each ovarian mass to its characteristic ultrasound or histopathologic appearance.
pairs: Hyperechoic Rokitansky nodule with acoustic shadowing from teeth or hair
Unilocular cyst with homogeneous low-level 'ground-glass' internal echoes
Thin-walled, unilocular, completely anechoic simple cyst < 3 cm
Bilateral multi-cystic 'soap bubble' ovaries driven by massive hCG
Large multilocular cystic mass with thin septations and clear fluid
explain: Acoustic characteristics on pelvic sonography identify specific benign ovarian lesions.

prompt: Match each physical exam sign of pregnancy to its anatomical description.
pairs: Bluish-violet discoloration of the cervix, vagina, and vulva
Softening of the uterine isthmus on bimanual pelvic examination
Softening of the vaginal portion of the cervix
Irregular softening and enlargement of the uterine fundus at implantation site
Hyperpigmented macules on the forehead, malar eminences, and upper lip
explain: Classic physiological physical signs reflect hormone-induced hypervascularity and tissue softening.

prompt: Match each cervical screening result to its appropriate initial clinical management.
pairs: NILM with HPV negative at age 35
Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) at age 28
Immediate colposcopy or loop electrosurgical excision (LEEP)
Colposcopy, endocervical curettage, and endometrial biopsy
explain: ASCCP guidelines dictate risk-based management ranging from routine rescreening to excision.

prompt: Match each type of perineal laceration to its anatomical depth of tissue injury.
pairs: Involves only the vaginal mucosa and perineal skin
Extends into the perineal body muscles (bulbocavernosus/transverse perineal)
Involves the external and/or internal anal sphincter complex
Extends completely through the anal sphincters and rectal mucosa
Tear of the cervix typically at 3 or 9 o'clock requiring high suture ligation
explain: Obstetric perineal lacerations are graded from mucosal tears (1st) to rectal lumen entry (4th).

prompt: Match each abnormal placentation to its pathological depth of invasion.
pairs: Placenta covers or lies within 2 cm of the internal cervical os
Chorionic villi attach directly to myometrium without decidua basalis
Chorionic villi invade deeply into the myometrium
Chorionic villi penetrate completely through myometrium and uterine serosa
Fetal vessels run unprotected through membranes covering the internal os
explain: Placenta accreta spectrum grades depth of villous penetration into uterine wall layers.

prompt: Match each gynecologic malignancy to its most common histological subtype.
explain: Squamous and glandular epithelial malignancies predominate across distinct gynecologic tracts.

prompt: Match each ovarian tumor marker to its corresponding neoplastic entity.
explain: Specific serum biomarkers correlate with epithelial, germ cell, and sex cord-stromal tumors.

prompt: Match each cause of primary amenorrhea to its defining karyotype and phenotypic characteristics.
pairs: 46,XX; normal female breasts and pubic hair; absent uterus and upper vagina
46,XY; normal breasts; absent pubic hair; absent uterus; intra-abdominal testes
45,X0; short stature; webbed neck; streak gonads; primary hypogonadism
46,XY; female external genitalia; normal uterus; streak gonads; no breasts
46,XX; hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; anosmia; absent breast development
explain: Karyotype, breast presence, pubic hair, and internal uterine anatomy definitively differentiate amenorrheas.

prompt: Match each contraceptive method to its primary mechanism of action.
pairs: Suppression of ovulation via hypothalamic-pituitary FSH/LH inhibition
Thickening of cervical mucus and local endometrial glandular atrophy
Sterile foreign body inflammatory reaction toxic to sperm and oocytes
High-dose systemic progestin blocking the LH surge and suppressing ovulation
Continuous progestin release suppressing ovulation and thickening mucus
explain: Contraceptive efficacy relies on ovulation inhibition, cervical mucus thickening, or endometrial hostility.

prompt: Match each breast disorder to its characteristic clinical or pathological presentation.
pairs: Rubbery, mobile, well-circumscribed painless mass in a 22-year-old female
Unilateral spontaneous serosanguinous nipple discharge from a single duct
Rapidly enlarging large breast mass with leaf-like architecture on histology
Firm, irregular mass with skin retraction following breast trauma or surgery
Rapidly progressive warmth, erythema, edema, and peau d'orange appearance
explain: Benign fibroepithelial, papillary, and malignant inflammatory lesions present with distinct clinical hallmarks.

prompt: Match each type of urinary incontinence to its pathophysiological mechanism and first-line treatment.
pairs: Urethral hypermobility; treated first-line with pelvic floor Kegel exercises
Detrusor overactivity; treated with bladder training and antimuscarinics
Detrusor underactivity or bladder outlet obstruction; treated with catheterization
Continuous unprovoked leakage following obstructed labor or pelvic surgery
Combined features of both stress and urge incontinence
explain: Incontinence subtypes are classified by sphincter integrity, detrusor contractility, or fistulous tracts.

prompt: Match each molar pregnancy entity to its genetic origin and pathology.
pairs: 46,XX entirely paternal diploid; diffuse hydropic villi; no embryo
69,XXY triploid with maternal and paternal DNA; focal villous swelling; fetal parts
Malignant anaplastic syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts lacking chorionic villi
Intermediate trophoblasts producing human placental lactogen (hPL)
Molar villi directly invading deep into the myometrium with persistent high hCG
explain: Gestational trophoblastic diseases are categorized by ploidy, villous presence, and invasive capacity.

prompt: Match each maternal medication to its characteristic fetal teratogenic effect.
pairs: Renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, and calvarial defects
Nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses (chondrodysplasia punctata), and CNS defects
Neural tube defects (spina bifida), cleft lip, and developmental delay
Ebstein anomaly (downward displacement of the tricuspid valve)
Craniofacial anomalies, microtia, thymic aplasia, and conotruncal heart defects
explain: Established teratogenic pharmaceuticals cause organ-specific fetal dysmorphology.

prompt: Match each twin gestation type to its timing of zygotic cleavage.
pairs: Cleavage occurring on Days 1 to 3 post-fertilization
Cleavage occurring on Days 4 to 8 post-fertilization
Cleavage occurring on Days 8 to 12 post-fertilization
Incomplete cleavage occurring after Day 13 post-fertilization
Fertilization of two separate ova by two separate sperm
explain: The precise timing of embryo splitting determines chorionicity and amnionicity.

prompt: Match each congenital intrauterine infection (TORCH) to its classic neonatal hallmark.
pairs: Chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications
Periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, and sensorineural hearing loss
Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus
Hepatomegaly, snuffles, maculopapular desquamating rash, and osteochondritis
Erythroid aplasia, severe fetal anemia, and non-immune hydrops fetalis
explain: Congenital TORCH pathogens produce pathognomonic intracranial calcification patterns and structural defects.

prompt: Match each maneuver for managing shoulder dystocia to its anatomical description.
pairs: Hyperflexion and abduction of maternal thighs onto abdomen
Manual pressure on posterior surface of anterior fetal shoulder pushing toward chest
Manual pressure on anterior surface of posterior shoulder rotating 180 degrees
Delivery of the posterior fetal arm by grasping forearm and sweeping across chest
Cephalic replacement of fetal head into vagina prior to emergency cesarean
explain: Shoulder dystocia maneuvers systematically manipulate maternal pelvis or rotate fetal shoulder diameters.

prompt: Match each vulvar pathology to its characteristic clinical and histological feature.
pairs: Porcelain-white atrophic plaques with epidermal thinning and hyalinized dermis
Erosive, painful glazed erythema with Wickham striae and vaginal synechiae
Leathery lichenified thickened plaques caused by chronic rubbing/scratching
Velvety erythematous 'strawberries and cream' plaques with mucin-positive cells
HPV-associated warty or basaloid atypia in younger smoking women
explain: Vulvar dermatoses and pre-malignancies display characteristic morphological and histological patterns.

prompt: Match each type of abnormal uterine bleeding (FIGO PALM-COEIN classification) to its category.
pairs: Structural lesion of endometrial or endocervical mucosa
Structural presence of endometrial glands deep within the myometrium
Structural benign monoclonal smooth muscle neoplasm (fibroid)
Non-structural systemic bleeding disorder (e.g. von Willebrand disease)
Non-structural endocrine anovulation (e.g. PCOS, thyroid disorder)
explain: FIGO classifies abnormal uterine bleeding into structural (PALM) and non-structural (COEIN) causes.

prompt: Match each uterine leiomyoma (fibroid) anatomical location to its predominant clinical symptom.
pairs: Severe menorrhagia, abnormal bleeding, and impaired implantation / infertility
Heavy prolonged menstrual bleeding and bulk symptoms
Pelvic pressure, urinary frequency, and constipation without menorrhagia
Acute severe pelvic pain if the stalk undergoes acute torsion
Dyspareunia, vaginal discharge, and obstructed labor
explain: Fibroid symptoms correlate directly with proximity to the endometrial cavity vs external pelvic viscera.

prompt: Match each puerperal complication to its diagnostic clinical presentation.
pairs: Persistent spiking fevers despite 48-72 hours of broad-spectrum antibiotics
Transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism within 1 year postpartum
Ischemic necrosis of anterior pituitary causing failure of lactation and amenorrhea
Depressed mood, anhedonia, and functional impairment lasting > 2 weeks
Acute hallucinations, delusions of harming infant, and severe confusion
explain: Postpartum vascular, endocrine, and psychiatric emergencies exhibit distinct temporal courses.

prompt: Match each stage of Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (Quintero staging) to its ultrasound finding.
pairs: Severe oligohydramnios in donor (DVP < 2 cm) and polyhydramnios in recipient (DVP > 8 cm)
Absent visualization of the donor fetal urinary bladder over 60 minutes
Critically abnormal Doppler studies (absent/reversed umbilical end-diastolic flow)
Presence of fetal hydrops in one or both twins
Fetal demise of one or both twins
explain: Quintero staging stratifies TTTS severity from fluid discordance to Doppler failure, hydrops, and demise.

prompt: Match each congenital Müllerian uterine anomaly to its embryological etiology.
pairs: Complete failure of fusion of the two paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts
Partial failure of fusion of the paramesonephric ducts at the superior fundus
Normal fusion with failure of resorption of the midline fibrous inter-ductal septum
Mild, normal fundal indentation of < 1 cm with complete septal resorption
Complete developmental arrest or agenesis of one paramesonephric duct
explain: Müllerian duct development involves elongation, midline fusion, and central septal canalization.

prompt: Match each rare neuroendocrine ovarian tumor to its defining clinical secretion and feature.
pairs: Monodermal teratoma producing thyroid hormone causing thyrotoxicosis
Neuroendocrine teratoma producing serotonin causing carcinoid syndrome without liver metastasis
Sex cord-stromal neoplasm secreting testosterone causing rapid virilization
Sex cord-stromal neoplasm secreting inhibin B and estradiol
Highly malignant trophoblastic neoplasm secreting massive beta-hCG
explain: Functioning ovarian neoplasms secrete active biogenic amines, thyroid hormone, or steroid hormones.

prompt: Match each inherited cancer predisposition syndrome to its gynecologic cancer manifestation.
pairs: 40-60% lifetime risk of endometrial adenocarcinoma and 10% risk of ovarian cancer
40-50% lifetime risk of high-grade serous ovarian/fallopian tube carcinoma
15-25% lifetime risk of high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma
Ovarian sex cord tumors with annular tubules (SCTAT) and adenoma malignum of cervix
Increased lifetime risk of endometrial carcinoma and benign hamartomas
explain: Germline DNA repair defects confer heightened lifetime vulnerabilities to gynecologic malignancies.

prompt: Match each obstetric ultrasound biometric parameter to its primary anatomical landmark.
pairs: Axial plane at level of thalami and cavum septi pellucidi
Outer perimeter of the calvarium at level of thalami
Transverse section through stomach bubble and portal vein J-shape
Full length of the blunt femoral diaphysis excluding epiphysis
Maximal straight-line length from cephalic pole to rump in first trimester
explain: Standard biometric landmarks ensure accurate gestational dating and fetal growth assessment.

prompt: At how many gestational weeks is routine universal screening for gestational diabetes mellitus performed using the 50-g oral glucose challenge test?
explain: Screening is performed at 24 to 28 weeks gestation (midpoint 26 weeks).

prompt: What is the recommended daily intake of supplemental folic acid in milligrams for a low-risk woman planning pregnancy?
explain: 0.4 mg (400 mcg) daily is standard preconception supplementation.

prompt: What is the recommended daily intake of supplemental folic acid in milligrams for a woman with a history of a prior pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect?
explain: High-risk women require 4.0 mg daily starting 3 months prior to conception.

prompt: At how many gestational weeks is universal rectovaginal screening culture for Group B Streptococcus (GBS) performed?
explain: Universal screening occurs between 35 and 37 weeks gestation (midpoint 36 weeks).

prompt: At how many weeks of gestation is prophylactic anti-D immune globulin (RhoGAM) routinely administered to an unsensitized Rh-negative pregnant female?
explain: Standard antenatal prophylaxis is administered at 28 weeks gestation.

prompt: Within how many hours postpartum must a second dose of anti-D immune globulin be administered to an Rh-negative mother if the infant is Rh-positive?
explain: RhoGAM must be administered within 72 hours of delivery.

prompt: What is the systolic blood pressure threshold in mmHg that defines severe range hypertension in preeclampsia?
explain: Systolic BP >= 160 mmHg on two occasions defines severe-range hypertension.

prompt: What is the diastolic blood pressure threshold in mmHg that defines severe range hypertension in preeclampsia?
explain: Diastolic BP >= 110 mmHg defines severe-range hypertension.

prompt: What is the minimum 24-hour urine protein threshold in milligrams defining proteinuria in preeclampsia?
explain: Proteinuria in preeclampsia is defined as >= 300 mg per 24-hour urine collection.

prompt: What is the threshold platelet count in cells/µL below which thrombocytopenia constitutes a severe feature of preeclampsia?
explain: Platelet count < 100,000/µL defines severe preeclampsia.

prompt: What is the normal physiological upper limit of fetal heart rate baseline in beats per minute?
explain: Normal baseline fetal heart rate is 110 to 160 beats per minute.

prompt: What is the normal physiological lower limit of fetal heart rate baseline in beats per minute?
explain: Baseline FHR < 110 bpm defines fetal bradycardia.

prompt: At what cervical dilation in centimeters is active phase labor now officially defined according to contemporary ACOG guidelines?
explain: Active labor is modernly defined as beginning at 6 cm dilation.

prompt: What is the complete cervical dilation in centimeters marking the end of the first stage of labor?
explain: Complete dilation is 10 cm.

prompt: What is the blood loss volume threshold in milliliters defining postpartum hemorrhage following a vaginal delivery according to ACOG redefinition?
explain: ACOG redefined PPH as cumulative blood loss >= 1,000 mL regardless of delivery route.

prompt: What is the loading dose in grams of intravenous magnesium sulfate administered for eclampsia seizure prophylaxis?
explain: A loading dose of 4 to 6 grams IV is given over 15 to 20 minutes.

prompt: What is the continuous maintenance infusion rate in grams per hour of intravenous magnesium sulfate in severe preeclampsia?
explain: Maintenance infusion is standardly 1 to 2 grams per hour.

prompt: What is the therapeutic serum magnesium level in mg/dL targeted during magnesium sulfate infusion in severe preeclampsia?
explain: Therapeutic magnesium range is 4.8 to 8.4 mg/dL (midpoint ~6 mg/dL or 2.0-3.5 mmol/L).

prompt: At what serum magnesium concentration in mg/dL is loss of deep tendon reflexes typically first observed?
explain: Patellar reflexes disappear at magnesium levels around 8 to 10 mg/dL (midpoint 9 mg/dL).

prompt: What is the discriminatory zone threshold of serum beta-hCG in mIU/mL above which an intrauterine gestational sac should be visualized on transvaginal ultrasound?
explain: The discriminatory zone is standardly 1,500 to 2,000 mIU/mL.

prompt: What is the upper limit of normal postmenopausal endometrial stripe thickness in millimeters on transvaginal ultrasound beyond which biopsy is indicated?
explain: Endometrial thickness > 4 mm in a postmenopausal bleeding patient mandates tissue biopsy.

prompt: At what age in years should routine cervical cancer screening (Pap smear) commence in average-risk females?
explain: Cervical cancer screening begins universally at age 21.

prompt: At what age in years can routine cervical cancer screening be safely discontinued in an average-risk woman with adequate prior negative screening?
explain: Screening ceases at age 65 if adequate negative prior screening is documented.

prompt: What is the normal duration in days of the human menstrual cycle around which physiological variation is centered?
explain: Normal menstrual cycle length is 21 to 35 days (mean 28 days).

prompt: What is the normal duration of the luteal phase in days in a healthy ovulatory menstrual cycle?
explain: The luteal phase is remarkably constant at 14 days (13-15 days).

prompt: What is the average age of natural menopause in years in the United States?
explain: Average age of natural menopause is 51.4 years.

prompt: Before what age in years is cessation of menses defined as premature ovarian insufficiency (POI)?
explain: Menopause occurring before age 40 defines premature ovarian insufficiency.

prompt: What is the threshold Bishop score out of 13 above which a cervix is considered favorable for successful labor induction?
explain: A Bishop score >= 8 predicts high likelihood of vaginal delivery.

prompt: What is the gestational age in completed weeks defining full term pregnancy (early term threshold)?
explain: Full term begins at 37 weeks (37 0/7 weeks).

prompt: What is the gestational age in completed weeks defining post-term pregnancy?
explain: Pregnancy reaching 42 0/7 weeks is classified as post-term.

prompt: What is the threshold gestational age in weeks at or after which External Cephalic Version (ECV) is recommended for breech presentation?
explain: ECV is performed at >= 37 weeks gestation.

prompt: What is the gestational age in weeks at which elective delivery is recommended for uncomplicated monochorionic monoamniotic (MoMo) twins?
explain: MoMo twins are delivered electively by cesarean at 32 to 34 weeks (midpoint 33 weeks).

prompt: What is the gestational age in weeks at which elective delivery is recommended for uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic (MoDi) twins?
explain: MoDi twins are delivered at 36 0/7 to 37 0/7 weeks gestation.

prompt: What is the gestational age in weeks at which elective delivery is recommended for uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic (DiDi) twins?
explain: DiDi twins are delivered at 38 0/7 to 38 6/7 weeks gestation.

prompt: What is the normal amniotic fluid index (AFI) midpoint value in centimeters in the third trimester?
explain: Normal AFI is 8 to 24 cm (mean ~14 cm); < 5 cm is oligohydramnios, > 24 cm is polyhydramnios.

prompt: What is the amniotic fluid index threshold in centimeters below which oligohydramnios is diagnosed?
explain: An AFI < 5 cm (or single deepest pocket < 2 cm) defines oligohydramnios.

prompt: What is the amniotic fluid index threshold in centimeters above which polyhydramnios is diagnosed?
explain: An AFI > 24 cm (or single deepest pocket > 8 cm) defines polyhydramnios.

prompt: What is the crown-rump length (CRL) threshold in millimeters on transvaginal ultrasound above which absence of fetal cardiac activity confirms early pregnancy loss?
explain: A CRL >= 7 mm without a heartbeat establishes early pregnancy failure.

prompt: What is the mean sac diameter (MSD) threshold in millimeters on transvaginal ultrasound above which absence of an embryo confirms early pregnancy loss?
explain: An MSD >= 25 mm without an embryo establishes early pregnancy failure.

prompt: How many hours of sustained clinical improvement and afebrile state are required before discontinuing intravenous antibiotics in postpartum endometritis?
explain: Patients should be afebrile and symptom-free for at least 24 hours before stopping IV antibiotics.

prompt: What is the threshold fetal middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) in multiples of the median (MoM) that predicts moderate-to-severe fetal anemia?
explain: An MCA-PSV > 1.5 MoM indicates fetal anemia warranting invasive assessment.

prompt: What is the standard standard dose in micrograms of anti-D immune globulin (RhoGAM) administered in a full vial?
explain: A standard vial contains 300 mcg (1,500 IU) of anti-D globulin, protecting against 30 mL of fetal whole blood.

prompt: How many milliliters of fetal whole blood are neutralized by a standard 300 mcg dose of anti-D immune globulin?
explain: 300 mcg covers 30 mL of fetal whole blood (or 15 mL of packed fetal red cells).

prompt: What is the critical maternal anti-D antibody titer ratio at or above which intensive fetal surveillance with MCA-PSV Doppler is initiated?
explain: A critical titer of 1:16 (or 1:32 at some centers) triggers specialized fetal Doppler monitoring.

prompt: What is the threshold serum FSH level in mIU/mL in a woman under 40 years of age that supports a diagnosis of premature ovarian insufficiency?
explain: An FSH > 30-40 mIU/mL on two occasions at least 1 month apart confirms hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

prompt: Within how many minutes of maternal cardiac arrest should perimortem cesarean delivery be initiated to optimize maternal and fetal survival?
explain: The 4-minute rule mandates perimortem cesarean delivery initiation by 4 minutes, aiming for delivery by 5 minutes.

prompt: What is the normal umbilical artery Doppler systolic-to-diastolic (S/D) ratio threshold upper limit at 34 weeks gestation beyond which placental insufficiency is suspected?
explain: The normal umbilical artery S/D ratio decreases with advancing gestation and should be < 3.0 after 30-34 weeks.

prompt: How many years of surveillance following diagnosis of Ulcerative Colitis is the recommended interval before initiating surveillance colonoscopy for colorectal cancer in women?
explain: Surveillance colonoscopy begins 8 years after symptom onset in pancolitis.

prompt: Which form of cell death is characterized by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, apoptotic body formation, and intact plasma membrane without inciting inflammation?
explain: Apoptosis is a programmed, ATP-dependent form of cell death involving caspase cascades that packages cellular contents into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies without evoking acute inflammation.

prompt: In ischemic coagulative necrosis of the myocardium, what histological feature persists in the infarcted tissue for several days?
explain: Coagulative necrosis denatures both structural proteins and lysosomal enzymes, preserving cellular outlines ("tombstones") without nuclei for several days.

prompt: Which type of cellular adaptation is exemplified by the transformation of normal esophageal stratified squamous epithelium to nonciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells in chronic acid reflux?
explain: Barrett esophagus represents glandular metaplasia, a reversible reprogramming of stem cells to replace squamous with intestinal columnar epithelium to withstand acid.

prompt: What type of necrosis is uniquely characteristic of ischemic stroke and cerebral infarctions?
explain: The brain lacks a substantial collagenous stroma and is rich in hydrolytic lysosomal enzymes released by microglial cells, leading to enzymatic digestion and liquefactive necrosis.

prompt: Which cellular adhesion molecule on postcapillary venular endothelial cells mediates the initial rolling phase of neutrophil extravasation by binding Sialyl-Lewis X?
explain: Endothelial E-selectin and P-selectin bind sialyl-Lewis X carbohydrates on leukocytes to mediate loose, low-affinity rolling interactions along the vessel wall.

prompt: Which vasoactive amine is rapidly released by mast cell degranulation to cause arteriolar vasodilation and increased venular endothelial permeability?
explain: Preformed histamine stored in mast cell granules is released via IgE cross-linking or physical stimuli, inducing endothelial contraction and immediate postcapillary venular leak.

prompt: Which cell type is the principal histological hallmark of chronic granulomatous inflammation, characteristically forming multinucleated Langhans giant cells?
explain: Activated macrophages assume an abundant pink "epithelioid" cytoplasm under the influence of interferon-gamma and fuse to form Langhans multinucleated giant cells.

prompt: Which growth factor is the most potent stimulator of fibroblast migration, collagen deposition, and myofibroblast differentiation during tissue repair and fibrosis?
explain: TGF-beta is the master cytokine driving chronic fibrosis, suppressing collagenase activity and upregulating extracellular matrix production.

prompt: What triad of primary pathophysiological abnormalities defines Virchow's triad predisposing to intravascular thrombosis?
explain: Virchow triad encompasses endothelial injury, abnormal hemodynamics (stasis or turbulence), and hypercoagulability of the blood.

prompt: Which type of embolus is characteristically associated with traumatic fractures of long bones and presents with dyspnea, confusion, and petechial rash?
explain: Fat embolism syndrome occurs 24-72 hours following pelvic or long bone fractures due to marrow fat globules entering venous sinusoids.

prompt: Which tumor suppressor gene product, often called the "guardian of the genome," arrests the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint in response to DNA damage?
explain: TP53 upregulates p21 (CDKN1A), which inhibits cyclin D-CDK4 complexes, arresting the cell cycle to allow DNA repair or inducing apoptosis via BAX if damage is irreparable.

prompt: Which reciprocal chromosomal translocation is the cytogenetic hallmark of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), generating the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene?
explain: The Philadelphia chromosome represents t(9;22), fusing ABL1 on chromosome 9 with BCR on chromosome 22 to produce a constitutively active tyrosine kinase.

prompt: Which chromosomal translocation characterizes Burkitt lymphoma, juxtaposing the MYC proto-oncogene with the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter?
explain: Burkitt lymphoma carries t(8;14), which places c-MYC under control of the strong Ig heavy chain enhancer on chromosome 14, driving rapid B-cell proliferation.

prompt: What serum tumor marker is elevated in non-seminomatous testicular germ cell tumors and hepatocellular carcinoma?
explain: AFP is produced by fetal yolk sac and liver, serving as a reliable clinical biomarker for hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumors.

prompt: Which hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by antigen-antibody immune complex deposition in vascular walls, followed by complement activation and neutrophil-mediated vasculitis?
explain: Type III hypersensitivity involves circulating immune complexes (e.g., SLE, serum sickness, poststreptococcal GN) that deposit and trigger complement-mediated tissue destruction.

prompt: Which autoantibodies are most sensitive for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and which are most specific?
choices: Anti-nuclear antibodies are most sensitive; Anti-dsDNA and Anti-Smith are most specific
Anti-dsDNA is most sensitive; ANA is most specific
Anti-Ro/SSA is most sensitive; Anti-La/SSB is most specific
Anti-centromere is most sensitive; Anti-Scl-70 is most specific
explain: ANA has >95% sensitivity (best screening test), while anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies have high specificity for SLE.

prompt: What pathognomonic staining property defines amyloid deposits when stained with Congo red and viewed under polarized light microscopy?
explain: Amyloid fibril cross-beta-pleated sheet conformation produces distinct apple-green birefringence under cross-polarized light after Congo red staining.

prompt: What is the most common chromosomal mechanism causing Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)?
choices: Maternal meiotic nondisjunction during meiosis I
Paternal meiotic nondisjunction during meiosis II
explain: Approximately 95% of Down syndrome cases arise from maternal meiotic nondisjunction, primarily occurring during maternal meiosis I.

prompt: Which histological feature is observed 1 to 3 days after an acute myocardial infarction?
choices: Coagulative necrosis with dense neutrophilic infiltration
Contraction band necrosis with early edema only
Dense fibrovascular granulation tissue with collagen
explain: Neutrophils peak at 24 to 72 hours (1-3 days) post-MI, infiltrating coagulatively necrotic myocardium to clear necrotic debris.

prompt: What myocardial complication of acute transmural myocardial infarction occurs most commonly between days 3 and 14 due to macrophage-mediated tissue softening?
explain: Macrophage clearing of necrotic myocytes produces structural wall weakening at 3 to 14 days, risking free wall rupture, interventricular septal rupture, or papillary muscle rupture.

prompt: Which pathognomonic histological lesion characterizes acute rheumatic carditis, consisting of granulomatous foci with Anitschkow "caterpillar" cells?
explain: Aschoff bodies are myocardial granulomas containing Anitschkow cells (activated histiocytes with wavy "caterpillar" chromatin) specific to acute rheumatic fever.

prompt: What is the primary predisposing etiology for acute non-traumatic aortic dissection involving the ascending aorta (Stanford Type A)?
explain: Chronic systemic hypertension is the single most common risk factor for aortic dissection, causing cystic medial degeneration of the aortic media.

prompt: Which large-vessel vasculitis predominantly affects elderly females, involves branches of the carotid artery, and carries an acute risk of irreversible blindness?
explain: Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of the temporal and ophthalmic arteries; involvement of the ophthalmic branch can cause ischemic optic neuropathy and blindness.

prompt: Which subtype of emphysema is strongly linked to cigarette smoking and preferentially involves the respiratory bronchioles of the upper lung lobes?
choices: Paraseptal (distal acinar) emphysema along the pleura
explain: Smoking-associated emphysema selectively destroys the central respiratory bronchioles (centriacinar) with an upper-lobe predilection; panacinar emphysema is linked to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

prompt: What pathognomonic microscopic structures are seen in the sputum of chronic asthma patients, representing eosinophil membrane-derived crystalline bipyramidal proteins?
explain: Charcot-Leyden crystals are hexagonal bipyramidal crystals derived from eosinophil galectin-10/lysophospholipase; Curschmann spirals are whorled mucus plugs.

prompt: Which diffuse parenchymal lung disease is characterized histopathologically by non-caseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and elevated serum ACE levels?
explain: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease characterized by tightly formed non-caseating granulomas, bilateral hilar adenopathy, and hypercalcemia via 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

prompt: Which subtype of primary lung carcinoma is strongly associated with non-smokers, arises peripherally, and commonly harbors activating EGFR or ALK mutations?
explain: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung malignancy overall and among non-smokers; it arises in peripheral lung tissue and is frequently driven by EGFR, KRAS, or ALK alterations.

prompt: Which glomerular disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, showing normal light microscopy and diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy?
explain: Minimal change disease shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence, and widespread podocyte effacement on EM, responding promptly to corticosteroids.

prompt: What pattern of immunofluorescence is pathognomonic for Goodpasture syndrome (Anti-GBM disease)?
choices: Linear IgG deposits along the GBM
explain: Goodpasture syndrome involves autoantibodies directed against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, yielding unbroken linear deposition of IgG along the GBM.

prompt: What is the most common primary renal malignancy in adults, classically arising from proximal convoluted tubular epithelium and exhibiting clear lipid-rich cytoplasm?
explain: Clear cell RCC accounts for 75-80% of renal malignancies, characteristically linked to loss of the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p.

prompt: Which chronic inflammatory bowel disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas, and cobblestone mucosal architecture?
explain: Crohn disease can affect any segment of the GI tract from mouth to anus with discontinuous "skip" transmural ulceration, fistulas, and non-caseating granulomas.

prompt: Which chronic inflammatory bowel disease is confined to the mucosa and submucosa, begins in the rectum, and extends continuously proximally?
explain: Ulcerative colitis exhibits contiguous mucosal inflammation extending from the rectum into the colon with crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps, and loss of haustra ("lead pipe").

prompt: What histological feature in a small intestinal mucosal biopsy confirms the diagnosis of celiac disease?
choices: Intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia, and villous atrophy
Transmural lymphoid aggregates with fissuring ulcers
Lamina propria distention by PAS-positive foamy macrophages
explain: Celiac disease presents with duodenal intraepithelial CD8+ T-cell infiltration, crypt elongation/hyperplasia, and blunting or total atrophy of intestinal villi.

prompt: What distinctive eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions composed of cytokeratin intermediate filaments are seen inside degenerating hepatocytes in alcoholic steatohepatitis?
explain: Mallory-Denk bodies are tangled clumps of ubiquitinated intermediate keratin filaments found inside ballooned hepatocytes in alcohol-induced and metabolic steatohepatitis.

prompt: Which chronic autoimmune liver disease is characterized by granulomatous destruction of medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts and high-titer anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA)?
explain: PBC is an autoimmune liver disease affecting middle-aged women, characterized by AMA seropositivity and progressive interlobular bile duct destruction.

prompt: What is the most common subtype of thyroid malignancy, characterized histologically by Orphan Annie eye nuclei, psammoma bodies, and nuclear pseudoinclusions?
explain: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, recognized by ground-glass clear nuclei ("Orphan Annie"), nuclear grooves, and concentric calcifications (psammoma bodies).

prompt: Which thyroid neoplasm arises from neuroendocrine calcitonin-secreting parafollicular C cells and is associated with germline RET mutations in MEN 2A and 2B?
explain: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from neural crest-derived C cells, secretes calcitonin, deposits amyloid stroma, and is associated with MEN2 RET proto-oncogene mutations.

prompt: Which neuroendocrine tumor of the adrenal medulla arises from chromaffin cells, secretes catecholamines, and exhibits a "Zellballen" nesting pattern on histology?
explain: Pheochromocytoma consists of nests ("Zellballen") of polygonal chromaffin cells surrounded by sustentacular cells, causing episodic headaches, diaphoresis, and hypertension.

prompt: Which morphological finding on peripheral blood smear is diagnostic of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) seen in TTP, HUS, and DIC?
choices: Spherocytes with loss of central pallor
Target cells with excess cell membrane
explain: Mechanical shearing of red blood cells across microvascular fibrin thrombi shears erythrocytes into fragmented schistocytes (helmet cells).

prompt: What pathognomonic binucleated giant cell with prominent eosinophilic "owl-eye" nucleoli defines Hodgkin lymphoma histologically?
explain: Classic Reed-Sternberg cells are CD15+ and CD30+ crippled B-cells characterized by two mirror-image nuclei each bearing an owl-eye nucleolus.

prompt: Which cytogenetic abnormality characterizes acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, AML M3) and responds dramatically to all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)?
explain: Translocation t(15;17) fuses the PML gene with the retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARA) gene, arresting promyelocytes; ATRA forces terminal granulocytic differentiation.

prompt: Which myeloproliferative neoplasm is defined by the gain-of-function JAK2 V617F mutation in >95% of patients, manifesting with panmyelosis and elevated hematocrit?
explain: Polycythemia vera is driven by the JAK2 V617F tyrosine kinase mutation, causing constitutive cytokine-independent erythrocyte, granulocyte, and platelet production.

prompt: Which intracranial hemorrhage is typically caused by traumatic rupture of the middle meningeal artery and presents with a lucid interval followed by rapid coma?
explain: Epidural hematoma results from skull pterion fractures tearing the middle meningeal artery, producing a biconvex lentiform hyperdensity on non-contrast CT.

prompt: Which intracranial hemorrhage is caused by rupture of bridging cortical veins, commonly in elderly patients after minor head trauma, yielding a crescent-shaped hematoma?
explain: Subdural hematomas arise from tearing of bridging cortical veins traversing the subdural space, forming a concavo-convex crescentic collection that crosses suture lines.

prompt: What are the two core histopathological hallmarks of Alzheimer disease in cerebral cortical tissue?
choices: Beta-amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles
Intracellular alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies and ubiquitin inclusions
TDP-43 cytoplasmic aggregates and Bunina bodies
Spongiform vacuolation of neuropil and PrPSc plaques
explain: Alzheimer disease is defined by extracellular senile plaques composed of A-beta-42 peptides and intraneuronal neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau.

prompt: What pathognomonic cytoplasmic inclusion composed of alpha-synuclein is found within degenerating substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson disease?
explain: Lewy bodies are round, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions containing insoluble alpha-synuclein polymers that displace the nucleus in pigmented nigral neurons.

prompt: Which primary high-grade malignant brain tumor in adults crosses the corpus callosum ("butterfly glioma") and displays pseudopalisading necrosis on histology?
explain: Glioblastoma is a WHO Grade 4 astrocytoma showing microvascular endothelial proliferation and serpentine areas of pseudopalisading ischemic necrosis.

prompt: What intracellular pigment, known as the "wear-and-tear" aging pigment, accumulates in lysosomes as a result of lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids?
explain: Lipofuscin is an insoluble brownish-yellow granular pigment composed of oxidized lipids and proteins that accumulates progressively in aging myocardium and liver.

prompt: Which hemodynamic profile is characteristic of SEPTIC SHOCK?
choices: Decreased systemic vascular resistance, increased cardiac output, and warm extremities
Increased systemic vascular resistance, decreased cardiac output, and cold extremities
Increased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure with severe bradycardia and pulmonary edema
Decreased central venous pressure with severe hypertension
explain: Septic shock causes widespread vasodilation (low SVR) mediated by nitric oxide and cytokines, compensated by an early hyperdynamic high cardiac output state.

prompt: Which primary immunodeficiency is caused by a failure of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches to develop, leading to thymic hypoplasia and severe hypocalcemia?
explain: DiGeorge syndrome results from a 22q11.2 microdeletion impairing 3rd/4th pharyngeal pouch development, yielding absent parathyroids (hypocalcemia) and thymus (T-cell deficiency).

prompt: What underlying genetic defect causes cystic fibrosis, leading to abnormally thick and viscid exocrine secretions?
choices: Autosomal recessive mutation in the CFTR chloride channel gene (commonly delta-F508)
Trinucleotide CAG repeat expansion in huntingtin
explain: Cystic fibrosis is caused by CFTR gene mutations (most commonly deletion of phenylalanine at position 508), causing misfolded chloride channels and thick secretions.

prompt: What is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, typically presenting as a pedunculated gelatinous mass in the left atrium causing "ball-valve" mitral obstruction?
explain: Left atrial myxomas are benign mesenchymal neoplasms embedded in an acid mucopolysaccharide-rich stroma that can intermittently obstruct the mitral valve.

prompt: Which occupational pneumoconiosis is characterized by "eggshell" calcification of hilar lymph nodes and birefringent silica particles surrounded by dense concentric whorls of collagen?
explain: Silicosis causes dense concentric fibrotic nodules with polarized silica crystals, predominantly in upper lobes, with characteristic eggshell hilar nodal calcification.

prompt: Which renal disorder presents in diabetic patients with nodular glomerulosclerosis characterized by Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules?
explain: Diabetic glomerulosclerosis exhibits non-enzymatic glycation leading to efferent arteriolar hyalinosis, hyperfiltration, and PAS-positive mesangial Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules.

prompt: Which inherited colorectal cancer syndrome is caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes leading to microsatellite instability (MSI)?
explain: Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition due to defects in MSH2, MLH1, MSH6, or PMS2, predisposing to early right-sided colon cancer and endometrial carcinoma.

prompt: What genetic disorder of iron overload is characterized by autosomal recessive mutations in HFE (C282Y), leading to excessive intestinal iron absorption and "bronze diabetes"?
explain: Hereditary hemochromatosis results from impaired hepcidin regulation, causing systemic hemosiderin deposition in hepatocytes, pancreas, skin, and myocardium.

prompt: What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas, characterized by Hurthle cells, lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, and anti-TPO antibodies?
explain: Hashimoto thyroiditis is autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland with intense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, germinal centers, and metaplastic oncocytes (Hurthle cells).

prompt: Which monoclonal gammopathy is characterized by clonal plasma cell proliferation, lytic bone lesions, Bence Jones proteinuria, and hypercalcemia (CRAB criteria)?
explain: Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of marrow plasma cells secreting monoclonal IgG or IgA, causing hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, and "punched-out" bone lesions.

prompt: Which motor neuron disease causes combined upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron degeneration without sensory loss, with familial cases linked to SOD1 mutations?
explain: ALS produces both UMN (spasticity, hyperreflexia) and LMN (atrophy, fasciculations) signs without sensory or cognitive impairment; linked to SOD1 and C9orf72 mutations.

prompt: Which proto-oncogene encoding a small GTPase is the most frequently mutated oncogene in human cancers, notably pancreatic adenocarcinoma?
explain: KRAS point mutations impair intrinsic GTPase activity, locking the protein into a permanently GTP-bound active state that continuously drives cell proliferation.

prompt: What cellular process involves lysosomal degradation of the cell's own components to survive nutrient deprivation, regulated by ATG genes?
explain: Autophagy is an evolutionary conserved survival mechanism where intracellular organelles are sequestered in double-membrane autophagosomes and digested by lysosomes.

prompt: Which cytokine synthesized predominantly by macrophages is a key mediator of acute phase responses, fever, and cachexia in chronic illness?
explain: TNF-alpha stimulates hypothalamic PGE2 to induce fever, activates endothelial adhesion molecules, and suppresses lipoprotein lipase, causing cachexia.

prompt: What alternating macroscopic banding pattern of pale platelet/fibrin layers and dark red cell layers identifies an antemortem thrombus from a postmortem clot?
explain: Lines of Zahn represent alternating laminar deposits of platelets/fibrin and RBCs formed in flowing blood, confirming that the thrombus formed antemortem.

prompt: Which autoimmune disease is characterized by keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth) with anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies?
explain: Sjogren syndrome is an autoimmune destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands mediated by CD4+ T cells, presenting with sicca syndrome and anti-SSA/SSB.

prompt: Which genetic disorder is characterized by a 45,X karyotype, streak ovaries, short stature, webbed neck, and coarctation of the aorta?
explain: Turner syndrome (complete or partial monosomy X) presents with primary amenorrhea, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, lymphedema, and aortic coarctation.

prompt: Which cardiomyopathy is characterized by asymmetric septal hypertrophy, myofiber disarray, and mutations in sarcomeric proteins such as beta-myosin heavy chain?
explain: HCM is an autosomal dominant disease of sarcomere contractile proteins causing massive interventricular septal thickening, myocyte disarray, and sudden cardiac death in athletes.

prompt: What histological finding characterizes acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) on lung biopsy during the exudative phase?
choices: Diffuse alveolar damage with intra-alveolar hyaline membranes
Extensive caseating granulomas with central necrosis
Dense intra-alveolar eosinophilic proteinaceous exudate without inflammatory cells
explain: ARDS manifests histologically as diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) with endothelial/epithelial necrosis, edema, and fibrin-rich hyaline membranes lining alveolar ducts.

prompt: Which pediatric renal neoplasm is composed of a triphasic mixture of blastemal, stromal, and epithelial elements, associated with WT1 gene mutations on chromosome 11p?
choices: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney
explain: Wilms tumor is the most common pediatric renal malignancy, presenting with an asymptomatic flank mass and exhibiting triphasic histology driven by WT1 or WT2 alterations.

prompt: What is the most common site of origin for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST), which typically harbor activating mutations in the c-KIT (CD117) tyrosine kinase gene?
explain: GIST arises most frequently in the muscularis propria of the stomach (60%), originating from interstitial cells of Cajal driven by KIT or PDGFRA mutations.

prompt: Which autosomal recessive disorder is caused by ATP7B mutations, leading to copper accumulation in the liver, brain (basal ganglia), and Kayser-Fleischer corneal rings?
explain: Wilson disease is characterized by defective biliary copper excretion due to ATP7B mutations, causing low ceruloplasmin, liver cirrhosis, chorea, and copper corneal rings.

prompt: What syndrome results from an autonomous pituitary adenoma oversecreting growth hormone after the closure of epiphyseal growth plates in adults?
explain: In adults, GH excess cannot stimulate longitudinal bone growth; instead, it causes acral bone overgrowth, coarse facial features, visceromegaly, and insulin resistance.

prompt: Which inherited hemoglobinopathy results from a missense mutation in the beta-globin gene substituting valine for glutamic acid at codon 6 (Glu6Val)?
explain: Sickle cell disease results from a point mutation replacing hydrophilic glutamic acid with hydrophobic valine, causing polymerization of deoxygenated HbS into sickle shapes.

prompt: What vascular lesion is the most frequent cause of spontaneous, non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage, typically located at arterial branch points in the circle of Willis?
explain: Saccular berry aneurysms develop at branching bifurcations of the anterior communicating or middle cerebral artery; rupture causes thunderclap headache.

prompt: What pattern of tissue calcification occurs in necrotic or degenerating tissues in the presence of completely normal serum calcium and phosphate levels?
explain: Dystrophic calcification deposits calcium salts locally in damaged or dead tissues (e.g., calcific aortic stenosis, caseous granulomas) despite normal serum calcium.

prompt: Which plasma enzyme-derived peptide system generates bradykinin, producing marked arteriolar dilation, increased vascular permeability, and somatic pain?
explain: Hageman factor (XIIa) activates prekallikrein into kallikrein, which cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to liberate bradykinin.

prompt: What histological feature distinguishes a red (hemorrhagic) infarct from a white (pale) infarct?
choices: Occurrence in organs with dual blood supply or loose connective tissue (e.g., lung, intestine)
Occurrence in solid organs with end-arterial circulation (e.g., spleen, kidney)
Immediate total absence of extravasated erythrocytes
explain: Red infarcts occur in tissues with dual circulations (lungs, liver), loose stroma, or venous occlusion where blood continues to seep into necrotic parenchyma.

prompt: Which form of amyloidosis is derived from immunoglobulin light chain fragments produced by monoclonal plasma cell dyscrasias?
explain: AL amyloidosis arises from clonal plasma cells producing excess lambda or kappa immunoglobulin light chains that misfold into insoluble beta-pleated fibrils.

prompt: Which genetic disorder is caused by a 47,XXY karyotype, presenting with tall stature, testicular atrophy, gynecomastia, and elevated FSH/LH?
explain: Klinefelter syndrome is male hypogonadism with an extra X chromosome, resulting in dysgenesis of seminiferous tubules, low testosterone, and elevated gonadotropins.

prompt: What is the characteristic histological finding in polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) during its acute inflammatory phase?
choices: Transmural necrotizing inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis sparing pulmonary vessels
Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch
Leukocytoclastic vasculitis of postcapillary venules only
explain: PAN is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries showing segmental transmural fibrinoid necrosis; pulmonary arteries are classically spared.

prompt: Which malignant tumor of the pleura is strongly linked to chronic asbestos exposure, has a latency of 25-45 years, and stains positive for calretinin and WT1?
explain: Mesothelioma is a highly aggressive pleural neoplasm linked to amphibole asbestos exposure; calretinin, cytokeratin 5/6, and WT1 immunopositivity confirm diagnosis.

prompt: Which rapid progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) feature is observed on light microscopy, composed of proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating monocytes?
explain: Glomerular crescents represent proliferating parietal epithelial cells and macrophages along with fibrin exudate inside Bowman space, compressing the glomerular tuft.

prompt: Which type of gastric adenocarcinoma is characterized by diffuse infiltration of the gastric wall with mucin-filled signet-ring cells and loss of E-cadherin (CDH1)?
explain: Diffuse-type gastric cancer is driven by CDH1 loss, producing non-cohesive signet ring cells that infiltrate the submucosa and muscularis, creating a rigid "leather bottle" stomach.

prompt: What vascular disorder is caused by thrombotic occlusion of two or more major hepatic veins, leading to severe centrilobular congestion, hepatomegaly, and ascites?
explain: Budd-Chiari syndrome results from hepatic venous outflow obstruction (often associated with myeloproliferative disorders), causing acute liver congestion and ischemic injury.

prompt: What congenital disorder of adrenal steroidogenesis results from 21-hydroxylase deficiency, causing ambiguous genitalia in females and salt-wasting crises in neonates?
explain: Deficiency of 21-hydroxylase impairs cortisol and aldosterone synthesis while shunting steroid precursors into androgens, causing virilization and hypotension.

prompt: Which acute leukemia is characterized morphologically by blasts containing Auer rods and positive myeloperoxidase (MPO) staining?
explain: Auer rods are crystal aggregates of fused azurophilic granules containing myeloperoxidase, diagnostic of myeloid lineage (AML).

prompt: Which autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disease is caused by an unstable CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4?
explain: Huntington disease involves CAG repeats encoding an expanded polyglutamine tract, leading to toxic gain of function, caudate atrophy, chorea, and dementia.

prompt: Which childhood intraocular tumor is caused by bilateral loss-of-function mutations in both alleles of the RB1 gene on chromosome 13q14?
explain: Retinoblastoma exemplified Knudson's "two-hit hypothesis" of tumor suppressor genes; loss of both RB1 alleles drives retinal neuroblastic proliferation.

prompt: Which form of arteriolosclerosis is characterized by concentric, laminated "onion-skin" thickening of arteriolar walls with luminal narrowing in malignant hypertension?
explain: Severe, malignant hypertension produces hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with concentric smooth muscle proliferation and basement membrane duplication.

prompt: Which histological finding is seen in the lungs of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), displaying temporal and spatial heterogeneity?
choices: Usual interstitial pneumonia pattern with fibroblastic foci and honeycomb lung
Diffuse homogenous ground-glass alveolar septal thickening
Multiple non-caseating granulomas along bronchovascular bundles
explain: The UIP pattern is defined by patchy interstitial fibrosis, subpleural honeycombing, and microscopic fibroblastic foci juxtaposed with normal lung.

prompt: What type of urinary casts are pathognomonic for acute glomerulonephritis on microscopic urinalysis?
explain: RBC casts form when glomerular bleeding allows erythrocytes to enter nephrons and become entrapped in Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein.

prompt: Coagulative necrosis is the characteristic pattern of ischemic necrosis in all solid organs except the brain.
explain: Hypoxic cell death in solid organs (heart, kidney, spleen) produces coagulative necrosis; the brain uniquely develops liquefactive necrosis.

prompt: Apoptosis typically elicits a vigorous surrounding neutrophilic acute inflammatory reaction.
explain: Apoptosis is non-inflammatory; apoptotic cells are rapidly phagocytosed before cellular membranes rupture.

prompt: Hyperplasia can occur only in tissues capable of mitotic cellular division.
explain: Permanent nondividing tissues (e.g., myocardium, neurons) can undergo hypertrophy but cannot undergo hyperplasia.

prompt: Dystrophic calcification occurs exclusively in the setting of severe hypercalcemia.
explain: Dystrophic calcification occurs in necrotic or degenerating tissues in patients with completely normal serum calcium levels.

prompt: Caseous necrosis is pathognomonic for tuberculous mycobacterial infection.
explain: Caseous necrosis is characteristic of tuberculosis but not pathognomonic: it also occurs in systemic fungal infections such as histoplasmosis.

prompt: Enzymatic fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis is mediated by the release of activated pancreatic lipases.
explain: Activated lipases hydrolyze triglyceride esters into fatty acids, which combine with calcium to produce insoluble calcium soaps (saponification).

prompt: Metaplasia is an irreversible genetic transformation of one adult cell type into another.
explain: Metaplasia is a reversible adaptive phenotypic change that reverts if the noxious underlying stimulus is removed.

prompt: Lipofuscin accumulation causes significant functional impairment of myocardial contractility.
explain: Lipofuscin is a benign biomarker of cellular wear-and-tear and lipid peroxidation that does not intrinsically cause myocardial dysfunction.

prompt: Bcl-2 is a pro-apoptotic protein that promotes mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization.
explain: Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL stabilize the outer mitochondrial membrane, preventing release of cytochrome c into the cytosol.

prompt: Cytochrome c release from mitochondria triggers the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis by binding Apaf-1.
explain: Cytosolic cytochrome c complexes with Apaf-1 and procaspase-9 to form the apoptosome, initiating executioner caspase activation.

prompt: Lymphocytes are the predominant leukocyte population in the acute inflammatory exudate during the first 6 to 24 hours.
explain: Neutrophils respond most rapidly to chemokines, outnumbering mononuclear cells in the first 24 hours before macrophages predominate at 48 hours.

prompt: Transudates have a high protein concentration (>3.0 g/dL) and high specific gravity compared to exudates.
explain: Transudates are low-protein, low-cellularity fluids caused by altered hydrostatic/oncotic pressures; exudates are protein-rich from vascular permeability.

prompt: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (LAD-1) is caused by a congenital defect in fucosylation of sialyl-Lewis X.
explain: Defective CD18 prevents formation of functional LFA-1 and Mac-1 integrins, abolishing firm leukocyte arrest on vascular endothelium.

prompt: Interferon-gamma secreted by TH1 cells is the primary cytokine responsible for activating macrophages into epithelioid cells in granulomas.
explain: IFN-gamma induces classical M1 macrophage activation, promoting phagocytic killing and epithelioid transformation.

prompt: Granulation tissue is histologically identical to a granuloma.
explain: Granulation tissue is a reparative tissue consisting of proliferating capillaries, fibroblasts, and myofibroblasts; a granuloma is a chronic immune aggregate of epithelioid histiocytes.

prompt: Type I collagen is the initial structural collagen deposited in healing wounds and is later replaced by Type III collagen.
explain: Granulation tissue initially deposits pliable Type III collagen, which is remodeled over weeks by matrix metalloproteinases into tensile Type I collagen.

prompt: Keloids are exuberant fibrotic scars that remain strictly confined within the boundaries of the original wound.
explain: Hypertrophic scars remain confined to wound margins; keloids extend pathologically beyond original margins and rarely regress.

prompt: Histamine mediates prolonged, delayed endothelial vascular permeability lasting several days.
explain: Histamine induces an immediate, transient response lasting only 15 to 30 minutes.

prompt: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) acts on the hypothalamus to elevate the thermoregulatory temperature set point, inducing fever.
explain: Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, TNF) induce vascular endothelial COX-2 to generate PGE2, which shifts hypothalamic set point upward.

prompt: C5a is a potent chemotactic factor for neutrophils and monocytes as well as an anaphylatoxin.
explain: Complement component C5a promotes leukocyte chemotaxis, endothelial activation, and triggers mast cell degranulation.

prompt: Arterial thrombi typically form at sites of endothelial injury and grow in the direction of blood flow, away from the heart.
explain: Arterial thrombi propagate in a retrograde direction toward the heart, while venous thrombi propagate anterograde in the direction of blood flow.

prompt: Lines of Zahn are characteristic histological bands found within postmortem blood clots.
explain: Lines of Zahn form exclusively in flowing blood antemortem and distinguish true thrombi from postmortem "currant jelly" clots.

prompt: A saddle pulmonary embolus occludes the main pulmonary artery bifurcation, causing acute cor pulmonale and sudden death.
explain: Large emboli straddling the pulmonary bifurcation obstruct RV outflow, precipitating acute electromechanical dissociation and shock.

prompt: Cardiogenic shock is characterized by low systemic vascular resistance and low pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.
explain: Pump failure lowers cardiac output, triggering compensatory vasoconstriction (high SVR) and backwards fluid accumulation (high PCWP).

prompt: Red (hemorrhagic) infarcts occur characteristically in solid organs with end-arterial circulations such as the kidney and spleen.
explain: Pale (white) infarcts occur in solid end-arterial organs; red infarcts occur in dual-circulation organs (lung, gut) or with reperfusion.

prompt: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) causes both widespread microvascular thrombosis and severe consumptive bleeding.
explain: Uncontrolled thrombin generation consumes platelets, fibrinogen, and factors V and VIII, precipitating paradoxical diffuse hemorrhage.

prompt: Decompression sickness (the "bends") is caused by rapid liberation of dissolved nitrogen bubbles into the bloodstream.
explain: Ascending rapidly from depth reduces ambient pressure, causing inert nitrogen gas dissolved in tissues to form intravascular gas emboli.

prompt: Left-sided heart failure causes nutmeg liver due to passive chronic venous congestion of hepatic central veins.
explain: Elevated right atrial pressure transmits to hepatic veins, causing centrilobular sinusoidal congestion with sparing of periportal tracts.

prompt: Anasarca refers to severe, generalized full-body subcutaneous edema.
explain: Anasarca is gross generalized edema involving subcutaneous tissues, peritoneal space (ascites), and pleural cavities.

prompt: Neurogenic shock features peripheral vasoconstriction and severe reflex tachycardia.
