explain: HOCM and MVP uniquely INCREASE/lengthen with decreased preload (Valsalva strain); AS decreases; MR/AR increase with handgrip.

prompt: Match each respiratory disorder with its typical pulmonary function test (PFT) ratio profile:
pairs: FEV1/FVC < 0.70, increased TLC and RV, decreased DLCO
FEV1/FVC normal or increased (> 0.75), reduced TLC, reduced RV, markedly reduced DLCO
FEV1/FVC normal or increased, reduced TLC and FVC, NORMAL DLCO
FEV1/FVC < 0.70 with significant (> 12% and > 200 mL) reversibility post-bronchodilator
FEV1/FVC < 0.70 with normal or near-normal DLCO
explain: Obstructive = low FEV1/FVC; Restrictive intrinsic = normal ratio, low volumes, low DLCO; Restrictive extrinsic = normal DLCO; Asthma = reversible.

prompt: Match each renal tubular transport defect / tubulopathy with its clinical syndrome:
pairs: Loss of NKCC2 function in TAL; mimics loop diuretics (hypokalemia, alkalosis, hypercalciuria)
Loss of NCCT function in DCT; mimics thiazides (hypokalemia, alkalosis, hypocalciuria)
Gain of ENaC function in collecting duct; mimics hyperaldosteronism (hypertension with low renin and low aldo)
Defective alpha-intercalated H+ ATPase; inability to acidify urine (urine pH > 5.5, nephrocalcinosis)
Defective PCT HCO3- reabsorption (Fanconi syndrome); urine pH < 5.5 once systemic HCO3- drops
explain: Bartter = loop defect; Gitelman = thiazide defect; Liddle = constitutive ENaC; Type 1 RTA = urine pH > 5.5; Type 2 RTA = proximal HCO3- wasting.

prompt: Match each sensory receptor with its specific sensory nerve fiber classification and physiological pathway:
pairs: Type Ia fibers (large myelinated; monitor rate of muscle stretch; myotatic reflex)
Type Ib fibers (monitor muscle tension; inverse myotatic reflex)
Type II fibers (monitor static muscle length)
Fast sharp pain and cool temperature
A-delta fibers (thinly myelinated; rapid initial localized nociception)
Slow burning pain and warm temperature
C fibers (unmyelinated; slow dull ache, polymodal nociception)
explain: Ia = dynamic stretch; Ib = tension; II = static length; A-delta = fast pain; C = slow unmyelinated pain.

prompt: Match each congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) enzyme deficiency with its presentation:
pairs: Most common; low aldosterone and cortisol, high androgens; salt wasting, virilization, hypotension
Low aldosterone and cortisol, but 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) accumulates; hypertension and virilization
Loss of sex steroids and cortisol; high mineralocorticoids; hypertension, hypokalemia, XY pseudohermaphroditism
Blocks all active steroid synthesis; salt wasting, ambiguous genitalia in both sexes
Cannot synthesize estrogens; virilization of female fetus and maternal virilization during pregnancy
explain: 21-OH def = salt wasting + virilization; 11-OH def = hypertension + virilization; 17-OH def = hypertension + lack of androgens.

prompt: Match each gastrointestinal cell type with its primary hormone or peptide product:
explain: Parietal = HCl/IF; Chief = pepsinogen; G cells = gastrin; I cells = CCK; S cells = secretin.

prompt: Match each electrocardiographic interval or wave with its underlying cellular electrophysiology:
pairs: Atrial depolarization initiated by SA node firing
Ventricular depolarization (Phase 0 of ventricular action potentials)
Ventricular repolarization (Phase 3 mediated by outward K+ currents)
Conduction delay through the atrioventricular (AV) node
Plateau phase of ventricular action potentials (Phase 2; isoelectric state)
explain: P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; T = ventricular repolarization; PR segment = AV delay; ST = Phase 2 plateau.

prompt: Match each type of hypoxia with its diagnostic blood gas and oxygen content pattern:
pairs: Decreased arterial PaO2 and decreased oxygen saturation (SaO2)
Normal arterial PaO2, normal SaO2, but markedly decreased total oxygen content (CaO2)
Normal arterial PaO2, severely reduced functional SaO2, reduced total CaO2
Normal arterial PaO2, normal CaO2, but markedly reduced mixed venous PvO2
Normal arterial PaO2, normal CaO2, but elevated mixed venous PvO2 due to failure of cellular extraction
explain: Hypoxemic = low PaO2; Anemic = low Hb/CaO2 with normal PaO2; CO = normal PaO2, low SaO2; Ischemic = low tissue perfusion; Histotoxic = high venous PO2.

prompt: Match each acid-base compensatory formula with its clinical diagnostic application:
pairs: Assesses respiratory compensation in Metabolic Acidosis
Detects concurrent non-gap metabolic acidosis (< 1) or metabolic alkalosis (> 2)
Calculates expected respiratory hypoventilation for Metabolic Alkalosis
[HCO3-] rises 1 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg acute rise in PaCO2 above 40
[HCO3-] rises 3.5 to 4 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg chronic rise in PaCO2 above 40
explain: Winter = metabolic acidosis; Delta-delta = mixed gap disorders; Met alkalosis = 0.7xHCO3+21; Acute resp acidosis = 1 per 10; Chronic = 3.5-4 per 10.

prompt: Match each neurotoxin with its molecular mechanism of ion channel or receptor blockade:
pairs: Block voltage-gated Na+ channels, abolishing action potential generation
Bind and keep voltage-gated Na+ channels persistently open, preventing repolarization
Blocks voltage-gated K+ channels, prolonging action potential duration
Cleaves presynaptic SNARE proteins (SNAP-25, syntaxin), blocking acetylcholine release
Cleaves synaptobrevin in inhibitory Renshaw cells, preventing glycine/GABA release
explain: TTX = blocks Na+; Ciguatoxin = opens Na+; Dendrotoxin = blocks K+; Botulinum = blocks ACh release (flaccid); Tetanus = blocks glycine release (spastic).

prompt: Match each specialized cardiovascular hemodynamic phenomenon with its physiological mechanism:
pairs: Exaggerated drop in systolic BP (> 10 mmHg) during inspiration; caused by cardiac tamponade and pericardial constraint
Paradoxical rise in JVP during inspiration; caused by constrictive pericarditis impeding RV filling
Beat-to-beat alternation in arterial pulse amplitude at regular rhythm; sign of severe left ventricular failure
Biphasic systolic pulse with two peaks; classic for combined aortic stenosis and regurgitation or HOCM
Rapid upstroke with rapid collapse due to massive stroke volume and diastolic runoff in aortic regurgitation
explain: Pulsus paradoxus = tamponade; Kussmaul = constrictive pericarditis; Pulsus alternans = severe LV systolic failure; Bisferiens = AS/AR; Water-hammer = AR.

prompt: What is the canonical resting heart rate in a healthy adult human at rest?
explain: The standard reference resting heart rate for a healthy adult is 72 beats per minute (normal range 60-100 bpm).

prompt: What is the normal resting cardiac output in a healthy adult male of 70 kg?
explain: Normal resting cardiac output is approximately 5.0 L/min (calculated as stroke volume of 70 mL x heart rate of 72 bpm).

prompt: What is the normal resting stroke volume ejected by the left ventricle per beat in an average adult?
explain: Standard resting stroke volume is approximately 70 mL (EDV ~120 mL - ESV ~50 mL).

prompt: What is the normal resting left ventricular ejection fraction in a healthy adult?
explain: Normal resting ejection fraction is approximately 55-65% (canonical benchmark: 60%).

prompt: What is the standard normal resting systolic blood pressure in a healthy young adult at sea level?
explain: Standard baseline normal systolic blood pressure is 120 mmHg.

prompt: What is the standard normal resting diastolic blood pressure in a healthy adult?
explain: Standard baseline normal diastolic blood pressure is 80 mmHg.

prompt: What is the calculated mean arterial pressure (MAP) for a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg?
explain: MAP = DBP + 1/3(SBP - DBP) = 80 + 1/3(40) = 93.3 mmHg (standard: 93 mmHg).

prompt: What is the normal resting Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy young adult male per 1.73 m2 body surface area?
explain: Normal baseline GFR is approximately 125 mL/min (~180 liters of filtrate per day).

prompt: What is the normal resting respiratory rate in a healthy adult at rest?
explain: Normal resting adult respiratory rate is approximately 12 to 16 breaths/min (standard reference: 12 breaths/min).

prompt: What is the normal tidal volume (volume of air moved per quiet breath) in an average 70 kg adult male?
explain: Normal resting tidal volume is approximately 500 mL (~7 mL/kg).

prompt: What is the normal volume of anatomical dead space in the conducting airways of an average adult?
explain: Anatomical dead space is approximately 150 mL (roughly 2.2 mL/kg or 1 mL per pound of ideal body weight).

prompt: What is the normal physiological pH of arterial blood in a healthy human?
explain: Arterial blood pH is tightly regulated at 7.40 (normal range 7.35 to 7.45).

prompt: What is the normal arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) at sea level?
explain: Normal arterial PaCO2 is 40 mmHg (normal range 35 to 45 mmHg).

prompt: What is the normal arterial plasma bicarbonate concentration ([HCO3-]) in a healthy adult?
explain: Normal arterial serum bicarbonate concentration is 24 mEq/L (normal range 22 to 26 mEq/L).

prompt: What is the normal arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) in a healthy young adult breathing room air at sea level?
explain: Normal arterial PaO2 is approximately 95 mmHg (normal range 90-100 mmHg).

prompt: What is the typical resting membrane potential of a large mammalian nerve axon?
explain: The standard resting membrane potential of a typical large neuron is -70 mV.

prompt: What is the resting membrane potential of a healthy working human ventricular cardiomyocyte during Phase 4?
explain: Ventricular cardiomyocytes have a resting membrane potential of approximately -90 mV due to inward rectifier K+ (IK1) channels.

prompt: What is the approximate threshold membrane potential required to fire an action potential in a typical mammalian neuron?
explain: Threshold potential for opening voltage-gated Na+ channels is typically around -55 mV.

prompt: What is the normal extracellular sodium concentration in human serum?
explain: Normal serum sodium concentration is approximately 140 mEq/L (normal range 135 to 145 mEq/L).

prompt: What is the normal extracellular potassium concentration in human serum?
explain: Normal serum potassium is approximately 4.0 mEq/L (normal range 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L).

prompt: What is the typical intracellular potassium concentration inside a resting mammalian cell?
explain: Intracellular potassium concentration is approximately 140 mEq/L.

prompt: What is the normal extracellular chloride concentration in human serum?
explain: Normal serum chloride concentration is approximately 100 mEq/L (normal range 96 to 106 mEq/L).

prompt: What is the normal total plasma osmolarity in a healthy adult human?
explain: Normal serum osmolarity is approximately 285 to 295 mOsm/kg (canonical value: 290 mOsm/kg).

prompt: What percentage of total resting cardiac output is delivered to the kidneys (renal fraction)?
explain: The kidneys receive approximately 20-25% of total resting cardiac output (~1.0 to 1.2 L/min).

prompt: What is the normal filtration fraction (GFR divided by renal plasma flow, GFR / RPF) in a healthy human?
explain: Normal filtration fraction is approximately 20% (125 mL/min GFR / 625 mL/min RPF = 0.20).

prompt: What is the average 24-hour daily urine volume produced by a healthy adult with average water intake?
explain: Normal daily urine output averages approximately 1500 mL (1.5 liters) per day.

prompt: What is the normal PR interval duration on a standard surface electrocardiogram (ECG)?
explain: Normal PR interval is 120 to 200 ms (standard benchmark: 160 ms or 4 small boxes).

prompt: What is the normal upper limit of QRS complex duration on a standard surface ECG in adults?
explain: Normal QRS duration is less than 100 to 120 ms (benchmark upper normal limit is 100 ms or 2.5 small boxes).

prompt: What is the normal fasting blood glucose concentration in a healthy non-diabetic human adult?
explain: Normal fasting blood glucose ranges from 70 to 99 mg/dL (canonical reference: 90 mg/dL).

prompt: What is normal core human body temperature in degrees Celsius?
explain: Normal human core body temperature is 37.0 degrees Celsius (98.6 degrees Fahrenheit).

prompt: What is the normal resting Vital Capacity (VC) in a healthy 70 kg young adult male?
explain: Normal vital capacity in a healthy young adult male averages approximately 4500 mL (4.5 L).

prompt: What is the normal Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) in a resting adult male?
explain: Normal FRC (residual volume + expiratory reserve volume) is approximately 2400 mL (2.4 L).

prompt: What is the normal Total Lung Capacity (TLC) in a healthy young adult male?
explain: Normal total lung capacity is approximately 6000 mL (6.0 L).

prompt: What is the normal Alveolar PO2 (PAO2) breathing room air at sea level (calculated from the alveolar gas equation)?
What is the normal upper limit of the Alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient in a healthy young adult breathing room air?
explain: In young adults breathing room air at sea level, the normal A-a gradient is typically between 5 and 10 mmHg (age/4 + 4).

prompt: What is the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) percentage cutoff below which acute kidney injury is classified as prerenal azotemia?
explain: FENa < 1% indicates intact tubular sodium reabsorption characteristic of prerenal hypoperfusion.

prompt: What is the normal effective Renal Plasma Flow (eRPF) in an adult male estimated by PAH clearance?
explain: Normal resting renal plasma flow is approximately 600 to 650 mL/min (standard reference: 625 mL/min).

prompt: What is the normal maximum concentrating ability of human kidneys for urine osmolarity under maximal ADH stimulation?
explain: Under maximal dehydration and ADH release, the human renal countercurrent multiplier concentrates urine up to 1200 mOsm/kg.

prompt: What is the normal reference value for the serum anion gap calculated as [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-])?
explain: Normal serum anion gap without potassium is 8 to 12 mEq/L (canonical midpoint: 10 mEq/L).

prompt: What is the upper normal limit of the corrected QT interval (QTc) in adult males on ECG?
explain: Normal QTc in adult males is less than 440 ms; values > 450 ms in males or > 460 ms in females are prolonged.

prompt: What is the normal upper limit of intracranial pressure (ICP) in a resting, recumbent adult?
explain: Normal adult intracranial pressure in the supine position is 5 to 15 mmHg; pressures sustained > 20-22 mmHg require active treatment.

prompt: What is the normal serum ionized calcium concentration in healthy human plasma?
explain: Normal ionized (free) calcium is approximately 1.15 to 1.30 mmol/L (standard reference: 1.2 mmol/L or ~4.8 mg/dL).

prompt: What is the normal mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) in a healthy adult at rest at sea level?
explain: Normal resting mean pulmonary artery pressure is 10 to 18 mmHg (benchmark: 14 mmHg; pulmonary hypertension is defined as > 20 mmHg).

prompt: What is the normal mean capillary wedge pressure (PCWP), reflecting left atrial pressure, in a resting adult?
explain: Normal PCWP ranges from 6 to 12 mmHg (canonical midpoint: 8 mmHg).

prompt: What is the normal central venous pressure (CVP / right atrial pressure) in a resting supine adult?
explain: Normal right atrial pressure (CVP) ranges from 2 to 6 mmHg (canonical reference: 4 mmHg).

prompt: What is the basal gastric juice pH inside the human stomach during fasting?
explain: Resting fasting gastric acid maintains a pH between 1.5 and 2.0.

prompt: What is the normal resting ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) ratio for the entire lung as a whole?
explain: Total alveolar ventilation (~4.0 L/min) divided by total cardiac output (~5.0 L/min) yields a whole-lung V/Q ratio of 0.8.

prompt: What is the typical plasma glucose concentration threshold (transport maximum threshold) at which glucosuria first begins to appear in urine?
explain: While the theoretical transport maximum (TmG) corresponds to ~300 mg/dL, glomerulotubular splay causes glucose to first appear in urine around 180-200 mg/dL.

prompt: What is the approximate positive endolymphatic potential in the scala media of the cochlea relative to perilymph?
explain: The stria vascularis actively secretes K+, generating an endocochlear potential of +80 mV that provides the driving force for hair cell depolarization.

prompt: What is the maximum normal duration of the corrected QT interval (QTc) in adult females before it is considered pathologically prolonged?
explain: In adult females, a QTc > 460 ms (and > 470 ms in clinical risk stratification) is classified as prolonged.

prompt: What is the most common cause of acute appendicitis in children and young adults?
explain: Lymphoid hyperplasia is the primary etiology in children and young adults, whereas fecaliths are more common in older adults.

prompt: Which clinical sign is characterized by right lower quadrant pain elicited by palpation of the left lower quadrant?
explain: Rovsing sign is pain in the right lower quadrant during left lower quadrant deep palpation due to peritoneal irritation.

prompt: What is the initial imaging study of choice for suspected acute cholecystitis?
explain: Right upper quadrant ultrasound is the initial study of choice, exhibiting high sensitivity for gallstones, wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid.

prompt: Which hernia passes medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through Hesselbach triangle?
explain: Direct inguinal hernias protrude directly through the abdominal wall weakness in Hesselbach triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

prompt: Which hernia passes lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep inguinal ring?
explain: Indirect inguinal hernias enter the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels due to a patent processus vaginalis.

prompt: What is the classic triad of Charcot in acute cholangitis?
choices: Fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain
explain: Charcot triad consists of fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice, signaling ascending bacterial cholangitis.

prompt: Which sign involves cessation of inspiration upon deep palpation of the right upper quadrant?
explain: Murphy sign is arrested inspiration during subcostal RUQ palpation, characteristic of acute cholecystitis.

prompt: What is the most common cause of mechanical small bowel obstruction in patients with prior abdominal surgery?
explain: Postoperative peritoneal adhesions account for approximately 60-75% of small bowel obstructions in adults with surgical history.

prompt: Which condition presents with severe periumbilical pain completely out of proportion to physical examination findings?
explain: Pain out of proportion to abdominal exam is the classic hallmark of early acute mesenteric ischemia.

prompt: What is the primary initial step in the evaluation of a trauma patient according to ATLS?
choices: Airway maintenance with cervical spine protection
explain: The primary survey in ATLS strictly prioritizes Airway maintenance with cervical spine motion restriction (A).

prompt: What is the immediate treatment for a tension pneumothorax in an unstable patient before a chest tube can be placed?
explain: Immediate needle decompression (2nd intercostal space midclavicular line or 5th ICS anterior axillary line) converts tension pneumothorax to simple pneumothorax.

prompt: What anatomical landmark separates an upper gastrointestinal bleed from a lower gastrointestinal bleed?
explain: The ligament of Treitz (suspensory muscle of the duodenum) is the formal anatomical boundary between upper and lower GI bleeding.

prompt: Which type of shock is characteristically seen in acute cardiac tamponade?
explain: Cardiac tamponade impairs diastolic filling, producing obstructive shock.

prompt: What is Beck triad in cardiac tamponade?
choices: Hypotension, jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds
Fever, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice
explain: Beck triad consists of systemic hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and distant/muffled heart sounds.

prompt: Which type of thyroid carcinoma is the most common?
explain: Papillary thyroid carcinoma comprises over 80% of all thyroid cancers and has an excellent overall prognosis.

prompt: What histopathological feature is pathognomonic for papillary thyroid carcinoma?
choices: Orphan Annie eye nuclei and psammoma bodies
Amyloid stroma with positive calcitonin immunostaining
explain: Orphan Annie eye nuclei (optically clear chromatin) and psammoma bodies are characteristic of papillary thyroid cancer.

prompt: Which parameter is evaluated first during the FAST ultrasound exam in blunt abdominal trauma?
explain: The hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch) is the most dependent space of the upper peritoneum in the supine patient and the most sensitive single view.

prompt: In a patient with suspected compartment syndrome of the lower extremity, what is the definitive therapeutic procedure?
explain: Urgent surgical fasciotomy of the affected compartments is mandatory to prevent irreversible muscle ischemia and necrosis.

prompt: Which arterial aneurysm is the most common in the peripheral arterial system?
explain: Popliteal artery aneurysms are the most common peripheral aneurysms, frequently bilateral and associated with abdominal aortic aneurysms.

prompt: What is the classic diagnostic radiographic finding of sigmoid volvulus on plain abdominal X-ray?
explain: A massively dilated, inverted U-shaped loop pointing toward the right upper quadrant produces the classic 'coffee bean' appearance.

prompt: Which complication is the leading cause of death within the first 24 hours following major thermal burns?
explain: Massive capillary leak and plasma exudation cause profound burn shock (hypovolemic shock) in the first 24 hours without adequate resuscitation.

prompt: What is the recommended screening test for abdominal aortic aneurysm in men aged 65-75 with a history of smoking?
explain: USPSTF recommends a 1-time screening abdominal ultrasound in men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked.

prompt: What size threshold of an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm generally warrants elective surgical repair?
explain: Elective repair is recommended when an abdominal aortic aneurysm reaches 5.5 cm in men (or 5.0 cm in women) or grows >0.5 cm in 6 months.

prompt: Which nerve is at highest risk of injury during an open thyroidectomy, leading to hoarseness?
explain: Unilateral injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve impairs vocal cord abduction/adduction, resulting in persistent hoarseness.

prompt: Which surgical sign represents ecchymosis of the periumbilical region indicating retroperitoneal hemorrhage?
explain: Cullen sign is superficial periumbilical ecchymosis caused by hemoperitoneum or tracking of retroperitoneal bleeding.

prompt: What is the initial management for an unruptured sliding inguinal hernia that is easily reducible?
choices: Strict bed rest and an abdominal truss indefinitely
explain: An easily reducible inguinal hernia can be safely scheduled for elective outpatient herniorrhaphy or hernioplasty.

prompt: What is the first-line treatment for acute cholangitis once hemodynamic resuscitation is initiated?
choices: Intravenous antibiotics and emergent biliary decompression
explain: Urgent biliary decompression (typically via ERCP) and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics are life-saving in acute cholangitis.

prompt: Which condition is characterized by Reynolds pentad?
explain: Reynolds pentad includes Charcot triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) plus hypotension and altered mental status, representing septic shock from acute cholangitis.

prompt: What is the most common location of diverticulitis in Western populations?
explain: In Western populations, pseudodiverticula occur overwhelmingly in the sigmoid colon due to high intraluminal pressure.

prompt: Which nerve injury results in 'winged scapula' after axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer?
explain: The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior; injury leads to medial winging of the scapula.

prompt: Which structure is most commonly injured in blunt abdominal trauma in motor vehicle collisions?
explain: The spleen is the most frequently injured solid visceral organ in blunt abdominal trauma, closely followed by the liver.

prompt: What is the classic diagnostic triad of abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture?
choices: Abdominal/back pain, pulsatile abdominal mass, hypotension
Chest pain, syncope, muffled heart sounds
explain: The triad of acute severe abdominal or back pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass, and hypotension indicates rupture.

prompt: What is the gold standard imaging modality to diagnose acute diverticulitis and rule out complications like abscess or perforation?
explain: CT with IV contrast is the gold standard; colonoscopy and barium enemas are contraindicated acutely due to risk of perforation.

prompt: Which burn resuscitation formula specifies 4 mL × body weight (kg) × % total body surface area burned in the first 24 hours?
explain: The Parkland formula dictates 4 mL Ringer's lactate × kg × %TBSA over the initial 24 hours, giving half in the first 8 hours.

prompt: What is the definitive management for an acute epidural hematoma with significant midline shift?
choices: Burr hole drainage at bedside under local anesthesia
explain: Emergent surgical craniotomy and hematoma evacuation is the definitive treatment to relieve intracranial mass effect.

prompt: Which vessel is most commonly lacerated in an acute epidural hematoma following temporal bone fracture?
explain: Laceration of the middle meningeal artery underneath the pterion is the classic source of epidural hemorrhage.

prompt: Which vascular structure is torn in a traumatic subdural hematoma?
explain: Tearing of parasagittal bridging cortical veins as they cross the subdural space produces a crescent-shaped subdural hematoma.

prompt: What is the primary diagnostic test for suspected acute pulmonary embolism in a hemodynamically stable patient?
explain: CT pulmonary angiography is the definitive and preferred first-line imaging modality for stable patients suspected of acute PE.

prompt: What is the most appropriate next step for an acutely strangulated, non-reducible femoral hernia?
choices: CT scan with oral and intravenous contrast first
explain: Strangulated hernias require emergent surgical exploration; reduction attempts are contraindicated because ischemic bowel may be returned to the peritoneal cavity.

prompt: Which antibiotic regimen is standard for surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis in clean-contaminated elective colorectal operations?
explain: Cefazolin provides coverage against enteric gram-negative rods and skin flora, while metronidazole provides anaerobic coverage.

prompt: In a patient presenting with acute scrotal pain, absence of the cremasteric reflex strongly suggests which diagnosis?
explain: Absence of the ipsilateral cremasteric reflex is one of the most reliable clinical signs distinguishing testicular torsion from epididymitis.

prompt: What is the golden time window for surgical detorsion and orchiopexy to achieve high testicular salvage rates in testicular torsion?
explain: Testicular salvage rates exceed 90% if surgical detorsion is performed within 6 hours of symptom onset.

prompt: Which test is used during physical examination to detect an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear with the highest sensitivity?
explain: The Lachman test has superior sensitivity compared to the anterior drawer test for detecting acute ACL disruptions.

prompt: What is the most common cause of early postoperative fever occurring on postoperative days 1 to 2?
explain: Pulmonary atelectasis ('Wind') is the most frequent cause of fever within the first 24-48 hours after major surgery.

prompt: Which tumor marker is primarily used to monitor recurrence and response to treatment in colorectal cancer?
explain: CEA is the established serum tumor marker for monitoring recurrence in treated colorectal carcinoma.

prompt: Which serum tumor marker is most sensitive for monitoring pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma?
explain: Carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9) is elevated in over 80% of patients with advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

prompt: What is the primary management for a traumatic open pneumothorax ('sucking chest wound') at the scene?
choices: Completely occlusive dressing on all four sides
explain: A three-sided occlusive dressing acts as a flutter valve, allowing air to escape during expiration while preventing air entry during inspiration.

prompt: What is the classic physical examination finding of retroperitoneal rupture in acute pancreatitis presenting as flank ecchymosis?
explain: Grey Turner sign is flank ecchymosis resulting from retroperitoneal blood tracking along fascial planes.

prompt: Which inherited colorectal cancer syndrome is characterized by thousands of adenomatous colonic polyps and near 100% risk of cancer without colectomy?
explain: FAP is caused by germline APC mutations, leading to hundreds or thousands of polyps and mandatory prophylactic proctocolectomy.

prompt: What is the definitive surgical procedure of choice for resectable adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head?
explain: A pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) resects the pancreatic head, duodenum, proximal jejunum, gallbladder, and distal common bile duct.

prompt: Which type of groin hernia has the highest risk of strangulation and is more common in elderly females?
explain: Femoral hernias pass through the narrow, rigid femoral canal medial to the femoral vein, bearing a high risk of incarceration and strangulation.

prompt: What is the treatment of choice for acute suppurative parotitis that does not respond to conservative intravenous hydration and antibiotics?
explain: When conservative measures fail, surgical incision and drainage along the lines of the facial nerve is required to relieve compartment pressure.

prompt: Which electrolyte disturbance is the most urgent concern following total thyroidectomy due to accidental removal of parathyroid glands?
explain: Accidental devascularization or excision of the parathyroid glands causes profound hypocalcemia, causing perioral tingling, tetany, and laryngospasm.

prompt: What bedside physical exam sign for hypocalcemia involves tapping the facial nerve to elicit facial muscle twitching?
explain: Chvostek sign is ipsilateral facial muscle spasm elicited by tapping over the anterior branch of the facial nerve at the angle of the jaw.

prompt: A 45-year-old trauma victim receives 10 units of packed red blood cells within 2 hours. Which complication is most likely unless proactively monitored?
choices: Metabolic acidosis from lactate overload alone
explain: Citrate in stored blood chelates serum ionized calcium, leading to acute hypocalcemia and cardiac dysfunction during massive transfusion.

prompt: Which finding on diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) defines a positive result in blunt abdominal trauma?
explain: A positive DPL for blunt trauma is defined by aspiration of >10 mL gross blood, >100,000 RBCs/µL, >500 WBCs/µL, or presence of bile/food/bacteria.

prompt: In a patient with severe acute pancreatitis who develops fever and leukocytosis on day 10, what is the best next diagnostic step?
explain: Contrast-enhanced CT assesses for necrotizing pancreatitis and peripancreatic fluid collections; fine-needle aspiration or drainage may be guided if infected necrosis is suspected.

prompt: Which mechanism explains the development of Curling ulcer in severely burned patients?
choices: Severe mucosal ischemia secondary to hypovolemia and systemic stress
Direct thermal injury to gastric mucosa
explain: Curling ulcers are acute stress ulcers of the stomach and duodenum caused by systemic hypotension and splanchnic vasoconstriction in severe burns.

prompt: What is the primary indication for surgical placement of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter in deep venous thrombosis (DVT)?
choices: Initial presentation of unprovoked proximal DVT
explain: IVC filters are indicated when therapeutic anticoagulation is contraindicated, causes life-threatening bleeding, or fails to prevent recurrent PE.

prompt: Which zone of the neck in penetrating trauma extends from the cricoid cartilage to the angle of the mandible?
explain: Zone II of the neck spans from the cricoid cartilage to the angle of the mandible; it contains the carotid arteries, jugular veins, and larynx.

prompt: A patient presents with painless gross hematuria, a flank mass, and polycythemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explain: Renal cell carcinoma presents classically (though rarely in its full triad) with flank pain, hematuria, and a palpable mass, frequently accompanied by paraneoplastic erythropoietin production.

prompt: What is the most appropriate management for a clean surgical incision that suffers deep dehiscence with evisceration?
choices: Cover with moist sterile gauze and emergent return to operating room
Immediate bedside closure with retention sutures under local anesthesia
Application of negative pressure wound therapy (wound VAC)
explain: Evisceration requires covering exposed viscera with sterile saline-moistened dressings and emergent formal operative exploration and closure.

prompt: Which type of bile duct injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy involves complete transection of the common bile duct?
explain: Strasberg Type E injuries correspond to Bismuth classifications involving major circumferential transection or occlusion of the main common hepatic/bile ducts.

prompt: In a patient undergoing carotid endarterectomy, which cranial nerve injury manifests as deviation of the tongue toward the operative side?
choices: Facial nerve marginal mandibular branch (CN VII)
explain: The hypoglossal nerve courses through the carotid triangle; injury causes ipsilateral genioglossus weakness and tongue protrusion toward the injured side.

prompt: What is the definitive initial diagnostic test for suspected Boerhaave syndrome (esophageal perforation)?
explain: Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) swallow is preferred initially because extravasated barium can cause severe mediastinal fibrosis.

prompt: Which vascular condition is characterized by chronic postprandial abdominal pain, fear of eating ('food fear'), and significant weight loss?
explain: Chronic mesenteric ischemia ('intestinal angina') results from atherosclerotic narrowing of at least 2 of 3 splanchnic arteries, provoking postprandial pain.

prompt: Which maneuver involves temporary digital occlusion of the portal triad at the foramen of Winslow to arrest hepatic hemorrhage?
explain: The Pringle maneuver compresses the hepatic artery and portal vein within the hepatoduodenal ligament to control hepatic inflow hemorrhage.

prompt: Which surgical mobilization maneuver exposes the retroperitoneal duodenum and head of the pancreas?
explain: The Kocher maneuver incises the lateral peritoneal reflection of the duodenum to reflect it medially, exposing the retroperitoneum.

prompt: What is the most common cause of early small bowel obstruction within the first 30 days after laparotomy?
explain: Early postoperative mechanical SBO is typically caused by fibrinous adhesions, which generally respond to conservative nasogastric decompression.

prompt: Which surgical condition causes a triad of gallstone ileus: pneumobilia, small bowel obstruction, and an ectopic radiopaque gallstone?
explain: Rigler triad consists of small bowel mechanical obstruction, pneumobilia (air in biliary tree), and an ectopic gallstone in the right iliac fossa.

prompt: Where does an ectopic gallstone most commonly impact to cause gallstone ileus?
explain: The terminal ileum and ileocecal valve represent the narrowest segment of the small bowel, making it the most frequent impaction site.

prompt: What is the definitive treatment for acute acalculous cholecystitis in a critically ill, hemodynamically unstable ICU patient?
explain: Percutaneous cholecystostomy provides immediate bedside gallbladder decompression in patients too unstable to tolerate general anesthesia.

prompt: What is the recommended surgical management for a solitary follicular neoplasm on thyroid fine-needle aspiration (FNA)?
choices: Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection
Observation with repeat FNA in 3 months
explain: FNA cannot distinguish benign follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma (capsular/vascular invasion requires histology); diagnostic lobectomy is standard.

prompt: Which type of parotid gland neoplasm is the most common benign tumor?
explain: Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor) is the most frequent salivary gland tumor, representing ~70% of parotid neoplasms.

prompt: Which condition is diagnosed when an intra-abdominal pressure exceeds 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction?
explain: Abdominal compartment syndrome is defined by sustained intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg accompanied by new end-organ failure, requiring decompressive laparotomy.

prompt: What is the landmark for determining the depth of invasion in Breslow thickness for cutaneous melanoma?
choices: Granular layer to the deepest tumor cell
Stratum corneum to the subcutaneous fat
Papillary dermis to the deep reticular dermis
Basal lamina to the regional lymph nodes
explain: Breslow thickness measures the vertical depth in millimeters from the granular layer of the epidermis to the deepest malignant melanoma cell.

prompt: What is the recommended surgical margin for wide local excision of an invasive melanoma with Breslow thickness of 1.5 mm?
explain: For melanomas with thickness 1.01 to 2.0 mm, clinical guidelines recommend a 1 to 2 cm surgical margin down to muscular fascia.

prompt: Which surgical complication presents with watery diarrhea, fever, and leukocytosis 5 days after perioperative clindamycin?
explain: Clostridioides difficile overgrowth and toxin production causes pseudomembranous colitis following antibiotic exposure.

prompt: What is the primary surgical therapy for high-grade non-muscle invasive bladder cancer refractory to BCG immunotherapy?
explain: BCG-unresponsive high-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer mandates radical cystectomy to prevent progression to muscle-invasive or metastatic disease.

prompt: In a patient with pheochromocytoma, what is the crucial pharmacological preparation required before surgical adrenalectomy?
choices: Immediate high-dose intravenous hydrocortisone monotherapy before induction
explain: Alpha-blockade (e.g. phenoxybenzamine) must precede beta-blockade to prevent unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and catastrophic hypertensive crisis.

prompt: Which scoring system utilizes PaO2/FiO2, age, WBC count, and hemodynamic criteria to assess acute pancreatitis severity at admission and 48 hours?
explain: Ranson criteria evaluate 5 parameters at admission and 6 parameters at 48 hours to stratify pancreatitis severity and mortality risk.

prompt: Which type of aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta and requires emergency surgical intervention?
explain: Stanford Type A dissections involve the ascending aorta and carry high early mortality from rupture, tamponade, or acute aortic insufficiency; they mandate emergency surgery.

prompt: Which physical finding indicates retroperitoneal bleeding around the inguinal ligament?
explain: Fox sign is ecchymosis over the anteromedial aspect of the thigh near the inguinal ligament, reflecting retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

prompt: What is the preferred operative approach for an unstable patient with gunshot wounds to the abdomen and active massive bleeding?
explain: Damage control laparotomy emphasizes rapid control of hemorrhage and contamination, temporary abdominal closure, and resuscitation in the ICU before definitive reconstruction.

prompt: Which test is most specific for diagnosing a traumatic rupture of the diaphragm?
choices: CT scan of the chest and abdomen
Plain upright chest radiograph showing nasogastric tube in the left hemithorax
explain: Visualizing a coiled nasogastric tube or hollow viscus herniating into the left hemithorax on chest radiography or direct laparoscopy/thoracoscopy provides definitive proof.

prompt: In a patient undergoing hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) after cytoreductive surgery for pseudomyxoma peritonei, what is the origin of the primary lesion?
explain: Pseudomyxoma peritonei originates almost exclusively from low- or high-grade mucinous neoplasms of the vermiform appendix.

prompt: Which inherited cancer syndrome is caused by mutations in the RET proto-oncogene, featuring medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism?
explain: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2A (MEN 2A) features medullary thyroid carcinoma, bilateral pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia.

prompt: During parathyroidectomy, what intraoperative laboratory decline confirms successful resection of the hyperfunctioning parathyroid adenoma?
choices: >50% decrease in intact PTH at 10 minutes post-excision compared to pre-incision baseline
>20% decrease in intact PTH at 30 minutes
Normalization of total serum calcium within 5 minutes
explain: The Miami criterion requires a >50% drop in intact PTH from baseline at 10 minutes after adenoma excision.

prompt: In liver transplantation, what anatomical variation presents with a replaced right hepatic artery arising from the superior mesenteric artery?
explain: Michels Type III hepatic arterial anatomy describes a replaced right hepatic artery originating from the SMA, running posterior to the portal vein.

prompt: What is the primary management for Ogilvie syndrome (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction) when cecal diameter exceeds 12 cm and conservative management fails?
explain: Neostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) is the drug of choice for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction refractory to conservative therapy when cecal perforation threatens.

prompt: A femoral hernia is located superior to the inguinal ligament and lateral to the femoral vein.
explain: The femoral canal is bounded laterally by the femoral vein and superiorly by the inguinal ligament.

prompt: Acute appendicitis can be definitively ruled out by a normal white blood cell count.
explain: A normal WBC count does not exclude acute appendicitis; approximately 10-15% of confirmed cases have normal leukocyte counts.

prompt: In blunt trauma, ultrasound FAST examination is designed to identify free peritoneal fluid rather than specific parenchymal organ tears.
explain: FAST detects anechoic free fluid in dependent peritoneal and pericardial spaces.

prompt: The pancreas is the most frequently injured abdominal solid organ in blunt trauma.
explain: The spleen is the most commonly injured visceral organ following blunt abdominal trauma.

prompt: Tension pneumothorax should be confirmed on chest radiograph before needle decompression is performed.
explain: Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening clinical diagnosis requiring instant decompression; radiographic delays can prove fatal.

prompt: Indirect inguinal hernias occur medial to the inferior epigastric artery.
explain: Indirect hernias pass lateral to the inferior epigastric artery through the deep internal inguinal ring.

prompt: Postoperative atelectasis is the most common cause of fever on the first postoperative day.
explain: Atelectasis ('Wind') is the leading cause of low-grade fever within 24-48 hours after general anesthesia.

prompt: Clean-contaminated wounds carry an expected infection rate of greater than 50% without antibiotics.
explain: Clean-contaminated wounds (e.g. elective GI entry) have a baseline infection rate of 5-10%.

prompt: A patient with complete mechanical small bowel obstruction typically has obstipation and hyperactive high-pitched bowel sounds initially.
explain: Early mechanical SBO presents with hyperactive tinkling bowel sounds and inability to pass stool or flatus.

prompt: Endotracheal intubation is the definitive airway in trauma resuscitation.
explain: A cuffed endotracheal tube in the trachea secured with positive confirmation represents a definitive airway.

prompt: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is contraindicated in acute calculous cholecystitis.
explain: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the standard of care for acute cholecystitis, ideally performed within 72 hours of symptom onset.

prompt: A pulsatile abdominal mass is a cardinal sign of an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
explain: A prominent pulsatile midline abdominal mass is the classic physical examination finding of an AAA.

prompt: Hypocalcemia causes QT shortening on electrocardiogram.
explain: Hypocalcemia delays myocardial repolarization, causing characteristic QT segment prolongation.

prompt: Hyperkalemia produces prominent U waves on the electrocardiogram.
explain: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves are the earliest electrocardiographic sign of hyperkalemia.

prompt: Incarcerated hernias are hernias that can be easily reduced back into the abdominal cavity with gentle pressure.
explain: Incarcerated hernias are non-reducible; reducible hernias return easily into the cavity.

prompt: Strangulation implies vascular compromise and ischemia of the herniated contents.
explain: Strangulation is incarceration leading to arterial or venous compromise and tissue necrosis.

prompt: Melanoma depth is measured clinically by the diameter of the surface pigment alone.
explain: Melanoma prognosis is determined histopathologically by Breslow vertical depth of invasion in millimeters.

prompt: Needle thoracostomy in an adult trauma patient is placed in the 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line or 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line.
explain: Both sites are endorsed by ATLS 10th edition for emergent needle decompression.

prompt: Charcot triad (fever, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice) indicates acute appendicitis.
explain: Fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice constitute Charcot triad of cholangitis.

prompt: Epidural hematomas typically present as a crescent-shaped hyperdensity crossing cranial suture lines on CT.
explain: Epidural hematomas are biconvex (lens-shaped) and bounded by cranial sutures; subdural hematomas are crescentic.

prompt: Epidural hematomas typically cross cranial sutures on non-contrast head CT.
explain: Because subdural hematomas lie in the subdural space, they can spread along the entire hemisphere across suture lines.

prompt: A tracheostomy is the preferred emergency surgical airway in an acute trauma patient who cannot be intubated.
explain: Cricothyroidotomy is the emergency surgical airway of choice in acute trauma, not tracheostomy.

prompt: Acute mesenteric ischemia is characterized by severe abdominal pain with minimal abdominal tenderness on early physical exam.
explain: Pain disproportionate to physical examination is the classic hallmark.

prompt: The Parkland formula utilizes normal 0.9% saline as the resuscitation fluid of choice.
explain: Lactated Ringer's solution is the crystalloid fluid specified by the Parkland formula to minimize hyperchloremic acidosis.

prompt: A Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 or less indicates severe traumatic brain injury and warrants airway protection.
explain: GCS <= 8 signifies severe head injury and inability to protect the airway ('GCS of 8, intubate').

prompt: Compartment syndrome can occur even in the presence of palpable distal peripheral pulses.
explain: Capillary perfusion ceases at pressures well below systolic arterial pressure; distal pulses often remain intact until late.

prompt: A positive Murphy sign is elicited during expiration.
explain: Murphy sign is elicited when inspiration arrests during deep subcostal palpation.

prompt: Intravenous contrast is routinely required for non-contrast head CT in acute traumatic head injury.
explain: Acute intracranial hemorrhage is readily visible as hyperdense blood on non-contrast CT; contrast is unnecessary and delays care.

prompt: Carotid endarterectomy is indicated for symptomatic patients with less than 50% internal carotid artery stenosis.
explain: NASCET trial confirmed substantial stroke risk reduction with CEA for symptomatic high-grade (70-99%) stenosis.

prompt: The psoas sign in appendicitis is elicited by passive internal rotation of the flexed right hip.
explain: Psoas sign is elicited by passive extension of the right hip; passive internal rotation elicits the obturator sign.

prompt: The obturator sign is caused by irritation of the obturator internus muscle by an inflamed pelvic appendix.
explain: Passive internal rotation of the flexed hip stretches the obturator internus against the pelvic appendix.

prompt: In acute diverticulitis, urgent barium enema is the examination of choice to locate mucosal fistulae.
explain: Barium enema and colonoscopy are contraindicated in acute diverticulitis due to risk of free perforation.

prompt: A pneumoperitoneum visible under the diaphragm on an upright chest X-ray indicates visceral perforation.
explain: Free air under the diaphragm indicates gastrointestinal tract perforation requiring urgent surgical evaluation.

prompt: Surgical site infections typically manifest within the first 12 hours after surgery.
explain: Most surgical site infections develop between postoperative days 4 and 7, unless caused by Group A Streptococcus or Clostridium.

prompt: Group A Streptococcus and Clostridium species can cause fulminant surgical wound infections within 24 hours of operation.
explain: These organisms produce necrotizing soft tissue infections presenting with rapid onset, bronzing, and systemic toxicity within 24 hours.

prompt: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass is both a restrictive and malabsorptive bariatric surgical procedure.
explain: Roux-en-Y creates a small gastric pouch (restriction) and bypasses the duodenum and proximal jejunum (malabsorption).

prompt: Sleeve gastrectomy involves placing an adjustable silicone band around the upper stomach.
explain: Sleeve gastrectomy resects approximately 80% of the greater curvature of the stomach; silicone bands describe gastric banding.

prompt: The Pringle maneuver occludes the inferior vena cava to control retrohepatic venous bleeding.
explain: The Pringle maneuver compresses the hepatic artery and portal vein in the hepatoduodenal ligament, not the IVC.

prompt: Esophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome) most commonly occurs in the upper cervical esophagus.
explain: Violent retching creates high intraluminal pressure, tearing the left posterolateral distal esophagus 2-3 cm above the GE junction.

prompt: Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury results in vocal cord paralysis in an abducted position causing airway obstruction.
explain: Unilateral injury causes paramedian vocal cord positioning and hoarseness; bilateral injury causes airway compromise.

prompt: A surgical needle stick injury with Hepatitis C virus carries a higher transmission risk than with Hepatitis B virus in unvaccinated individuals.
explain: HBV has a ~30% transmission risk, HCV ~3%, and HIV ~0.3% following percutaneous exposure.

prompt: In deep venous thrombosis, phlegmasia cerulea dolens represents complete venous outflow occlusion that threatens limb viability.
explain: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is massive venous thrombosis causing critical limb ischemia, cyanosis, and gangrene.

prompt: Diverticulosis is the most common cause of massive lower gastrointestinal bleeding in adults over 60.
explain: Arterial bleeding from diverticula accounts for the majority of acute, painless severe hematochezia in the elderly.

prompt: Meckel diverticulum is located on the mesenteric border of the ileum.
explain: Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum situated on the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum.

prompt: Rule of 2s for Meckel diverticulum includes: 2% of population, 2 inches long, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve, and presents by 2 years of age.
explain: The rule of 2s is a classic teaching mnemonic for Meckel diverticulum characteristics.

prompt: The presence of heterotopic gastric mucosa in Meckel diverticulum is responsible for painless lower GI bleeding.
explain: Acid secreted by heterotopic gastric mucosa ulcerates adjacent ileal epithelium, leading to painless bleeding.

prompt: Direct inguinal hernias have a higher incidence of strangulation than femoral hernias.
explain: Direct inguinal hernias have a broad defect with low strangulation risk; femoral hernias have a tight canal and highest risk.

prompt: Hypovolemic shock is characterized by elevated central venous pressure and low systemic vascular resistance.
explain: Hypovolemic shock produces low central venous pressure (preload) and elevated systemic vascular resistance (compensatory vasoconstriction).

prompt: Septic shock in its early warm phase typically exhibits low cardiac output and high systemic vascular resistance.
explain: Distributive/septic shock features peripheral vasodilation (low SVR) and high compensatory cardiac output.

prompt: In an abdominal aortic aneurysm, risk of rupture increases exponentially when aneurysm diameter exceeds 5.5 cm.
explain: Laplace's law dictates that wall tension is proportional to diameter; rupture risk rises steeply beyond 5.5 cm.

prompt: Prophylactic antibiotic administration for elective surgery should be given within 60 minutes prior to surgical incision.
explain: Administering antibiotics within 60 minutes before skin incision ensures optimal tissue bactericidal concentrations.

prompt: A patient with a traumatic flail chest exhibits paradoxical chest wall motion during respiration.
explain: The isolated segment moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration due to intrathoracic pressure swings.

prompt: Flail chest requires fracture of at least three adjacent ribs in two or more places.
explain: This anatomical disruption creates a free-floating segment of the thoracic cage.

prompt: Sentinel lymph node biopsy is standard of care for staging clinically node-negative early invasive breast cancer.
explain: Sentinel node biopsy reliably detects axillary micrometastases while sparing patients morbid complete axillary dissection.

prompt: In acute pancreatitis, serum amylase levels correlate directly with the clinical severity and prognosis of the disease.
explain: Amylase and lipase magnitude do not correlate with pancreatitis severity; Ranson, APACHE II, or BISAP scores predict severity.

prompt: A left varicocele that fails to decompress in the supine position raises suspicion for a left renal cell carcinoma.
explain: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein; tumor thrombus in the left renal vein can obstruct testicular venous drainage.

prompt: The right testicular vein empties into the right renal vein.
explain: Unlike the left testicular vein, the right gonadal vein drains directly into the IVC.

prompt: Abdominal compartment syndrome is treated medically with high-volume crystalloid boluses.
explain: Additional crystalloids worsen bowel edema and intra-abdominal hypertension; decompressive laparotomy is the definitive therapy.

prompt: In a burn patient, deep partial-thickness burns are completely painless and do not blanch with pressure.
explain: Full-thickness (third-degree) burns are painless due to nerve destruction; deep partial-thickness burns retain dull pressure sensation.

prompt: Full-thickness burns destroy both the epidermis and the entirety of the dermis, requiring skin grafting.
explain: Because dermal appendages are destroyed, full-thickness burns cannot re-epithelialize and mandate excision and grafting.

prompt: A Marjolin ulcer is an aggressive squamous cell carcinoma arising within chronic non-healing burn scars or sinus tracts.
explain: Malignant transformation of chronic burn scars into aggressive SCC is termed a Marjolin ulcer.

prompt: Pheochromocytoma arises from chromaffin cells of the adrenal cortex.
explain: Pheochromocytoma originates from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, producing excess catecholamines.

prompt: Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) can readily differentiate follicular thyroid adenoma from follicular thyroid carcinoma.
explain: Cytology cannot assess architectural capsular or vascular invasion; histological tissue sections from formal resection are required.

prompt: Thyroglobulin is a specific serum tumor marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma.
explain: Medullary thyroid carcinoma originates from neuroendocrine parafollicular C-cells which secrete calcitonin.

prompt: In acute mesenteric ischemia due to superior mesenteric artery embolism, early surgical embolectomy can prevent bowel infarction.
explain: Prompt SMA embolectomy restores perfusion before irreversible full-thickness transmural gangrene develops.

prompt: A Richter hernia involves herniation of only a portion of the circumference of the bowel wall through a defect.
explain: In a Richter hernia, only the antimesenteric border of the bowel herniates, which can strangulate without causing complete mechanical obstruction.

prompt: A Littre hernia is defined as any hernia that contains a Meckel diverticulum.
explain: A Littre hernia specifically describes a hernia sac harboring a Meckel diverticulum.

prompt: An Amyand hernia contains a Meckel diverticulum within an inguinal hernia sac.
explain: Presence of the appendix in an inguinal hernia is eponymously named an Amyand hernia.

prompt: A De Garengeot hernia contains the vermiform appendix within a femoral hernia sac.
explain: An appendix within a femoral hernia sac is known as a De Garengeot hernia.

prompt: In laparoscopic surgery, carbon dioxide is preferred for insufflation because it is highly soluble in blood and does not support combustion.
explain: CO2 has high blood solubility (reducing gas embolism lethality) and is non-flammable during electrocautery.

prompt: The triangle of Calot is bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and the inferior border of the liver.
explain: These boundaries define the hepatobiliary triangle where the cystic artery and lymph node of Lund are located.

prompt: During cholecystectomy, the critical view of safety requires clearing the hepatocystic triangle of all fat and fibrous tissue and displaying two and only two structures entering the gallbladder.
explain: The two structures are the cystic duct and cystic artery, with the lower third of the gallbladder dissected off the liver bed.

prompt: Zenker diverticulum is a true traction diverticulum of the mid-esophagus.
explain: Zenker diverticulum is a false pulsion diverticulum occurring in Killian triangle above the cricopharyngeus muscle.

prompt: Killian triangle is an area of muscular weakness between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles.
explain: This anatomical defect in the posterior pharyngeal wall is the site of Zenker diverticulum herniation.

prompt: Surgical intervention for chronic subdural hematoma is indicated when there is neurological deficit or midline shift >5 mm.
explain: Symptomatic chronic subdural hematomas with mass effect warrant burr hole trephination or craniotomy.

prompt: An ankle-brachial index (ABI) of 1.1 indicates severe peripheral artery disease.
explain: An ABI of 0.91 to 1.30 is completely normal; ABI <0.90 indicates PAD, and ABI <0.40 indicates severe limb ischemia.

prompt: Rest pain in peripheral artery disease typically worsens when the patient elevates the legs.
explain: Elevation reduces hydrostatic perfusion pressure across arterial stenosis, worsening ischemic rest pain.

prompt: The Belsey Mark IV and Nissen fundoplication are surgical procedures used to treat refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease.
explain: Both are antireflux procedures designed to restore competency to the lower esophageal sphincter.

prompt: In trauma resuscitation, tranexamic acid (TXA) reduces mortality if administered within 3 hours of injury.
explain: CRASH-2 trial demonstrated that early antifibrinolytic therapy with TXA within 3 hours significantly reduces trauma mortality.

prompt: Prophylactic oophorectomy is indicated during every routine laparoscopic appendectomy in postmenopausal women.
explain: Routine oophorectomy during appendectomy is unwarranted without specific pathology or clear indications.

prompt: A pancreatic pseudocyst is lined by a true epithelial mucosal layer.
explain: A pseudocyst lacks an epithelial lining; its wall consists of fibrous and granulation tissue surrounding pancreatic fluid.

prompt: Gastric adenocarcinoma of the linitis plastica type is characterized by diffuse infiltration of signet ring cells resulting in a rigid, non-distensible stomach.
explain: Linitis plastica features diffuse scirrhous carcinoma infiltrating the gastric wall.

prompt: Cushing ulcer is a stress-related gastric ulcer associated with severe head trauma and elevated intracranial pressure.
explain: Elevated ICP stimulates vagal nuclei, leading to hypersecretion of gastric acid and ulceration.

prompt: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) characteristically harbor activating mutations in the KIT (CD117) receptor tyrosine kinase.
explain: Approximately 85% of GISTs have oncogenic mutations in KIT (CD117) and respond to imatinib therapy.

prompt: Intussusception in adults is most commonly idiopathic and successfully treated with air enema reduction alone.
explain: Adult intussusception is caused by an organic lead point (malignancy or polyp) in over 90% of cases and requires formal resection.

prompt: In hepatic resection, segment I corresponds to the caudate lobe, which possesses independent venous drainage directly into the inferior vena cava.
explain: Couinaud segment I (caudate lobe) receives portal and arterial branches from both left and right triads and drains directly into the IVC.

prompt: The Calot node (Lund lymph node) lies in the hepatocystic triangle and is a key anatomical landmark for identifying the cystic artery.
explain: The cystic lymph node of Lund consistently overlies the cystic artery in the triangle of Calot.

prompt: Gastrinomas in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome are most commonly located within the 'gastrinoma triangle' bounded by the cystic duct, junction of the 2nd/3rd duodenum, and neck of the pancreas.
explain: Over 80% of gastrinomas arise within the Stabile gastrinoma triangle.

prompt: In transplant rejection, hyperacute rejection is mediated by donor-specific preformed recipient antibodies and occurs within minutes to hours of graft reperfusion.
explain: Pre-existing anti-HLA or ABO antibodies bind donor graft vascular endothelium, causing microvascular thrombosis and ischemic necrosis.

prompt: A left-sided colon cancer obstruction can be safely and definitively relieved by simple appendectomy.
explain: Left-sided obstruction requires colonic decompression, stenting, resection, or diverting colostomy; appendectomy does not relieve colonic obstruction.

prompt: Order the standard sequence of the ATLS primary survey in trauma resuscitation.
items: Airway maintenance with cervical spine protection
explain: ATLS prioritizes ABCDE sequence for primary resuscitation.

prompt: Order the standard clinical progression of acute appendicitis from symptom onset to physical signs.
items: Somatic sharp pain localized to McBurney point
Peritoneal signs with rebound tenderness and guarding
explain: Luminal obstruction initiates distension (visceral pain), progressing to transmural inflammation irritating parietal peritoneum (somatic pain).

prompt: Order the normal sequential phases of wound healing.
items: Proliferative phase with angiogenesis and collagen synthesis
explain: Wound healing proceeds predictably from hemostasis to remodeling.

prompt: Order the steps of a routine laparoscopic appendectomy.
items: Identification and mobilization of the appendix and cecal base
Mesoappendix division and skeletonization with energy device
Ligation and transection of the appendiceal base
Specimen extraction in an endobag and port site closure
explain: Standard laparoscopic appendectomy follows systematic port insertion, mobilization, ligation, and contained extraction.

prompt: Order the steps of basic surgical knot tying and wound closure.
items: Needle entry perpendicular to skin edge
Suture passage through opposite wound margin
Instrument throw creating first knot loop
Square knot placement with opposing second throw
Suture cut leaving appropriate tail length
explain: Clean apposition requires perpendicular entry, equal depth, and squared throws.

prompt: Order the evaluation algorithm for an unstable blunt trauma patient.
items: Identify free fluid in Morison pouch with persistent hypotension
Transfer immediately to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy
explain: Unstable trauma patients with positive FAST bypass CT and proceed directly to laparotomy.

prompt: Order the steps in managing an acute tension pneumothorax.
items: Recognize clinical signs of respiratory distress, hypotension, and absent breath sounds
Perform immediate needle decompression in the 2nd ICS MCL or 5th ICS AAL
Auscultate for rush of air and hemodynamic improvement
Prepare sterile field and local anesthesia for chest tube
Place tube thoracostomy in the 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line
explain: Needle decompression relieves immediate tension; formal chest tube provides definitive ongoing drainage.

prompt: Order the sequence of pre-operative preparation for an elective abdominal case.
items: NPO status confirmation for solid foods
Prophylactic intravenous antibiotic infusion within 60 minutes of incision
Surgical safety time-out before skin incision
explain: Standard perioperative checklist enforces patient safety, fasting, infection prevention, and time-out.

prompt: Order the stages of bowel recovery after major abdominal surgery from first to last.
items: Small intestinal motility recovery within 24 hours
First bowel movement and tolerance of solid food
explain: The small intestine recovers first, followed by the stomach, and lastly the colon.

prompt: Order the steps of a laparoscopic cholecystectomy achieving the Critical View of Safety.
items: Cephalad fundus traction and lateral infundibulum retraction
Dissection of the hepatocystic triangle clearing all fat and fibrous tissue
Separation of the lower third of the gallbladder from the liver bed
Visualization of exactly two structures entering the gallbladder (cystic duct and artery)
Application of clips and division of the cystic duct and artery
explain: The critical view of safety demands clearing the triangle and liver bed before any structure is clipped or divided.

prompt: Order the sequence of diagnostic workup for a suspicious solitary thyroid nodule.
items: High-resolution neck ultrasound evaluating nodule characteristics
Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy for suspicious features
Surgical lobectomy or total thyroidectomy if malignant
explain: Workup begins with functional status (TSH), anatomical imaging (ultrasound), cytological sampling (FNA), and resection if indicated.

prompt: Order the steps of tube thoracostomy (chest tube insertion).
items: Position patient and identify the 5th intercostal space at the anterior/mid-axillary line
Administer local anesthesia to skin, subcutaneous tissue, and pleura
Make transverse skin incision and blunt dissect over the rib upper border

Monitor resuscitation adequacy by targeting urine output of 0.5 to 1.0 mL/kg/hr

Perform emergency subtotal colectomy if refractory life-threatening bleeding persists

Mobilization of the right colon from the retroperitoneum taking the mesocolon intact
Resection of the terminal ileum (10 cm) and right colon
Primary ileocolic anastomosis (stapled or hand-sewn) and mesenteric defect closure

Perform surgical balloon catheter thromboembolectomy (Fogarty catheter)
Perform prophylactic four-compartment fasciotomy of the leg to prevent reperfusion compartment syndrome

Heparinize patient systemically and place proximal aortic cross-clamp below renal arteries
Place distal clamps on common iliac arteries and open the aneurysm sac
Sew synthetic Dacron tube graft, backbleed vessels, release clamps, and close aneurysm wall over graft
explain: Proximal control below renal vessels and distal iliac clamping precede opening the sac and inlying graft replacement.

End-to-side or piggyback anastomosis of donor hepatic veins to recipient IVC
End-to-end anastomosis of donor portal vein to recipient portal vein
Microvascular surgical anastomosis of the hepatic artery using surgical loupes/microscope
Duct-to-duct biliary anastomosis or Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
explain: Vascular reconstruction proceeds from outflow (hepatic veins) to inflow (portal vein then hepatic artery) and finally biliary reconstruction.

Transection of distal esophagus with negative frozen section margin
Creation of a Roux jejunal limb 40-50 cm in length
End-to-side esophagojejunostomy and distal jejunojejunostomy reconstruction
explain: Oncologic gastrectomy requires D2 lymph node dissection followed by Roux-en-Y reconstruction with tension-free esophagojejunostomy.

prompt: What is the constant factor (in mL/kg/%TBSA) used in the Parkland burn formula for crystalloid resuscitation in the first 24 hours?

prompt: What is the normal adult minimum urine output threshold in mL/kg/hour that indicates adequate kidney perfusion during surgical resuscitation?
explain: Target urine output in resuscitated adult surgical patients is >= 0.5 mL/kg/hr.

prompt: What is the maximum possible score on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)?
explain: GCS ranges from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully awake and oriented).

prompt: What is the minimum possible score on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)?
explain: The lowest score on the GCS is 3 points.

prompt: What is the threshold diameter in centimeters at which elective repair is typically recommended for an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm in a male?

prompt: According to the Rule of Nines in adult burns, what percentage of total body surface area is assigned to the entire head and neck?
explain: The adult head and neck represents exactly 9% of TBSA.

prompt: According to the Rule of Nines in adult burns, what percentage of total body surface area is assigned to one entire upper extremity?

prompt: According to the Rule of Nines in adult burns, what percentage of total body surface area is assigned to the anterior trunk?
explain: The anterior torso accounts for 18% of TBSA.

prompt: According to the Rule of Nines in adult burns, what percentage of total body surface area is assigned to one entire lower extremity in an adult?
explain: Each adult lower extremity accounts for 18% of TBSA.

prompt: According to the Rule of Nines in adult burns, what percentage of total body surface area is assigned to the perineum?

prompt: What is the maximum normal diameter of the appendix in millimeters on ultrasound or CT beyond which appendicitis is suspected?
explain: An outer diameter >6 mm is considered abnormal and supportive of acute appendicitis.

prompt: What is the golden time window in hours for surgical exploration and detorsion to achieve high salvage in acute testicular torsion?
explain: Salvage rates exceed 90% if operated within 6 hours of pain onset.

explain: Prophylactic antibiotics must be completely infused within 60 minutes of skin incision.

prompt: What is the normal lower limit of the Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) below which peripheral artery disease is diagnosed?
explain: An ABI <0.90 is diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease.

prompt: What is the Alvarado score cut-off value out of 10 points that strongly indicates acute appendicitis warranting surgical consultation?
explain: A score >= 7 on the Alvarado scale indicates high probability of appendicitis.

prompt: What percentage of calculated Parkland burn formula fluids should be administered in the first 8 hours following injury?
explain: Half (50%) of the calculated 24-hour volume is given in the first 8 hours.

prompt: What is the threshold internal carotid artery stenosis percentage in symptomatic patients that establishes an indication for carotid endarterectomy?
explain: Symptomatic stenosis >= 70% derives the greatest absolute risk reduction from CEA.

prompt: In massive transfusion protocol, what is the ideal ratio of Packed Red Blood Cells to Fresh Frozen Plasma in trauma resuscitation?
explain: Balanced damage control resuscitation targets a 1:1:1 ratio of PRBCs, FFP, and platelets.

prompt: What is the threshold compartment pressure in mmHg at or above which tissue perfusion is critically compromised and fasciotomy is indicated?
explain: An absolute compartment pressure >= 30 mmHg (or delta pressure <= 30 mmHg) mandates fasciotomy.

prompt: What is the intra-abdominal pressure threshold in mmHg defining intra-abdominal hypertension (Grade I)?
explain: Intra-abdominal hypertension is defined as sustained IAP >= 12 mmHg.

prompt: What is the sustained intra-abdominal pressure threshold in mmHg that defines abdominal compartment syndrome when accompanied by organ failure?
explain: Sustained IAP >20 mmHg with new organ failure defines abdominal compartment syndrome.

prompt: What is the normal mean intracranial pressure (ICP) upper limit in mmHg for a resting adult?
explain: Normal resting adult ICP ranges from 5 to 15 mmHg.

prompt: At what intracranial pressure threshold in mmHg is intervention generally initiated in severe traumatic brain injury to prevent herniation?
explain: Current Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines recommend treating ICP above 22 mmHg.

prompt: What is the minimum cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) target in mmHg in managing adult traumatic brain injury?
explain: Maintaining CPP between 60 and 70 mmHg optimizes cerebral oxygenation.

prompt: How many hours after symptom onset is the recommended upper limit for administering intravenous tranexamic acid (TXA) to improve trauma survival?
explain: CRASH-2 trial showed benefit only when TXA was administered within 3 hours of trauma.

prompt: What is the surgical margin width in centimeters recommended for wide local excision of a cutaneous melanoma with Breslow thickness between 1.01 and 2.0 mm?
explain: Clinical guidelines mandate a 1 to 2 cm margin (median 1.5 cm) for lesions 1-2 mm thick.

prompt: What is the surgical margin width in centimeters recommended for melanoma in situ?
explain: Melanoma in situ is treated with a 0.5 cm margin.

prompt: What is the cecal diameter threshold in centimeters on plain radiograph beyond which the risk of impending cecal perforation dramatically increases in obstruction?
explain: A cecal diameter >12 cm carries high risk of ischemia and perforation.

prompt: How many pairs of ribs are typically involved in a traumatic flail chest injury as a minimum requirement?
explain: Flail chest requires >= 3 contiguous ribs fractured in >= 2 places.

prompt: What is the minimum volume in milliliters of acute pericardial fluid that can produce tamponade physiology in sudden traumatic hemopericardium?
explain: Because the pericardium is non-compliant acutely, as little as 100-200 mL can cause fatal tamponade.

prompt: What percentage decrease in intact parathyroid hormone at 10 minutes post-excision compared to baseline confirms curative resection of a parathyroid adenoma?
explain: The Miami criterion requires a >50% drop in intact PTH at 10 minutes post-excision.

prompt: What is the normal transit time in hours of the small intestine from ingestion to the ileocecal valve?
explain: Normal small bowel transit time averages 3 to 5 hours.

prompt: What is the minimum red blood cell count per microliter on diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) that signifies a positive test in blunt abdominal trauma?
explain: A count >100,000 RBCs/µL indicates a positive DPL in blunt abdominal trauma.

prompt: What is the minimum white blood cell count per microliter on diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) that indicates a positive test in trauma?
explain: A count >500 WBCs/µL on DPL fluid denotes a positive finding.

prompt: How many Couinaud functional liver segments are recognized in hepatic surgery?
explain: The liver is anatomically divided into 8 independent functional segments.

prompt: What is the standard insufflation pressure in mmHg used for creating carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum in adult laparoscopic surgery?
explain: Routine adult laparoscopic pneumoperitoneum is maintained between 12 and 15 mmHg.

prompt: What is the recommended dietary fiber intake in grams per day for secondary prevention of recurrent diverticulitis?
explain: Guidelines recommend 30-35 grams of daily dietary fiber to maintain soft stools.

prompt: What is the threshold chest tube output in milliliters of blood immediately upon insertion that constitutes an indication for emergent exploratory thoracotomy?
explain: Initial chest tube evacuation >1,500 mL of blood warrants emergency thoracotomy.

prompt: What is the normal resting portal venous pressure in mmHg?
explain: Normal portal venous pressure is 5 to 10 mmHg (mean ~7 mmHg).

prompt: What is the HVPG threshold in mmHg above which the risk of acute variceal bleeding dramatically increases?
explain: Variceal bleeding occurs almost exclusively when HVPG exceeds 12 mmHg.

prompt: How many days prior to elective surgery should aspirin be discontinued if complete platelet recovery is desired?
explain: Platelet lifespan is 7-10 days, so withholding aspirin for 7 days allows full platelet turnover.

prompt: How many hours prior to surgery should unfractionated intravenous heparin be stopped before general anesthesia to normalize coagulation?
explain: IV unfractionated heparin has a half-life of 60-90 minutes and is stopped 4-6 hours preoperatively.

prompt: What is the target international normalized ratio (INR) threshold or below generally required prior to elective major surgery?
explain: An INR <= 1.5 is standard to safely proceed with major operative procedures.

prompt: What is the half-life in minutes of intact parathyroid hormone in human circulation?
explain: The rapid half-life of intact PTH (3-5 minutes) enables reliable intraoperative monitoring.

prompt: What percentage of patients with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) will develop colorectal cancer by age 50 if left untreated without colectomy?
explain: FAP carries an absolute 100% lifetime risk of colorectal cancer without prophylactic colectomy.

prompt: What is the length in centimeters of the standard alimentary (Roux) limb constructed in a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass for morbid obesity?
explain: A standard Roux limb is constructed at 75 to 150 cm (commonly 100 cm) in length.

prompt: What is the cold ischemia time limit in hours for donor liver preservation prior to transplantation?
explain: Liver graft function deteriorates significantly when cold ischemia time exceeds 12 hours.

prompt: What is the maximum tolerable warm ischemia time in minutes for a deceased-donor kidney graft prior to cold perfusion?
explain: Warm ischemia beyond 30 minutes sharply increases primary graft non-function and delayed graft function.
